value.text: A Bicyclist was seriously injured Wednesday morning after a crash involving a vehicle in Port St. Lucie, according to Port St. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Port St. Lucie police said officers responded around 6:40 a.m. to the area of Southwest Rosser Boulevard and Southwest Meridian Avenue for a crash involving a car and a cyclist. Investigators said a man riding a bicycle was traveling in the roadway on Southwest Rosser Boulevard when the crash happened. When officers arrived, the cyclist was unconscious but breathing and was wearing a helmet. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he was listed in critical but stable condition. Authorities said he is expected to survive. Traffic in both directions near the crash scene was shut down for a time as officers investigated, and drivers were redirected to nearby side streets. The crash remains under investigation. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

LUCIE COUNTY – While there were surprises across the state at the conclusion of the 2026 Primary Election held Aug. 18, Florida voters’ reputation of bucking the national trend of automatically reelecting incumbents proved true in several local races. One of the only two candidates assured victory last night was current Port St. Lucie Planning Zoning Board Chairman Jim Norton, who will assume the Port St. Lucie District 3 Council Seat being vacated by Anthony Bonna, who is resigning to run for the Florida House District 85 seat. Toby Overdorf, R-Palm City himself is vacating that position to make a bid for the Florida Senate in 2028. Norton received 52.26 percent of the total 37,056 votes cast in that race according to official results posted by the St. Lucie County Supervisor or Elections, while the other two candidates, Fritz Masson-Alexandre and Peter D. Overhuls, received 24.89 percent and 22.85, respectively. Since there was no primary for either Republican Candidate Bonna or the sole Democratic Candidate Wayne Richter in the District 85 seat, both now advance to the Nov. For the city’s District 1 City Council Seat being vacated by Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan who chose not to seek reelection after completing a decade on the Board, Candidate Rick Meltzer got 42.02 percent of the total 37,196 votes. He was followed by Indony P. Jean Baptiste with 22.13 percent and Eric Reikenis and Kevin Zimmerman, who received 5,591 votes and 7,744 votes, respectively. Because neither candidate got the 50 percent-plus-one vote required by Florida statute in non-partisan races, Meltzer and Baptiste now head to a runoff election in November. Lucie Mayoral Primary Race, current Mayor Shannon Martin did prove her incumbent advantage with 47.71 percent of the total 39,247 votes cast against Challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Reikenis, who received 15,629 and 7,744 votes, respectively. Martin and Giordano now head to a Nov. In the Democratic Primary Race for the District 4 County Commission Seat, Jean Eddy Leroy got 50.66 percent of the 20,898 votes cast, while Candidate Roger N. Messer received 49.34 percent. Leroy now faces Incumbent and current Chairwoman Jamie Lee Fowler and Candidate Nicholas Burgos – who is running with no party affiliation – on Nov. Lucie County School District races, Incumbent Debbie Johnson Hawley was the other winning candidate last night, retaining her District 1 seat with 55.00 percent of the total 53,520 votes cast against Challenger Brian K. Capp, who received 24,082 votes. In the District 5 seat race, Challenger Lisa Kessler got 37.54 percent of the 53,295 total votes cast. Incumbent Troy Ingersoll – who’s completing a decade on the Board – received 37.24 percent, while Charles V. Cerami, got 25.22 percent. Ingersoll and Kessler now head to a runoff in November. This year the City Commission of Fort Pierce did not hold a Primary Election because no challenging candidates qualified to run against either Commissioner Michael Broderick or Commissioner Arnold Gaines, who are both up for reelection. The City Charters allows them to both re-assume their respective offices during the second regular meeting after the Nov. For the Florida governor and lieutenant governor races, Byron Donalds and Jay Collins topped the crowded field of 11 candidates in the Republican Primary, with Donalds getting 53.41 percent of the local votes cast and Collins receiving 23.06 percent. In the Democratic Primary, David Jolly topped the field of six Democratic candidates, getting 56.19 percent of the total votes. His closest challenger, Dayna Marie Foster, received 15.39 percent of the vote. Donalds will will now face Jolly on Nov 3. In the Democratic Primary race for the U.S. Senator Seat vacated by Marco Rubio when he was appointed by President Donald Trump to be secretary of state, Angie Nixon defeated Alexander Vindman with 54.50 percent of the total 22,310 local votes cast. In the Republican Primary for that seat, Ashley Moody got 79.77 percent of the local votes cast for the four candidates, while Chris Gleason got 14.72 percent of the remaining votes. Ashley will now face Nixon in November for the final two years of Rubio’s term. As far as the Florida District 21 Democratic Primary Race, Bernard Taylor got 55.56 percent of the total 21,862 votes cast, with James T. Martin getting 44.4 percent. Martin, however, won the state overall and will now face Incumbent Republican Candidate Bryan Mast on Nov. According to the Ballotpedia Website that has analyzed statewide races nationally for the last three years, the incumbency reelection rate remained at 90 percent or higher in all but the 11 states of Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Kansas, Maine, Minnesota, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Virginia and Washington. The State of Florida, however, had the lowest victory rate of incumbents nationally, with only 63 percent of incumbents successfully being reelected during the same time period. Lucie County is growing fast, and new Census estimates show much of that growth is centered in Port St. Census Bureau estimates put St. Lucie County's population at 402,449 as of July 1, 2025 , up from 329,226 in 2020. That's an increase of more than 73,000 residents, or 22.2%, in just over five years. For comparison, neighboring Palm Beach County grew from 1,492,191 residents in 2020 to an estimated 1,575,726 in 2025 an increase of about 5.6%. Lucie County has grown at roughly four times the rate of Palm Beach County since 2020. Lucie County started the decade with less than one-quarter of Palm Beach County's population, but has added nearly as many residents. RELATED: Census data shows St. Lucie surging while Palm Beach growth nearly stops Much of St. Lucie County's population is concentrated in Port St. The Census Bureau estimates 268,062 people now live in Port St. Lucie, meaning the city accounts for roughly two-thirds of the county's entire population. Lucie has also grown faster than the county overall. The city's population is up nearly 31% from its 2020 estimates base of 204,826. So what's drawing people there? Jason Coley with Atlantic Shores Realty, Expertise ERA Powered, said affordability remains one of the biggest factors he sees among his clients. "It's been picking up big time," Coley said. "People are moving here because we have a heck of a deal with the bang for your buck. You can get a really nice house." Coley works throughout the Treasure Coast and into Palm Beach County, but said about 60% of his business is in St. He said his clients moving into the area are coming from both outside Florida and communities farther south in South Florida. "A lot of them are coming from down south," Coley said. "They're coming from Broward, Palm Beach. They can just get much more of a home up in our area than they can down south." Coley said his own clients are roughly split between people relocating from out of state and those coming from other parts of Florida. He said he also sees buyers coming from Miami-Dade County. For some South Florida buyers, he believes the decision to continue north into St. Lucie County instead of buying in Palm Beach County comes down largely to price. "I just strictly think it is pricing," Coley said. "When they look at what they're going to be able to get and what they can afford, it just makes it that much harder for them to really have the family dream of what they want." According to Coley, a buyer spending between $400,000 and $500,000 in St. Lucie County can find a four-bedroom, two-bathroom home with a two-car garage on a quarter-acre lot. See also: Florida left lane law: Deputies crack down on slow drivers lingering in the fast lane He estimated a comparable newer home in Palm Beach County could cost between $600,000 and $800,000, though prices vary significantly by neighborhood, property and market conditions. Coley said he sees a range of people making the move, from retirees to young couples and families looking for more space. For some buyers, living farther north also means a longer commute. Coley said some of his clients are willing to make that tradeoff, while others are able to work remotely. "A lot of people are working from home nowadays when we talk to people," Coley said. "They're either working remote or willing to make that drive just to have a nicer house." New construction helping attract buyers New construction is another part of Port St. Communities in and around Tradition continue to add homes as builders compete for buyers. Coley said some builders are offering incentives such as closing-cost assistance and temporary or permanent mortgage-rate buydowns, which can make new construction more attractive to buyers facing higher borrowing costs. "They're giving them cash to close, which is like covering their closing costs," Coley said. "And they're also buying down their interest rates." The exact incentives and mortgage rates vary by builder, development, buyer and loan. Coley also believes Port St. Lucie's expanding selection of restaurants, entertainment and other amenities is helping make the city more attractive to families. "I think it's just drawn people in because it's newer," Coley said. Another report highlights Port St. Lucie's growth The Census numbers are not the only recent data highlighting Port St. A private analysis from workplace technology company Blink recently ranked Port St. cities in an index examining population growth and indicators of small-business activity. The analysis considered population growth along with retail, food and hospitality business density, workforce growth, online search activity and walkability. The report cited Census data showing Port St. Lucie added 11,880 residents between 2023 and 2024. The Blink ranking should not be confused with an official Census ranking of America's fastest-growing cities. It is a private analysis that combines population growth with several economic and business-related factors. The newer Census estimates now put Port St. Lucie's population above 268,000. See also: West Palm Beach man arrested after police say he faked coma to cover up $190K embezzlement With more people arriving, the question becomes whether St. Lucie County can maintain its affordability advantage as demand increases. Coley said he does not expect interest in the area to disappear anytime soon. "My crystal ball is broken, so I can't tell you for sure if it'll last," Coley said. "But I will say that people have to live somewhere." When asked whether he sees Port St. Lucie's growth stopping soon, his answer was simple. "I don't see it anytime soon."

Lucie County Fire District board met today to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation. After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it. The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing. Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying, "It was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate." Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September. A man the Martin County Sheriff's Office referred to as a "brazen" robber is now facing felony charges, accused of a jewelry theft at the Treasure Coast Mall. It happened at Royal Jewelers, a kiosk inside the mall, on July 20. Security video from the mall shows a man standing at the counter of the kiosk. Chris Morales of the Martin County Sheriff’s Office identified the man as 25-year-old Dezmone Johnson. "He actually comes up and pretends to be a customer, engages with the clerk for a few minutes," Morales said. According to Morales, Johnson walked away at one point before returning to ask for a closer look at the jewelry. "The clerk brings out a tray of, let's say, seven or eight less expensive necklaces according to him, and he just grabs the tray and runs out," Morales said. The clerk at the store can be heard screaming as the suspect runs away with the necklaces. According to the police report, the necklaces are valued between $850 and $4,500 each, totaling more than $22,000 in stolen jewelry. Cameras outside the mall showed investigators the vehicle Johnson drove away in. "We were able to get the tag from that vehicle, making it pretty easy for us. The vehicle came back to an address in Lauderhill, so down in Broward County," Morales said. Detectives visited a pawn shop near the Lauderhill address and stopped in to ask if Johnson was a customer. "Lo and behold, the owner says, 'Yeah, he was just in here trying to pawn a few necklaces.' Again, making it pretty easy for our detectives," Morales said. Johnson was arrested shortly afterward. Morales expressed relief at the arrest, saying even though this specific robbery was not violent, the next one might have been. "I would say there's a great chance of that. He has a history of violence. He has access to weapons in his criminal history. I'm sure he's not afraid to use that in future endeavors," Morales said. Johnson is charged with robbery and grand theft. He spent a short time in the Broward County jail and is currently free on bond as he awaits trial. Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. Monster Jam is returning to Amerant Bank Arena in Sunrise this weekend with monster trucks, freestyle stunts and family-friendly entertainment that transforms the home of the Florida Panthers into a dirt-filled arena.Crews brought in about 70 truckloads of dirt to convert the hockey arena into a Monster Jam course, according to driver Tony Ochs of JCB DIGatron.“Isn’t it amazing how they can transform this thing from a hockey arena to a dirt track, back to a hockey arena within a matter of hours?” Ochs said during an interview with WPTV’s T.A. “When this thing’s all said and done with, these guys will have this thing loaded out of here maybe four hours.”Monster Jam events are scheduled for Aug. 22-23 at Amerant Bank Arena in Sunrise. The Kings Academy made headlines last year when the school announced it would leave the Florida High School Athletic Association and enter the Sunshine State Athletic Association for the first time. Multiple people were hospitalized Thursday morning after a school bus collided with a pickup truck just south of Greenacres, according to Palm Beach County Fire Rescue.The crash happened around 6:35 a.m. at the intersection of West Lantana Road and Plantation Boulevard in front of Palm Beach Plantation. Joaquín García High School were on the bus at the time, and none of them were taken to the hospital.However, all four people in the truck suffered serious injuries and required rescue efforts to free them from the wreckage. They were all taken to a local trauma center.Nineteen different fire rescue units responded to the scene. Fire rescue crews arrived within four minutes of the initial 911 call and began treating the trapped victims even before they could be freed from the vehicle."The last person was out of the vehicle at about 7:20 a.m., so it was an extensive extrication," said Capt. Tom Reyes with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. "There were other people that came out sooner than that, but this was this was a significant incident. We had our special operations teams come here, and they went right to work working on it. More importantly, we did start with patient care even before they were out of the vehicle."The cause of the crash remains under investigation by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Reyes said it's unclear what led to the collision.The eastbound lanes of Lantana Road near Plantation Boulevard remain closed while authorities conduct their investigation, with westbound traffic reduced to two lanes. Officials advise drivers to avoid the area for the remainder of the morning as the investigation is expected to be lengthy.The school district has contacted the families of all students involved. Below is the statement sent to all families of Dr. Joaquín García High School:"Good morning, Dr. Joaquín García High School families, I am writing to inform you that Bus CO48 was transporting ten students when it was involved in a traffic crash this morning near Lantana Road and Hagen Ranch Road.All ten students on board are safe and did not require medical intervention on scene of the crash. They were transported to school and met directly by our school nurse to check on their well-being when they arrived at school. Emergency medical services and School Police responded to the school to assist.Because experiencing an incident like this can be unsettling, counseling resources and support services are available on campus today for any student who may need to speak about their experience."

This week, I found myself somewhere that's all about agriculture, family, and lots of Florida oranges. Let me tell you about my incredible day at Al's Family Farms in Fort Pierce!I was with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau, who knows this area like the back of her hand. Lucie County at Al's Family Farms right here in Fort Pierce," she explained. "This is a generational family farm, three generations now, 50 years of serving up just the freshest Florida produce. The reason why I brought you here is because I cover this area. Lucie County is home to me. It is so special."WATCH: What I learned during my visit really stuck with me. But you can trust Al's to pick, pack and ship your citrus from the family itself.Now, Brooke had something special planned for me— indulging in a Sunshine Shake.But before I could get my hands on that famous Sunshine Shake, Brooke had other plans: Trying a Georgia peach.And let me tell you, I didn't even wait for permission. A Miami woman was arrested in Martin County after allegedly posing as a bank representative to scam residents out of thousands of dollars, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. Newly released aerial footage shows sheriff's deputies following the suspect, 32-year-old Monquie Turnbull, on I-95 before stopping her vehicle. Body camera footage captured Turnbull exiting her car and being questioned by deputies. "You’re going to be placed under arrest," a deputy said in the footage. Budensiek said Turnbull drove from Miami to Martin County, where she approached two residents, claiming their debit cards were compromised and needed to be turned in for replacement. "They stated that their card was compromised and they needed to turn their card in and they were going to replace their card for them," Budensiek said. One resident was scammed out of hundreds of dollars. "The victim notices pretty quick that not long after the suspect left, there’s $3,180 now missing from her account," Budensiek said. While investigators were handling that case, they received a second 911 call matching the suspect’s description and vehicle. Deputies began their search. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "She was located as she came eastbound on Bridge Road and then she turned around and was going westbound on Bridge Road, which is the video you saw her getting arrested," Budensiek said. Officials later discovered Turnbull had entered the jail with about $3,200 hidden in one of her body parts. "She took our first victim’s card, withdrew $3,180, and that’s the exact amount recovered from inside her person in the jail," Budensiek said. The sheriff urged residents to be cautious if someone comes to their home claiming to be from a bank and asking for credit cards. "This particular incidence, this was all the money that this lady had, this was her rent money, it was everything that she had, and she handed it over to a scammer," Budensiek said. Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, a Vero Beach hairdresser, was killed outside her home on Aug. 16 by Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, of Sebastian, who then fled the area and was subsequently arrested in West Virginia. Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, a Vero Beach hairdresser, told fellow co-workers at a salon where she worked that she did not want anything to do with Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, of Sebastian, who later allegedly shot her outside her Vero Beach home on Aug. 16, Sheriff Eric Flowers said. The gun that Indian River County Sheriff’s Office found near the scene of the homicide of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, belonged to the ex-wife of Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, now charged with first-degree murder in Kriskewicz’s death. Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, was taken into custody on Aug. 19, at a motel in Dunbar, West Virginia by U.S. Marshals deputies for Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, which has charged Waggle with first-degree murder. Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, is facing a first-degree murder charge in the fatal shooting on Aug. 16 of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, outside her Vero Beach home in the 500 block of 1st Street, Vero Beach. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY – Indian River County Sheriff’s Office is now working to bring a murder suspect, arrested on Aug. 19 in West Virginia, to face a first-degree murder charge in Indian River County in the homicide death of a Vero Beach hairdresser, Sheriff Eric Flowers said at a press conference on Aug. Marshals deputies arrested Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, of Sebastian at a motel in Dunbar, West Virginia, about six miles west of Charleston, on Aug. Waggle was being sought by the sheriff’s office as a “person of interest” in the homicide of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, outside her home in the in the 500 block of 1st Street, Vero Beach. 16, detectives responded to a 911 call about a woman lying in the roadway at that address. Deputies located Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures. She was transported to a local trauma center, where she was later pronounced deceased. Waggle, who apparently was traveling alone, is suspected of traveling by a Greyhound bus from an unknown location to Orlando where he then rode in an Uber to a location near Kriskewicz’s home in Vero Beach, Flowers said. Waggle was in Vero Beach for no more than 15 minutes, during which “he murdered her in cold blood in the street,” Flowers said. He had specifically traveled to Vero Beach with the full intention of killing Kriskewicz, Flowers noted. Waggle and Kriskewic interacted during that 15 minutes but it is not known what was said, Flowers said. Kriskewic was concerned about Waggle, with whom she had a relationship with at one time, to the point of telling co-workers “if he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I’m not here,” Flowers said. Waggle left the gun behind, ordered another Uber to take him to Orlando, where he then rode another Greyhound bus to North Carolina and then made his way to a motel in West Virginia, Flowers said. Detectives are still working to piece together specifics about Waggle’s travel patterns before and after the murder, Flowers said. Detectives recovered the gun they believe was used to kill Kriskewicz. In tracing the gun, they found it was registered to Waggle’s ex-wife in West Virginia. She was taken into custody and led detectives to Waggle at the motel, Flowers said. It is not clear whether any charges will be filed against the ex-wife. “Our team has worked relatively non-stop for the last couple of days,” Flowers said. In addition, the agency’s Real Time Crime Center and the Flock network of license plate readers helped detectives track Waggle to the motel, Flowers said. Flowers also praised the partnership the agency has with the Marshals office and witnesses who contributed information which led to Waggle’s arrest. The case is still an active investigation, Flowers said. “There’s still so much more to do in this investigation. We have a case to build.” Your comment has been submitted. The city's Downtown Development Authority reports that 95% of shops on Atlantic Avenue are classified as small businesses, making rent affordability a critical factor for the corridor's future.The Downtown Development Authority (DDA) acknowledges that business operating costs are rising but says rent increases are not the only factor behind recent business closures along the avenue. For some families, finding the right place for their children to learn, grow and connect can be a challenge. Lucie organization is bringing together music, art, dance and therapy — creating a space where students of all abilities can find their voice.WATCH BELOW: House of Music PSL opens doors for students of all abilitiesStephen Lepore has been part of the House of Music PSL since 2021, when he first joined as a student. Now, he works there as a program assistant."My name is Stephen Lepore and I'm from right here in Port St. Lucie, but many of my friends call me Mr. Hollywood," Lepore said."As a program assistant I help put the staff organize stuff, helping people get ready for class," Lepore said.He plays piano and drums and was preparing a song for an upcoming Christmas recital."House of Music, they always make me feel welcomed, they always make me feel right at home," Lepore said.That feeling of belonging is something families say they find throughout the House of Music. Ashley Aguirre first came to the organization about two years ago, looking for a speech therapist for her daughter, Alia."We started with speech classes for her, then she started the early education music group classes and that allowed her, because I'm a stay-at-home mom and a homeschooler, for her to get some fellowship," Aguirre said.Alia now takes piano and ballet, and her younger brother has joined the music group classes, too."Listening to a teacher that's not mom, so all of us. It's really been such a blessing and an answered prayer for the whole family," Aguirre said.That sense of connection extends to students with special needs. Johnny Ortiz is nonverbal and has mobility disabilities. After aging out of other services at 21, his mom, Jenifer, brought him to the House of Music."Having somebody who actually believes in him, because they push him to the limits and seeing how much he's grown," Jenifer said.She says the progress can show up in ways big and small — even something as simple as throwing a ball."I tried playing ball with him all the time and I would throw at him and the ball would just roll over, and I don't know what Lucas did, but now he throws back and forth," Jenifer said."The high fives and all that, that really helps him," Jenifer said.For founder Maive Arndt, the House of Music wasn't the plan. After decades as a music teacher and therapist in Brazil, she moved to the United States with her family, expecting to only stay a year."This is not easy, especially for me. I was 43 years old when we moved here and start from zero with language, the culture," Arndt said.She says she tried to find work in music, but doors kept closing. In 2017, she and her family took a chance and opened the House of Music PSL."The families start to ask us, you need to do other things because my kids want to stay here," Arndt said.Today, its programs reach children and adults through music, dance, art, speech, special-needs services and sports."We think about our families, we think about our kids…we work with so much love," Arndt said.For the families there, that love has made them feel seen, supported and celebrated."They believe in him, sometimes more than I do, which is amazing. I feel like they're family," Jenifer said.House of Harmony is their nonprofit organization. The nonprofit is committed to providing access to music and arts education, offering community programs and outreach, supporting neurodivergent individuals through music therapy and creating inclusive and inspiring learning environments. A man the Martin County Sheriff's Office referred to as a "brazen" robber is now facing felony charges, accused of a jewelry theft at the Treasure Coast Mall. It happened at Royal Jewelers, a kiosk inside the mall, on July 20. Security video from the mall shows a man standing at the counter of the kiosk. Chris Morales of the Martin County Sheriff’s Office identified the man as 25-year-old Dezmone Johnson. "He actually comes up and pretends to be a customer, engages with the clerk for a few minutes," Morales said. According to Morales, Johnson walked away at one point before returning to ask for a closer look at the jewelry. "The clerk brings out a tray of, let's say, seven or eight less expensive necklaces according to him, and he just grabs the tray and runs out," Morales said. The clerk at the store can be heard screaming as the suspect runs away with the necklaces. According to the police report, the necklaces are valued between $850 and $4,500 each, totaling more than $22,000 in stolen jewelry. Cameras outside the mall showed investigators the vehicle Johnson drove away in. "We were able to get the tag from that vehicle, making it pretty easy for us. The vehicle came back to an address in Lauderhill, so down in Broward County," Morales said. Detectives visited a pawn shop near the Lauderhill address and stopped in to ask if Johnson was a customer. "Lo and behold, the owner says, 'Yeah, he was just in here trying to pawn a few necklaces.' Again, making it pretty easy for our detectives," Morales said. Johnson was arrested shortly afterward. Morales expressed relief at the arrest, saying even though this specific robbery was not violent, the next one might have been. "I would say there's a great chance of that. He has a history of violence. He has access to weapons in his criminal history. I'm sure he's not afraid to use that in future endeavors," Morales said. Johnson is charged with robbery and grand theft. He spent a short time in the Broward County jail and is currently free on bond as he awaits trial. A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel, ending a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in Indian River County. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures, according to the sheriff's office. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide. Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. "She had actually told her co-workers, 'If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him, I'm not here,'" Flowers said. "She had broken things off with him, he had moved away and somehow she knew that he could potentially be coming to the area." WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers gives update on Vero Beach homicide arrest According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from an unknown location to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning. "You see that video of him walking, he was dropped off around the corner, he made his way in, we've got him on video, on Ring doorbells, on a variety of different security cameras," Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators. The sheriff's office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle's movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. "At this moment, we don't have charges on her, but we are actively speaking with her," Flowers said. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife, according to the sheriff's office. Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. "I'm not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia," Flowers said. "So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this." The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic's body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night — a timeline Flowers called "unbelievable police work." Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement. Waggle will be extradited back to Indian River County to face the first-degree murder charge. Lucie man faces multiple charges involving a minor after officers served a search warrant at a home Thursday morning, authorities said. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. at a residence in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. During the operation, officers arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz without incident Police said Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. The response drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Authorities said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry into the home. "It's a diversion to either make entry. When conducting a high-risk operation, these are utilized just for the safety of both the officers and the individual," police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation and say they are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active. "As a father of three myself, we take it very serious anytime there is a child involved," Martinez said. Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrest of Matthew Waggle in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewic on First Street in Vero Beach early Sunday morning. Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewic and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation. “He was there for 10, 15 minutes tops. He murdered her in cold blood in the street,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a news conference. Flowers said Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle to her co-workers at a hair salon. “She had actually told her co-workers out at the hair salon, ‘If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I’m not here,’” Flowers said. The sheriff credited the controversial Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle. “Without Flock, I’m not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia. So for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system,” Flowers said. Waggle was found at a motel in West Virginia, and officials said the gun used in the shooting belonged to Waggle’s ex-wife. “She was at the hotel, the same hotel that we got him at. So they were definitely in communication. We don’t know to what extent, what she knew. We don’t know if she knew his plans. All those are things that our detectives will be asking,” Flowers said. The sheriff added that Waggle’s ex-wife is still being questioned and is not currently facing any charges. Small business owners and longtime residents are raising concerns that rising commercial rents along Delray Beach's Atlantic Avenue are threatening the mom-and-pop shops that help define the popular downtown corridor, according to business owners and community members who contacted WPTV.Gail DelVecchio, a Delray Beach resident who has visited the area for decades and lived there full-time for the past four years, said she reached out to WPTV because she fears the trend could undermine the character that makes Atlantic Avenue a destination."They've done such a great job bringing it back," DelVecchio said. It's just a great happening place and I hate to see that ruined."WATCH:Amanda Perna, owner of boutique A Little Wild on Atlantic Avenue, shared similar concerns in an email to WPTV. Perna said tenants who have operated businesses on the strip for a decade are being pushed out due to rent increases.The issue comes as Delray Beach's downtown continues to attract visitors and new development, potentially creating pressure on commercial real estate prices. The city's Downtown Development Authority reports that 95% of shops on Atlantic Avenue are classified as small businesses, making rent affordability a critical factor for the corridor's future.The Downtown Development Authority (DDA) acknowledges that business operating costs are rising but says rent increases are not the only factor behind recent business closures along the avenue. However, the authority was unable to provide WPTV with specific data on average commercial rent costs along Atlantic Avenue or the current number of vacant storefronts. According to the DDA, many empty commercial spaces along Atlantic Avenue are currently undergoing renovations by new tenants, and overall commercial vacancy rates remain low compared to other cities in South Florida.The city and Downtown Development Authority continue to monitor the situation as they work to balance economic growth with preserving the small-business character that defines much of Atlantic Avenue's appeal.Small business owners or employees on Atlantic Avenue are welcome to share their stories— email Victor Jorges at victor.jorges@wptv.com.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." See also: Deputies arrest man, 27, accused of traveling to meet 14-year-old in Hallandale Beach Another commenter said to the chief, "I don't know how you sleep at night." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

A leadership change is on the way for the School District of Indian River County. Moore’s tenure as superintendent ends on June 30, 2027. A judge has thrown out three code enforcement violations against Subculture Coffee, but the City of Delray Beach is still prohibiting the popular coffee shop from hosting its community events, according to a letter sent to the owner.A Palm Beach County Circuit Court judge reversed the city’s orders, ruling that Delray Beach failed to follow its own established rules for such enforcement actions.WATCH: Parking saga continuesThe owner, Rodney Mayo, says just after he paid a separate $10,000 overdue fee and celebrated the court’s decision, he was hand-delivered a letter from the assistant city attorney informing him the events were still not allowed.“Tuesday I thought we’re all back on and we’re all good,” Mayo told WPTV. “Then I get a hand-delivered letter that says just because you won the appeal, does not mean that you are allowed to do these events.”The Court’s RulingThe appeals court found that the city’s Special Magistrate rulings against Subculture Coffee lacked the required written findings of fact and conclusions of law.According to the court’s opinion, Delray Beach's own operating guidelines mandate these formal sections in all rulings. Because they were absent, the court reversed the orders and sent the case back to the city’s Special Magistrate for proper proceedings.This legal battle comes after the city raised concerns about overflow parking, arguing Subculture’s popular open mics, poetry nights, and other gatherings make it more of a venue than a coffee shop.City's Position and Taxpayer CostThe dispute is now back in the city's hands. Commissioner Juli Casale told WPTV the case is being sent back to be rewritten with the proper legal language.According to the city attorney, this legal fight has cost Delray Beach taxpayers approximately $22,000 so far.Mayo, who said his community events have been on pause for a year, expressed frustration.“I’ve asked over and over why are other establishments allowed to do this and we’re not and it’s been silent,” Mayo said.Owner Weighs Next StepsWith the case returning to the city, Mayo faces a difficult choice. His tenure currently ranks as the second longest among Florida's appointed district school superintendents.He said during his time leading the district, SDIRC advanced from 38th to 5th among Florida's 67 school districts based on District Grade, earned 4 consecutive A district grades, and grew the share of schools earning an A or B from 47 percent to 100 percent. The district also achieved a 96 percent high school graduation rate and was named the No. 1 Best Place to Teach in Florida by Niche for 2026. Moore said was named the 2025 Florida Superintendent of the Year and a national finalist."These accomplishments tell an extraordinary story of improvement, but they are not the story itself. They are the evidence of the story," Moore said in the release. "The story is what happens when beliefs become behaviors, behaviors become habits, and habits become coherent systems of work."As Moore enters his final school year, he identified two priorities: ensuring every SDIRC school earns an A grade and positioning the district to become the No. 1 school district in Florida."We have spent close to seven years proving that dramatic improvement is possible," he said. "This year, I want us to demonstrate just how far a mature, coherent, high-performing system can go."Following his departure, Moore said he intends to explore opportunities to help other leaders and school systems create conditions for exceptional student outcomes.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The man accused of grabbing an entire display of gold chains from a jewelry kiosk at Treasure Coast Square Mall and fleeing on foot has been arrested and has already bonded out of jail, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . According to the sheriff's office, the robbery happened July 20 at the Royal Jewelers kiosk near the mall's main entrance in Jensen Beach. Investigators say a man approached the counter and asked to see several gold chains, trying some on before handing them back and walking away. He briefly left the mall, then returned and told the employee his girlfriend thought the chains he'd looked at were too expensive, asking to see cheaper options. When the employee pulled out a new display holding 9 gold chains, deputies say the man suddenly grabbed the entire display out of her hands and ran. He fled through the same entrance he'd come in, past a Ruby Tuesday and Port Barna Restaurant, and got into a silver Ford Fusion that was later seen on nearby surveillance video heading south on Federal Highway. The sheriff's office says the stolen merchandise was worth more than $22,000. Three of the necklaces were later recovered, two of them found on the ground near the mall's south exit, leaving six chains valued at roughly $13,000 still missing. Investigators say a Sheriff's Office crime scene unit lifted fingerprints and palm prints from the glass display counter where the suspect had been handling the chains, along with DNA from necklaces he tried on and a pair of sunglasses that fell off while he was running. Deputies say those prints matched 25-year-old Dezmone Karlde' Rome Johnson of Lauderhill. The sheriff's office says Johnson already had an open felony warrant out for a probation violation at the time of the robbery. Investigators say he was also spotted the following day at a Broward County pawn shop with a woman who may have pawned one of the stolen chains. An arrest warrant was approved and filed in the Martin County case, and Johnson was taken into custody July 31 by the Broward County Sheriff's Office with the help of the U.S. Marshals Fugitive Task Force. He recently bonded out of the Broward County Jail on separate charges. Sheriff John Budensiek explains why the arrest came more than a week after the robbery. "The next day, we had fingerprints from our suspect. Immediately we had a tag from the car in a description, but we wanted to kind of put it all together and do it the right way, as opposed to hastily running out and making an arrest that could or could not be beat in a court," said Budensiek. See also: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The sheriff described Johnson as having an extensive criminal history, including prior arrests involving firearms charges and resisting. "He's been through the system, but he's used to the revolving door system," Budensiek said. "That's not going to be the case here. If you steal $22,000 worth of anything from one of our Martin County businesses or residences, the 19th Circuit will lock you up, and you're likely to do prison time here in our circuit." Budensiek said Johnson will face the Martin County charges in addition to the felony probation violation warrant out of Broward County, and said investigators don't yet know why Johnson specifically targeted the Treasure Coast Square Mall. He also cautioned that mall kiosks like Royal Jewelers can be especially vulnerable, since they typically have fewer security cameras and safeguards than storefront businesses, and said this year alone the mall has seen multiple snatch-and-grab incidents targeting kiosks. He encouraged vendors to ask for identification or proof of funds from customers requesting to see high-value merchandise.

After two of the largest animal hoarding cases in recent Martin County history, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City is now caring for over 100 animals connected to two separate hoarding investigations in Stuart and Palm City.One case involved 108 cats and dogs rescued from a Stuart home owned by 77-year-old Gail Giustino. WPTV previously reported that deputies found horrific conditions at Giustino's home on Southwest Meadowlark Circle in July, with no working air conditioning, little ventilation and up to a foot of animal feces covering the floor.The second case involved 36 Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home after deputies described severe neglect conditions. Paige O'Donnell was arrested and faces 72 criminal charges after WPTV's investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe. Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris.Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said American Humane has been assisting the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast with shelter operations and veterinary support following the rescues.The Border Collies rescued from the Palm City home are undergoing what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath. "We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."He said even small signs — including a tail wag or playful behavior — can signal major progress."The first little tail wag," Perea said, "is an indication that something's going right."Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said in the Stuart case that investigators believed Giustino thought she was helping animals, despite the dangerous conditions inside the home. In the Palm City case, O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood," according to court documents."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," he said.Perea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under the law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrest of Matthew Waggle in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewic on First Street in Vero Beach early Sunday morning. Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewic and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation. “He was there for 10, 15 minutes tops. He murdered her in cold blood in the street,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a news conference. Flowers said Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle to her co-workers at a hair salon. “She had actually told her co-workers out at the hair salon, ‘If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I’m not here,’” Flowers said. The sheriff credited the controversial Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle. “Without Flock, I’m not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia. So for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system,” Flowers said. Waggle was found at a motel in West Virginia, and officials said the gun used in the shooting belonged to Waggle’s ex-wife. “She was at the hotel, the same hotel that we got him at. So they were definitely in communication. We don’t know to what extent, what she knew. We don’t know if she knew his plans. All those are things that our detectives will be asking,” Flowers said. The sheriff added that Waggle’s ex-wife is still being questioned and is not currently facing any charges. The man accused of grabbing an entire display of gold chains from a jewelry kiosk at Treasure Coast Square Mall and fleeing on foot has been arrested and has already bonded out of jail, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . According to the sheriff's office, the robbery happened July 20 at the Royal Jewelers kiosk near the mall's main entrance in Jensen Beach. Investigators say a man approached the counter and asked to see several gold chains, trying some on before handing them back and walking away. He briefly left the mall, then returned and told the employee his girlfriend thought the chains he'd looked at were too expensive, asking to see cheaper options. When the employee pulled out a new display holding 9 gold chains, deputies say the man suddenly grabbed the entire display out of her hands and ran. He fled through the same entrance he'd come in, past a Ruby Tuesday and Port Barna Restaurant, and got into a silver Ford Fusion that was later seen on nearby surveillance video heading south on Federal Highway. The sheriff's office says the stolen merchandise was worth more than $22,000. Three of the necklaces were later recovered, two of them found on the ground near the mall's south exit, leaving six chains valued at roughly $13,000 still missing. Investigators say a Sheriff's Office crime scene unit lifted fingerprints and palm prints from the glass display counter where the suspect had been handling the chains, along with DNA from necklaces he tried on and a pair of sunglasses that fell off while he was running. Deputies say those prints matched 25-year-old Dezmone Karlde' Rome Johnson of Lauderhill. The sheriff's office says Johnson already had an open felony warrant out for a probation violation at the time of the robbery. Investigators say he was also spotted the following day at a Broward County pawn shop with a woman who may have pawned one of the stolen chains. An arrest warrant was approved and filed in the Martin County case, and Johnson was taken into custody July 31 by the Broward County Sheriff's Office with the help of the U.S. Marshals Fugitive Task Force. He recently bonded out of the Broward County Jail on separate charges. Sheriff John Budensiek explains why the arrest came more than a week after the robbery. "The next day, we had fingerprints from our suspect. Immediately we had a tag from the car in a description, but we wanted to kind of put it all together and do it the right way, as opposed to hastily running out and making an arrest that could or could not be beat in a court," said Budensiek. See also: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The sheriff described Johnson as having an extensive criminal history, including prior arrests involving firearms charges and resisting. "He's been through the system, but he's used to the revolving door system," Budensiek said. "That's not going to be the case here. If you steal $22,000 worth of anything from one of our Martin County businesses or residences, the 19th Circuit will lock you up, and you're likely to do prison time here in our circuit." Budensiek said Johnson will face the Martin County charges in addition to the felony probation violation warrant out of Broward County, and said investigators don't yet know why Johnson specifically targeted the Treasure Coast Square Mall. He also cautioned that mall kiosks like Royal Jewelers can be especially vulnerable, since they typically have fewer security cameras and safeguards than storefront businesses, and said this year alone the mall has seen multiple snatch-and-grab incidents targeting kiosks. He encouraged vendors to ask for identification or proof of funds from customers requesting to see high-value merchandise.

Marshals took a person of interest into custody Wednesday night in connection with the shooting death of a 52-year-old woman in Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced. Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian, was arrested at a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia. Detectives are working to return him to Indian River County. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office identified the victim as Dawn Kriskewic . Investigators are treating her death as a domestic violence homicide. At approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday, the sheriff's office received a 911 call reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street. Deputies located Kriskewic with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home. Sheriff Eric Flowers identified Waggle as the person of interest and said investigators believe Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle following the shooting. Flowers called the incident a tragedy and said detectives used resources such as Flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts. "At this point we're not sure, but this could be a domestic violence incident. It's a loss of life that's so unnecessary," Flowers said. "So our team is committed to working on that." Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home. "My brother actually heard the shot," Cardenas said. Cardenas said he hopes an arrest comes soon. "I just hope that they find the suspect," Cardenas said. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. School District of Indian River County Superintendent Dr. Moore announced Wednesday he will conclude his tenure with the district effective June 30, 2027, after nearly seven years of service. “I am proud of what we have accomplished, but even more so of what we have built together,” Moore said. “Serving as Superintendent of Schools has been one of the greatest privileges of my professional life. Nearly seven years later, my belief in the power of public education to transform lives is stronger than ever.” Moore said in a news release that he shared his decision with school board members and his Cabinet Leadership Team before informing district and school leaders and broader SDIRC staff. His tenure currently ranks as the second longest among Florida’s appointed district school superintendents. He said during his time leading the district, SDIRC advanced from 38th to 5th among Florida’s 67 school districts based on District Grade, earned 4 consecutive A district grades, and grew the share of schools earning an A or B from 47 percent to 100 percent. The district also achieved a 96 percent high school graduation rate and was named the No. 1 Best Place to Teach in Florida by Niche for 2026. Moore said was named the 2025 Florida Superintendent of the Year and a national finalist. “These accomplishments tell an extraordinary story of improvement, but they are not the story itself. They are the evidence of the story,” Moore said in the release. “The story is what happens when beliefs become behaviors, behaviors become habits, and habits become coherent systems of work.” As Moore enters his final school year, he identified two priorities: ensuring every SDIRC school earns an A grade and positioning the district to become the No. 1 school district in Florida. “We have spent close to seven years proving that dramatic improvement is possible,” he said. “This year, I want us to demonstrate just how far a mature, coherent, high-performing system can go.” Following his departure, Moore said he intends to explore opportunities to help other leaders and school systems create conditions for exceptional student outcomes. Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. FORT PIERCE – The Fort Pierce City Commission Monday said no for the third time to a proposal to settle a citizen lawsuit over the Little Jim Bait and Tackle property. Commissioner Arnold Gaines, himself an attorney, suggested that a settlement demand that Little Jim’s current operator be given the right to match the outcome of any future bids to lease the city-owned property, would violate state law. Public entities are required to competitively bid the awarding of things like property leases to get the best outcome for taxpayers. Gaines suggested giving Little Jim’s current operator an automatic “right of first refusal” would violate the principle of competitive bidding. Instead, commissioners unanimously decided to offer a counter settlement that says they are willing to forgo a claim for the city’s legal costs involved in defending the lawsuit – a minimum $3,600 – if plaintiff Kevin Keene will drop his action. Keene, a Fort Pierce resident, said he filed suit against the city in October as an attempt to give citizens more authority in determining how city-owned waterfront property is used. Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. The current operator, Salty Baitshack 3, has continued business there on a month-to-month lease for more than a year. Lucie County judge has twice dismissed Keene’s lawsuit, but gave him an opportunity to refile. Keene’s latest settlement offer would: – Require the city to suspend any new Requests for Proposals (RFP) for awarding the next long-term Little Jim lease until all issues with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection have been resolved. – Require the city to agree to put any future sale or long-term lease of publicly owned waterfront property to a citywide vote. – Give Little Jim’s current operator the right to match the highest bid resulting from an RFP process. With the Republican nomination secured, Byron Donalds is moving from winning the primary to defending the policy fine print.In a recent one-on-one interview, Donalds outlined his positions on four issues likely to follow him into November: property taxes, insurance, school vaccine requirements and data centers.The first three help define his governing pitch. The fourth is already opening a sharp divide with Democratic nominee David Jolly.Watch report from Forrest SaundersProperty-tax relief, with more promisedDonalds supports Amendment 3, the property-tax proposal headed to voters this fall, but calls it only a first step.The measure would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for Floridians who establish permanent residency by the end of 2026. It would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%.New residents would face a five-year phase-in before qualifying for the full exemption.The Florida Division of Elections lists the measure under the revised title, “Increased Homestead Exemption; Lower Cap on Increases in Non-Homestead Property Assessments.” A judge ordered the original title and summary rewritten after finding the wording misleading.Donalds said the amendment would provide needed relief, particularly for seniors and working families, but suggested Florida should eventually consider a system that treats counties differently based on property values and economic output.“It might be time for Florida to have a multi-tiered taxing system,” Donalds said, contrasting large counties such as Miami-Dade and Orange with smaller counties including Putnam, Wakulla and Gadsden.He did not spell out how the tiers would work or how local governments would replace lost revenue.A legislative financial analysis estimates Amendment 3 would reduce local non-school property-tax revenue by nearly $5 billion in its first full fiscal year. The recurring impact is projected to approach $11.9 billion by the 2031-32 fiscal year.The amendment needs approval from at least 60% of voters.Insurance: A 20% to 25% pledgeDonalds is making an ambitious promise on property insurance, saying regulatory changes could lower costs by another 20% to 25%.“We have to reform the regulatory side of insurance in our state,” Donalds said. “We think we can push costs down in Florida another 20 to 25%.”His ideas include changing the Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund, lowering reinsurance costs and making home-hardening grants more efficient.Donalds specifically pointed to the catastrophe fund’s 25% cash buildup factor, which insurers pay on top of actuarially calculated premiums. Florida law has required the factor since the 2013-14 contract year.Donalds said the state could eliminate the charge or create a formula that turns it down when the fund has healthy reserves and raises it when the balance falls.The detailed proposal is still coming. Donalds did not provide an independent analysis showing how the changes would produce the promised savings or how quickly homeowners would see them.Vaccines: More choice, but not a full repealOn school vaccines, Donalds is taking a more cautious position than Gov. Ron DeSantis and Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo, who have pushed to eliminate all childhood vaccine mandates.Donalds supports giving parents more discretion and spreading vaccinations over a longer schedule. But he stopped short of endorsing the elimination of core requirements for polio and measles, mumps and rubella, commonly known as MMR.“In terms of polio vaccines or measles or mumps or rubella, there’s more study, there’s more data I want to look at before that decision is made,” Donalds said.Florida’s standard school requirements remain in place. State law requires immunization against polio, diphtheria, measles, rubella, pertussis, mumps and tetanus. A 2026 effort to expand exemptions passed the Senate but stalled in the House.Donalds’ position still favors more parental choice, but leaves him short of the complete rollback sought by Florida’s current governor and surgeon general.Data centers become the main eventDonalds is standing behind data-center development despite resistance from both parties.He argues the facilities are necessary infrastructure for artificial intelligence, aerospace, medicine, government services and other parts of Florida’s future economy. He also warns that bans and moratoriums could send investment and high-paying jobs elsewhere.“Capital goes where it’s valued,” Donalds said. “When you start throwing out the word ban or moratorium, what you’re really saying is that maybe Florida is not the place to do business.”Donalds would allow the facilities with safeguards. A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel, ending a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in Indian River County.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene.After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators.The sheriff's office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle's movements across state lines. An overwhelming number of people have posted comments on WPTV's Facebook page, calling for the death penalty for suspended Palm Beach County clerk Mike Caruso following his arrest on alleged sexual abuse charges, so we're getting answers.The question of whether the suspended Palm Beach County Clerk and Comptroller could face the death penalty comes down to the details of how a state law is written — and whether his charges qualify him for it.WATCH BELOW: Could Mike Caruso face death penalty? Ron DeSantis, who appointed Caruso, weighed in on the possibility of the death penalty after the arrest."We're the first state to reintroduce the death penalty for pedophiles, and I'm proud that I signed that into law and I'm proud that we have very strong penalties for people that abuse children and if he's convicted he's going to be in a world of hurt," DeSantis said.DeSantis was referring to the 2023 Florida Capital Sexual Battery Law — a law Caruso himself voted in favor of when he was a state representative. The law allows prosecutors to seek the death penalty for adults convicted of sexually battering a child under the age of 12.Caruso was arrested on five felony charges related to child sex abuse, including kidnapping, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious exhibition, luring or enticing a child, and child abuse causing mental injury. A Florida investor tells Scripps News Group Tampa Bay reporter Michael Paluska that artificial intelligence has become his most valuable business partner — one that never takes a day off, never calls in sick, and never asks for a paycheck.Alex Jandick, owner of 131 Cash Home Buyers in St. Petersburg, says he now relies on an AI agent called Claude to handle nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation — from marketing to bookkeeping — saving him more than $41,000 a year.Before making the switch, Jandick was paying $2,500 a month for marketing and nearly $1,000 a month for a bookkeeper."Did you tell them that you replaced them with AI?" Paluska asked."Nope. I just let them go," Jandick said.Claude currently handles both for $100 a month."So what does Claude do now for the marketing side?" Paluska asked."Everything, everything that I tell it to," Jandick said. "I sit in my office, and I tell a robot, Claude, what to do."After spending about two weeks setting up and fine-tuning the system, Jandick said the results were immediate."It's like holy smokes! This is — it was everything that I had wanted to get done at a cheaper rate for a year," Jandick said.Now, Jandick says he and Claude essentially split the workload. A human still has to verify the information and input the correct prompts. But the AI takes it from there."I put in 25 to 30 hours a week, and I have Claude probably putting in 25 to 30 hours a week," Jandick said.Jandick is the sole employee of his company, meaning no workers were displaced when he made the switch. Still, after posting online about his AI-driven savings, he faced criticism."I get that there's going to be haters out there," Jandick said.He pushed back directly."I'm saving $41,000 per year; for me, that is an incredible amount of money. That's my kids' college savings funds."The broader question of how many jobs AI could eliminate remains unsettled. According to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report, AI will displace 92 million jobs globally by 2030. However, the same report projects 170 million new roles will open up — a net gain of 78 million jobs worldwide. A separate 2026 Goldman Sachs study estimates 300 million jobs globally are exposed to automation by AI, though that research did not cite specific numbers for job gains.For Jandick, the technology has changed more than just his bottom line. He said he used to feel isolated working alone. Now, he tells Paluska, that has changed."Before Claude, I did get lonely," Jandick said. Now, I wake up in the morning with a bit more energy. I'm more excited because it's like I don't have to work so hard to break even each month. You know, it does take a little bit of legwork to get all set up and everything, but I have not found anything that is a better cost cutter than AI at this point," Jandick said.
