A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel, ending a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in Indian River County. WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers gives update on Vero Beach homicide arrest Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures, according to the sheriff's office. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide. Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. "She had actually told her co-workers, 'If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him, I'm not here,'" Flowers said. "She had broken things off with him, he had moved away and somehow she knew that he could potentially be coming to the area." According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from West Virginia to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning. "You see that video of him walking, he was dropped off around the corner, he made his way in, we've got him on video, on Ring doorbells, on a variety of different security cameras," Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators. The sheriff's office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle's movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. "At this moment, we don't have charges on her, but we are actively speaking with her," Flowers said. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife, according to the sheriff's office. Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. "I'm not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia," Flowers said. "So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this." The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic's body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night — a timeline Flowers called "unbelievable police work." Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement. Waggle will be extradited back to Indian River County to face the first-degree murder charge. A man accused of traveling to Indian River County with the intent to kill his ex-girlfriend, a Vero Beach hairdresser, was captured in West Virginia after a four-day investigation that authorities say was aided by license plate reader technology. The investigation began Sunday morning, when authorities found Dawn Kriskewic’s body in a roadway in the southern part of the county. Officials said investigators initially did not know who she was and had not previously encountered her. By Wednesday night, authorities had tracked Waggle to a motel in West Virginia and taken him into custody. This has been an absolutely incredible case for them to put this together and make all of this happen in such a short amount of time, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a news conference. Authorities said Kriskewic had ended her relationship with Waggle before the shooting and had warned coworkers at the hair salon that she wanted no contact with him. She had actually told her coworkers at the hair salon, If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I’m not here,’ the sheriff said. Investigators believe Waggle traveled to the area specifically to kill Kriskewic. Waggle came here to Indian River County fully intent on shooting and killing Dawn, the sheriff said. That was his entire premise. According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus to Orlando before taking an Uber to Indian River County. Surveillance footage, including Ring doorbell video and other security cameras, captured him walking toward Kriskewic’s residence after being dropped off nearby. Authorities said Waggle and Kriskewic had a brief interaction before he shot her and fled. He walked to the residence. They had a brief interaction. He shot her, and then he fled that area, the sheriff said. Investigators said Waggle then took an Uber back to Orlando, boarded another Greyhound bus and traveled to North Carolina before eventually making his way to West Virginia. Authorities said no one appeared to have traveled with him. Investigators interviewed the Uber drivers who transported Waggle and found that he had a single bus ticket. Sheriff credits network of license plate readers The sheriff credited the agency’s Real Time Crime Center and a network of license plate readers with helping investigators piece together Waggle’s movements and locate him. For everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this, the sheriff said. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system. The sheriff clarified that Flock is one brand of automated license plate reader used by law enforcement. We’ve made so many cases, and we’ve protected this community as a result of this, and this is just another example of that, he said. Investigators also focused on Waggle’s ex-wife, who was in West Virginia and had been communicating with him. Authorities said the Real Time Crime Center determined she had been making calls to a specific motel. Investigators eventually found Waggle at that same motel. The sheriff said the gun believed to have been used in the killing belonged to Waggle’s ex-wife and that she knew he had it. Two detectives were sent to West Virginia to interview both Waggle and his ex-wife and determine how much she knew about his plans and what assistance, if any, she provided. She was at the hotel, the same hotel that we got him at, the sheriff said. So they were definitely in communication. We don’t know what extent, what she knew. We don’t know if she knew his plans. Authorities said the investigation remains active as detectives continue working to establish Waggle’s movements before and after the shooting, including where his trip began, how he traveled from North Carolina to West Virginia and the circumstances surrounding his stay at the motel. The sheriff also praised witnesses who came forward during the investigation, saying their cooperation helped detectives build the case. Waggle is expected to be returned to Florida, although the timing could depend on whether he agrees to extradition or challenges the process. There’s still so much more to do in this investigation, the sheriff said. We’ve got a case to build.

The man accused of grabbing an entire display of gold chains from a jewelry kiosk at Treasure Coast Square Mall and fleeing on foot has been arrested and has already bonded out of jail, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . According to the sheriff's office, the robbery happened July 20 at the Royal Jewelers kiosk near the mall's main entrance in Jensen Beach. Investigators say a man approached the counter and asked to see several gold chains, trying some on before handing them back and walking away. He briefly left the mall, then returned and told the employee his girlfriend thought the chains he'd looked at were too expensive, asking to see cheaper options. When the employee pulled out a new display holding nine to ten gold chains, deputies say the man suddenly grabbed the entire display out of her hands and ran. He fled through the same entrance he'd come in, past a Ruby Tuesday and Port Barna Restaurant, and got into a silver Ford Fusion that was later seen on nearby surveillance video heading south on Federal Highway. The sheriff's office says the stolen merchandise was worth more than $22,000. Three of the necklaces were later recovered, two of them found on the ground near the mall's south exit, leaving six chains valued at roughly $13,000 still missing. Investigators say a Sheriff's Office crime scene unit lifted fingerprints and palm prints from the glass display counter where the suspect had been handling the chains, along with DNA from necklaces he tried on and a pair of sunglasses that fell off while he was running. Deputies say those prints matched 25-year-old Dezmone Karlde' Rome Johnson of Lauderhill. The sheriff's office says Johnson already had an open felony warrant out for a probation violation at the time of the robbery. Investigators say he was also spotted the following day at a Broward County pawn shop with a woman who may have pawned one of the stolen chains. An arrest warrant was approved and filed in the Martin County case, and Johnson was taken into custody July 31 by the Broward County Sheriff's Office. He bonded out of jail August 8. It's not yet clear which agencies were directly involved in tracking Johnson down and making the arrest; CBS12 is working to confirm those details. The Martin County Sheriff's Office has also said the case could be turned over to Broward County for additional charges related to dealing in stolen property, pending review of the pawn shop surveillance footage. CBS12 News is speaking with Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek and will provide updates when they become available.

The Miami woman accused of posing as a bank representative to scam a Martin County senior is now facing an additional charge after deputies say she tried to smuggle thousands of dollars in cash into jail hidden in an unexpected hiding spot her lady parts. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Monquie Love Turnbull never mentioned she was carrying $3,180 in cash concealed in her body when she was arrested, and the money wasn't discovered until she was being processed into the jail. The sheriff's office has since confirmed the cash is the same money taken from one of her alleged scam victims. Sheriff John Budensiek said Turnbull revealed she had the money inside her body when she complained of pain during a jail phone call to an unknown man. "Our detectives went back over to the jail. They interviewed her yet again. She admitted to having money inside of her. She said at that point it was only $400. And then later, as they interviewed her a little more, she said it was $3,180," said Budensiek. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office , the case began Monday when 31-year-old Monquie Love Turnbull showed up at an elderly victim's home claiming the person's bank account had been compromised. She told the victim she was with the bank and offered to take the debit or credit card off their hands to dispose of it safely. The victim grew suspicious of the encounter and contacted law enforcement, giving deputies time to track Turnbull down before she left the county. Arrest affidavits show the scheme was more coordinated than initially known. Investigators say an unidentified male caller, posing as a Chase Bank fraud representative, told the victim her account had been compromised and that someone would come to her home to collect and destroy her card before a replacement arrived. Turnbull, using the alias "Monica," then arrived at the home, verified herself with a code relayed from the caller, and collected the card, cutting it in half in front of the victim and placing the pieces in a manila envelope. The victim told deputies she grew uneasy and wrote down Turnbull's license plate number as she left. Minutes later, the victim's bank account was drained through a $3,000 withdrawal and a $180 ATM withdrawal, a total of $3,180. "In this particular instance, this was all the money that this lady had. This was everything that she had. And she handed it over to a scammer," said Budensiek. While deputies were investigating that report, the sheriff's office says they were alerted to a second call identifying Turnbull as a possible suspect in a nearly identical incident targeting another victim the same day. That attempt was caught on a Ring doorbell camera, but the second victim's family member grew skeptical and refused to hand over the card. That victim also provided a plate number and vehicle description, which helped investigators track Turnbull down. Deputies located the vehicle, a gray two-door Nissan Altima, on Bridge Road in Hobe Sound near the I-95 interchange and conducted a traffic stop. Body camera footage shows deputies pulling her over during the stop and placing her under arrest, with the arresting deputy telling her she was being taken into custody for a scheme to defraud. The first victim was brought to the scene and positively identified Turnbull as "Monica" from about 15 feet away. A search of the vehicle turned up a surgical mask and multiple yellow envelopes matching witness descriptions. Turnbull was booked on charges including scheme to defraud, grand theft, fraudulent use of a credit or debit card without consent involving a victim 60 or older, fraudulent use of ID without consent, and felony use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. Investigators say her cellphone and Apple Watch were seized, and a search warrant for the devices is pending. The Sheriff says there are still missing details in this investigation. She stated that she is part of a larger organization. We can't verify that one way or the other, and then the other question we have is: How does she know where to go? She went to two Chase Bank customers. Just random addresses, but it doesn't look to be that random," Budensiek said. See also: Suspended PBC clerk Mike Caruso makes first appearance on child sex abuse charges Turnbull now faces a charge of introducing contraband into a corrections facility on top of her original charges. She's being held on a $500,000 bond. The investigation remains open, including efforts to identify the second suspect who made the phone calls. The Martin County Sheriff's Office is renewing its warning to residents, especially seniors, not to let anyone into their home who wasn't scheduled to be there, and never to hand over cash, credit cards or valuables to someone who shows up unannounced. Anyone approached by someone claiming to represent a bank, financial institution or other organization asking for valuables or access to their home is urged not to comply and to call 911 instead.

The man driving the SUV sustained traumatic injuries and was taken to a local hospital. Cameras catching drivers who illegally pass stopped school buses or speed through school zones are generating millions of citations across Florida — and a growing wave of legal challenges.For nearly 3 years, Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp have been tracking the problems with these new automated school cameras and the millions of dollars they generate. But legal fights over these cameras are proving to be a bumpy road.Miami-based Attorney Gino Moreno filed 3 lawsuits last year after our investigation found drivers hit with $225 school bus camera fines had no way to challenge their fines because the cameras started rolling without the proper due process in place.WATCH Legal challenges over school bus and school speed zone cameras are hitting roadblocks"They were getting handed out tickets, and there was no way for the drivers to contest it," Moreno said.Since then, his cases have hit a wall.In Polk County, a judge dismissed his federal case. In Miami-Dade, a revised complaint is pending, and in Hillsborough County, his client, Stanley Shultz, is still waiting to see if his case will move forward."I mean, this has certainly been disheartening, but we're hopeful," Moreno said.Shultz, who lives in Plant City, was fined for illegally passing a school bus — even though video from his citation shows the bus’s warning lights never flashed. Shultz appeals the fine, but a judge in Tallahassee upheld it, despite state law requiring appeals must be heard by “local hearing officers.”So Shultz is fighting back, accusing the county of not following state rules for appeal hearings."I felt that I was guilty before even going into the hearing," Shultz said about his hearing with the Tallahassee judge.Legal questions over these new cameras extend beyond school buses. Our investigation also found concerns over school speed zone cameras, with drivers fined when school was not in session or when signs directing them to slow down when flashing never flashed.Questions also emerged about the camera devices themselves. The radar inside the cameras, which state law requires to be approved by the state, is not approved. The state maintains it's exempt.Attorney Ira Karmelin with The Ticket Clinic has successfully used that argument to get school speed zone tickets thrown out — but he says judges are now starting to side with the state’s claim of exemption, even though the exemption refers to a radar’s design, not the device itself."You don't want a radar that's so powerful that it's actually harming people by the radar beams," Karmelin said about why the devices require state approval to begin with.Since the cameras began operating in Florida, they’ve generated well over 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in paid fines as of earlier this year. While these legal challenges continue to hit roadblocks, judges have left the door open for appeals or new legal arguments.“This is something that will impact a lot of people, so we know that judges are taking this seriously,” Moreno said.

With less than three months until election day, the U.S. Senate race in the key battleground state of Michigan remains essentially deadlocked, according to a new AARP poll released Thursday.Democrat Abdul El Sayed narrowly leads Republican Mike Rogers 48-47, the poll showed, well within the survey’s 3.3% margin of sampling error. Five percent of likely voters remain undecided in the Senate race.Michigan’s Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson holds a slightly larger lead in the gubernatorial race. She leads Republican nominee Rep. John James by five points, 49-44, with six percent still undecided.While both contests remain tight, the U.S. Senate race is “extremely close,” according to Matt Hogan, a partner with the Democratic polling firm Impact Strategies who conducted the poll alongside GOP pollster Bob Ward of Fabrizio Ward.As was the case in other states polled by AARP, voters over 50, particularly older women, remain a key constituency that could swing the race in either direction.Significant partisan age gaps are apparent in both the Senate and gubernatorial races: El Sayed trails Rogers by 9 points among voters over 50 but leads by 16 points with those aged 18-49; Jocelyn similarly leads James among younger voters by 13 points but trails James by one among those over 50.RELATED STORY | Midterm poll shows Democrats with advantage on generic midterm ballot“50-plus voters are really driving the difference in the margin between these two races,” Hogan said.El Sayed’s struggle with older voters is particularly apparent when looking at older swing voters — those who, in the survey, did not indicate support for only the Democratic or Republican ticket but rather split their support between the parties or were undecided in one or more races.Rogers leads such voters by a whopping 33 points in the Senate contest, while Benson leads the group by 28 in the gubernatorial race, amounting to the “biggest difference we’ve seen in swing voters 50-plus in any of our polls,” Hogan noted.And while voters of all partisan backgrounds reported high interest in voting, older voters hold a slight edge in terms of enthusiasm; 86% of those 50-plus rated themselves a 10-out-of-10 in terms of their motivation to show up to the polls, compared to just 71% of voters under 50.As with other battleground races and national surveys of American voters, the economy and cost of living remain the number one issues for voters of both parties, followed by threats to democracy, immigration and border security and taxes and government spending.For older voters, the solvency of Social Security and Medicare are of key interest, as are the cost of health care and policies to help seniors live independently at home as they age.While foreign policy issues dominated the Democratic primary for Senate – with El Sayed repeatedly attacking his then-opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, over her support for Israel and significant backing by pro-Israel PACs – matters of foreign policy ranked seventh among voters’ most important issues.“This is not an issue that is really driving the midterm elections more broadly,” Ward told Scripps News.The AARP poll of 877 randomly sampled likely Michigan voters from Aug.

Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. "She volunteered 300 to 400 hours building her home, doing financial education, and then she purchased her home at a 0% interest mortgage based on 30% of her income and not the market."Hamilton and her grandson walked into the home expecting an empty house but instead found every room completely furnished and personalized."We were surprised," Hamilton said. It was just an empty box, and now there's things like coffee makers and juicers and TVs and every drawer, every cabinet has something in it."The home makeover was coordinated by the iTHINK Community Foundation and dozens of volunteers who worked behind the scenes to prepare the surprise reveal.Stephen Johnson, AVP of administration and marketing for iTHINK Financial, said the organization partnered with Habitat for Humanity as part of the foundation’s ongoing community investment efforts."Our iTHINK Community Foundation is how we made this happen,” Johnson said. Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. FORT PIERCE – The Fort Pierce City Commission Monday said no for the third time to a proposal to settle a citizen lawsuit over the Little Jim Bait and Tackle property. Commissioner Arnold Gaines, himself an attorney, suggested that a settlement demand that Little Jim’s current operator be given the right to match the outcome of any future bids to lease the city-owned property, would violate state law. Public entities are required to competitively bid the awarding of things like property leases to get the best outcome for taxpayers. Gaines suggested giving Little Jim’s current operator an automatic “right of first refusal” would violate the principle of competitive bidding. Instead, commissioners unanimously decided to offer a counter settlement that says they are willing to forgo a claim for the city’s legal costs involved in defending the lawsuit – a minimum $3,600 – if plaintiff Kevin Keene will drop his action. Keene, a Fort Pierce resident, said he filed suit against the city in October as an attempt to give citizens more authority in determining how city-owned waterfront property is used. Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. The current operator, Salty Baitshack 3, has continued business there on a month-to-month lease for more than a year. Lucie County judge has twice dismissed Keene’s lawsuit, but gave him an opportunity to refile. Keene’s latest settlement offer would: – Require the city to suspend any new Requests for Proposals (RFP) for awarding the next long-term Little Jim lease until all issues with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection have been resolved. – Require the city to agree to put any future sale or long-term lease of publicly owned waterfront property to a citywide vote. – Give Little Jim’s current operator the right to match the highest bid resulting from an RFP process. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." See also: Deputies arrest man, 27, accused of traveling to meet 14-year-old in Hallandale Beach Another commenter said to the chief, "I don't know how you sleep at night." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

Florida voters’ reputation of bucking the national trend of automatically reelecting incumbents proved particularly true in Indiantown, with three incumbents swept off the Board by voters yesterday, and the county as a whole reflected a desire to restore formerly elected officials to power. That was also evident in the Primary races for three of the seats on the Stuart City Commission, an election cycle made more transformational by the April 30 resignation of Collins as then mayor of Stuart to seek the District 2 Martin County Commission vacated by Commissioner Stacey Hetherington who chose not to seek re-election. In Collins’ bid for the latter, he received 48.99 percent, or 14,657 votes, of the total 29, 916 votes cast in that race. The two other candidates, Susan O’Rourke and Althea Wiley, got 40.33 percent and 10.68 percent, respectively. In the District 2 County Commission race, Current Chairwoman and Incumbent Sarah Heard won her seventh term on the Board, with 47.53 percent, or 14,219 votes, out of a total of 29,914 cast in that race. Her challengers John Dial and John “Kaz” Kanzanjian, got 44.93 percent and 7.53 percent, respectively. The City Commission races saw a lot of intense campaigning this year, partly due to the fact that Collins’ departure left a power vacuum on that Board resulting in a series of 2-2 failed votes due to the lack of his swing slower-growth vote. His Group 3 seat, however, was claimed by former City Commissioner Merritt Matheson, who several times over the last year railed against the restrictive policies implemented by the slow-growth majority led by Collins. Matheson particularly lamented that majority’s opposition to any funding or support of a Brightline train station downtown. The chances of that possibility got slimmer this month, when Martin County did not get its desired grant funding from the state to pursue the station without the city’s help. Matheson received 58.20 percent or 2,084 votes, of the total 3,581 cast in that race. The other candidate, Derreck Ogden ran on a strictly slow-growth platform and got 41.80 percent. The Group 1 Seat Race was a lot closer, however, with Incumbent Campbell Rich getting 50.25 percent, or 1780 of the total 3,542 votes cast. His challenger, Will Laughlin, received 49.75 percent. Because the difference was just under the state-mandated 0.5 percent, a formal recount is mandatory. While Rich consistently opposed much of Collins’ and the slow-growth majority’s actions over the past few years, Laughlin ran on a platform dedicated to slowing or stopping the growth and resisting the state’s efforts at eroding home rule. If the recount affirms Rich’s victory and with Matheson’s comeback to the Board, the remaining slow-growth commissioners may find themselves in the minority in the future. As far as the Stuart Commission’s Group 5 Seat Race, incumbent Eula R. Clarke – who’s served on the Board since 2011 – received 52.12 percent or 1,867 of the total 3,582 votes cast. Her challengers Dayne Oldenborg and Kylie Micciche got 32.08 percent and 15.80 percent respectively. Both of them had run on slower-growth platforms and the preservation of local waterways. The 2026 Primary Election in the Village of Indiantown basically routed the Council of incumbents, beginning with current Mayor Carmine Dipaolo who lost Seat 3 to Challenger Christa Miley, who received 59.38 percent of the total 832 votes cast. Dipaolo himself received 32.09 percent, while Candidate Octavius Thompson got 8.53 percent. That trend continued onto the Seat 4 Race, where former Village Councilman Anthony D. Dowling received 51.59 percent or 437 of the total 847 votes cast. Incumbent Angelina Perez got 32.11 percent, while Challenger Ana Farias received 16.29 percent. Current Seat 5 Councilwoman and Incumbent Karen Onsager fared no better, losing her reelection bid to former Village Councilwoman Janet Hernandez. While Hernandez got 63.68 percent of the total 837 votes cast, Onsager got 36.32 percent. On the other hand, the three incumbents up for reelection on the Martin County School Board successfully fended off challenges to their seats. Because the elections are non-partisan, the winners must follow the state’s 50-percent-plus-one-vote rule in order to claim victory in the Primary Election. In the District 1 Race, Incumbent Cristia Li Roberts got 49.69 percent with 14,061 votes out of a total 28,296 cast. Her challengers, Cherie White and Charles J. “Chuck” Winn, received 26.98 percent and 23.33 percent of the votes, respectively. Because Roberts fell just under the statutory minimum requirements, She will once again face White on Nov. School Board District 3 Incumbent Jen Russell fared much better, receiving 63.70 percent or 18,210 votes out of a total 28,588 cast. Her Challenger Jackie Gary Clarke got 36.30 percent. The District 4 Seat will also go to a runoff after Incumbent Amy B. Pritchett got 42.76 percent with 12,228 votes out of a total 28,599 cast. Her primary challenger was former School Board Member Anthony “Tony” Anderson who got 41.37 percent, while Challenger Milly Blanco got 15.87 percent. Pritchett will now face Anderson again in the November General Election. The Martin County incorporated towns of Jupiter Island and Sewall’s Point did not hold primary elections this year. For the Florida governor and lieutenant governor races, Byron Donalds and Jay Collins topped the crowded field of 11 candidates in the Republican Primary, with Donalds getting 48.37 percent of the local votes cast and Collins receiving 22.04 percent. In the Democratic Primary, David Jolly topped the field of six Democratic candidates, getting 69.03 percent of the total votes. His closest challenger, Dayna Marie Foster, received 11.74 percent of the vote. Donalds will will now face Jolly on Nov 3. In the Democratic Primary race for the U.S. Senator Seat vacated by Marco Rubio when he was appointed by President Donald Trump to be secretary of state, Angie Nixon defeated Alexander Vindman statewide, although the latter got 58.73 percent of the total 8,714 local votes cast. In the Republican Primary for that seat, Ashley Moody got 79 percent of the local votes cast for the four candidates, while Chris Gleason got 14.48 percent of the remaining votes. Ashley will now face Nixon in November for the final two years of Rubio’s term. As far as the Florida District 21 Democratic Primary Race, James T. Martin got 52.98 percent of the total 8,529 votes cast, with Bernard Taylor getting 47.2 percent. Martin will now face Incumbent Republican Candidate Brian Mast on Nov. According to the Ballotpedia Website that has analyzed statewide races nationally for the last three years, the incumbency reelection rate remained at 90 percent or higher in all but the 11 states of Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Kansas, Maine, Minnesota, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Virginia and Washington. The State of Florida, however, had the lowest victory rate of incumbents nationally, with only 63 percent of incumbents successfully being reelected during the same time period. Abandoned and derelict boats are piling up at Wildcat Cove off North Hutchinson Island in Fort Pierce, and residents say the vessels are creating dangerous conditions on the water.WATCH BELOW: 'Flotilla of garbage. Needs to go,' Kevin Fitzgerald tells WPTV's Tyler HatfieldKevin Fitzgerald, who regularly navigates the waterway between Wildcat Cove and Jack Island Preserve, described to WPTV’s Tyler Hatfield what he sees on the water."It's just like a boat junkyard," Fitzgerald said.Fitzgerald counted at least 15 boats in the cove, including vessels that have sunk."I see a couple of boats ahead of me where there was just one sunk, and now there's two sunk on top of each other," he said. “There's a boat a catamaran, that's on a sandbar.”Fitzgerald said navigating the area is especially dangerous after dark."Most of them don't have lights," he said. "You come up on a boat when it's dark, it's right in front of you. You got to swerve or get out of the way. You got to watch for anchor lines and different things like that."Fitzgerald called the situation dangerous."It's like a minefield," he said.His friend Bart Plymale was also on the water and shared the same concern."It's a maze," Plymale said.Plymale said he is also worried about environmental damage from the abandoned vessels."There's fuel on these boats or oil and whatever engines that are left on them, that's all ending up in the water right now," Plymale said.WPTV went looking for answers from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.FWC said enforcement action in surrounding counties and new anchoring requirements in St. Lucie County appear to be contributing factors to the influx of boats at Wildcat Cove.FWC said it is actively investigating and that officers are in contact with at-risk vessel owners to bring their boats back into compliance. The agency said citations have been issued and vessels deemed derelict are going through the legal process before removal can be authorized.Fitzgerald said he wants the cove cleared."Flotilla of garbage. At least 15 boats," Fitzgerald said.

Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin and challenger Steven Giordano will face off in the November general election after neither candidate secured the 50% threshold needed to win outright in Tuesday’s primary race, according to election results. Martin, the incumbent mayor, captured nearly 48% of the vote while Giordano received approximately 35%, forcing a runoff between the top two candidates. Third candidate Eric Strazzeri was eliminated from the race after receiving nearly 17% of the vote. Both candidates addressed how an ongoing investigation into campaign signs may have affected Tuesday’s results. The investigation has been a focal point in the mayoral campaign leading up to the primary. “If it would’ve happened earlier, I think the results would’ve swayed better to our race,” Giordano told WPTV at his election watch party at My Brother’s BBQ, where family and friends gathered to celebrate advancing to the general election. Martin acknowledged the investigation’s potential impact during a phone interview with WFLX. “I do think that had something to do with it, but I’m going to keep focused on the issues and not on other things that are not important to the campaign,” Martin said. “I’m going to keep focusing on the issues that are important to residents and demonstrate to them how I want to continue working for them over the next four years.” Martin, who has served as Port St. Lucie’s mayor, said she plans to let her track record with the city speak to voters as the campaign moves forward. The incumbent emphasized her experience leading the city and her commitment to continuing her work for residents. Giordano outlined his campaign priorities for the November race, focusing on supporting local youth programs and local businesses. I’m the people’s mayor and the people’s voice. I’m very excited to be in this position,” Giordano said. The November general election will determine who leads Port St. Lucie for the next four years. Voters will choose between Martin’s experience as the current mayor and Giordano’s vision for change in city leadership. WFLX will continue following both candidates as they campaign leading up to the November general election. Lucie County Fire District board met today to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation. After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it. The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing. Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying, "It was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate." Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September. Lucie voters are deciding Tuesday who they want to lead one of Florida's largest cities, with growth, traffic, development and the future of the city among the major issues in the mayoral race. CBS12 News sat down with incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin and challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Strazzeri ahead of Election Day, asking them the same questions about some of the biggest concerns facing Port St. Lucie and what they would do if elected. Their answers reveal different approaches to managing a city that continues to grow. Lucie's growth Giordano said he believes the city needs to slow development and focus on whether existing infrastructure can handle what is already being built. "I want to slow down the growth and make sure that our infrastructure can handle what we already have," Giordano said. He said the city needs to make sure its drainage systems, roads and traffic infrastructure can keep up with development. Giordano also said he wants the city to focus more heavily on supporting local businesses and attracting higher-paying jobs. Martin said one challenge is that many development rights were granted decades ago and cannot simply be taken away by the current City Council. "What a lot of people don't realize still is that the developer rights were granted over 20 years ago," Martin said. "Where the developers do have those rights that were granted and those entitlements, we can't make that change." Martin pointed to Rosser Lakes Preserve as an example of an area where the city was able to prevent additional development. She said a developer wanted to build 86 homes on the property, but the city instead acquired the land to preserve it as green space. Lucie has acquired more than 280 acres of green space since January 2025. Strazzeri said he supports what he calls responsible growth but believes infrastructure should be in place before communities are developed. "Our roads, our schools, our utilities, our emergency services need to be in place prior to them developing in these communities because they're playing catch up right now," Strazzeri said. Traffic All three candidates acknowledged traffic as a major issue, but offered different approaches. Giordano called traffic in St. Lucie West a "nightmare" and said he wants a new traffic study examining roadways, traffic signals and signal timing. "It takes almost 30 minutes to get from one end to the other," Giordano said of St. "That's totally unacceptable." He said the city should examine where roads could be widened, whether medians need to be removed and where other changes could improve traffic flow. Martin pointed to projects already underway, including work on Floresta Drive and Port St. Lucie Boulevard South, roundabouts in Torino and planned intersection improvements at Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway, Savona Boulevard and Gatlin Boulevard. She said roundabouts can help move vehicles more efficiently and the city is extending turn lanes where possible. "We're going to continue to look at all of our areas and do those intersection improvements so that we can keep the flow of traffic going to reduce that traffic congestion," Martin said. Strazzeri said the city needs to be "proactive and not reactive," calling for better traffic signal coordination, adaptive signal technology and road expansion where possible. "We have to ensure that the infrastructure keeps pace with the development," Strazzeri said. Who should pay for growth? The candidates also addressed concerns over whether developers are paying enough toward the infrastructure needed to support new development. Giordano said developers should be held accountable for infrastructure needs associated with their projects. "They need to pay their fair share if they're going to be coming here and developing," Giordano said, adding that if a project requires sidewalks or lights, developers should be responsible for those needs. Martin pushed back on the idea that developers are not already paying toward infrastructure. "All the developers are required to pay mobility or impact fees for roads, for parks, for law enforcement and for civic space," Martin said. She said the city periodically reviews and increases those fees, but noted state law limits how much municipalities can levy through impact and mobility fees. Strazzeri said he also believes developers should carry more of the burden associated with growth. "The developers have to pay their fair share," Strazzeri said. "This should not be pushed off to the residents." He said roads, schools, emergency services and utilities should be addressed as part of the development process. Property taxes, CDDs and housing costs Martin also addressed a distinction she said residents should understand when looking at what they pay to live in Port St. She said the city does not control housing prices or interest rates, but does control its own property tax rate. Lucie has lowered its property tax rate each year for the past 11 years, reducing the rate by 25% over that period. She also said 22% of a resident's property tax bill goes to the city, with the remainder going to other taxing authorities. Martin also addressed Community Development District assessments, or CDDs, which are common in parts of Tradition. She said those assessments are determined by their respective CDD boards, not the Port St. On housing affordability, Giordano said higher-paying jobs are an important part of making it possible for residents to afford homes. "We need to bring the jobs," Giordano said. Strazzeri acknowledged the city does not control the housing market or interest rates but said it can work on affordable housing and ensuring housing options exist for everyday workers. "Everybody deserves the right to afford a home," Strazzeri said. Giordano also tied housing affordability to the need for higher-paying jobs. He said he wants to attract investors, medical centers and technology companies to Port St. We need those $100,000 jobs for our community, Giordano said. Why do we have to travel to West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale or Miami? Strazzeri also said attracting higher-paying jobs could help residents afford to stay in the city. He said he would like to see Port St. Lucie become a technology hub rather than having residents leave for higher-paying work elsewhere. Trash collection Trash service is another issue that has generated debate in Port St. The city currently provides garbage collection once a week. Lucie voters will also get a chance to weigh in on trash service in the November general election, when a nonbinding question will ask whether residents support twice-weekly garbage pickup. Giordano said he supports allowing residents to decide service frequency and proposed creating a city-run trash operation instead of outsourcing collection. He estimated the city currently spends roughly $61 million outsourcing trash service and said he believes a city operation could provide the service for around $55 million while creating jobs. Those cost estimates are Giordano's and were not independently verified by CBS12 News. Strazzeri said he remains frustrated with trash service and also believes voters should have a say in how often their trash is collected. "We're paying more for less service, whereas previously we were paying less and getting more service," Strazzeri said. He said he has heard from residents who want twice-a-week pickup and others who prefer different service levels. The city has previously said twice-weekly collection would require more equipment and workers and would cost residents approximately $130 more per household each year. Soccer stadium and a downtown for Port St. Lucie One of the clearest differences between the candidates involves the planned minor league soccer stadium and the broader effort to create a downtown-like destination. Martin supports the project and said the stadium is intended to serve as an anchor for redevelopment on the city's east side. She said the city is not paying for the stadium itself, its operations or maintenance, or debt associated with it. "It's supposed to be the anchor to start attracting all those different uses of the retail, the shopping, the hotels to really redevelop that entire area so that we can have that walkable downtown-like destination point," Martin said. Giordano opposes the stadium and said he would try to stop it if possible. "If I can stop the soccer stadium, I will stop it," Giordano said. However, he said that if the project cannot be stopped, he would work to make the venue as profitable as possible by using it for concerts, graduations and other community events. Giordano said he does support creating a downtown and floated attracting investors and even a Seminole Hard Rock casino as possibilities. Strazzeri said he is not opposed to a downtown but does not believe it or the soccer stadium should be the city's priority right now. "I would really like to improve the roads," Strazzeri said. "I would like to bring, you know, Trader Joe's, a Topgolf, higher-paying jobs." He said Port St. Lucie should first focus on quality of life and other needs. "I'm not saying that I'm against a downtown, but right now we need to focus on other things," Strazzeri said. Water quality Water quality also came up during the candidate interviews. Giordano said he wants the city to stop chemical spraying in lakes and waterways, pointing to a fish kill at Sawgrass Lakes as an example of his concern. He attributed the deaths to spraying and said the practice would stop if he becomes mayor. Strazzeri similarly said he would prefer natural approaches, including aeration or dredging, over what he described as harsh chemicals. "I would prefer to find natural ways to fix these issues rather than using these harsh chemicals and killing the fish," Strazzeri said. Martin pointed to the city's existing water-quality programs, including the McCarty Ranch Water Quality Project, stormwater baffle boxes and other projects aimed at reducing nutrients and pollution. "We constantly have projects going that are all about water quality," Martin said. What would they prioritize in office? Martin said her top priority if reelected would continue to be public safety, followed by infrastructure, reducing traffic congestion and maintaining quality of life. She also pointed to what she considers accomplishments during her time in office, including lowering the city's millage rate, reducing city debt by more than $400 million and adding parks. Giordano said that during his first 100 days, he would focus on Flock license plate readers and red-light cameras as well as traffic patterns and signal timing. He said he would seek new traffic data to determine where the city can reduce congestion. Strazzeri said his first year would focus on increasing transparency between City Hall and residents. He proposed creating a small-business owner committee and holding quarterly town halls where residents could hear about upcoming city plans and provide feedback before decisions are made. He said he would also focus on higher-paying jobs and additional entertainment and dining options. Martin has served as Port St. Lucie's mayor for the past five years and previously served on the City Council. She was first elected in 2010 and said she has lived in Port St. Before elected office, Martin worked as a paralegal. Giordano said he has lived in Port St. Lucie since 1989, grew up and attended school in the city and has nearly 20 years of public-service experience. He said he spent about a decade with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, later worked in security at the nuclear power plant and is a local business owner. Strazzeri said he moved to Port St. He served in the Army, deployed to Iraq as a combat engineer and later transitioned into information technology and cybersecurity. He said he decided to run after his son died from cancer and his experiences led him to believe residents needed a stronger voice in local government. Why should voters choose them? Martin points to her experience. "I have the knowledge, experience, and the results-driven leadership in order to continue to make that happen, to continue to make Port St. Lucie the best it possibly can be," Martin said. Giordano describes himself as an alternative to longtime political leadership. I'm a local business owner," Giordano said. "I want to bring a different style of leadership that works for the community." Strazzeri said his campaign is centered on transparency and accountability. Lucie deserves leadership that's transparent, accountable, and independent and is only responsible to the people and not special interests," Strazzeri said. Lucie voters will make that decision Tuesday. Election Day information The Port St. Lucie mayoral race is nonpartisan, meaning candidates do not run with a political party affiliation. Polls close Tuesday at 7 p.m. If one candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, that candidate wins the mayoral race outright. If no candidate receives more than 50%, the top two vote-getters will advance to the November general election. CBS12 News will be tracking the Port St. Lucie mayoral race and election results throughout the night.

Christopher "Doc" Collins won the open Martin County Commission District 2 seat, defeating Susan O'Rourke and Althea Wiley in Tuesday's election. Because all three candidates were Republicans and no Democrat qualified for the race, it was held as a Universal Primary Contest, meaning Tuesday's vote decided the seat outright with no November general election to follow. Collins received 14,657 votes, or about 49 percent. O'Rourke received 12,065 votes, about 40 percent, and Wiley received 3,194 votes, nearly 11 percent. Collins, a chiropractor and former Stuart city commissioner and mayor, stepped down from the Stuart City Commission earlier this year to run for the county seat, a move required under the city's charter before he could qualify for another elected office. He ran largely on a platform of slow growth, calling for tighter restrictions on new development across the county. During his time on the Stuart City Commission, Collins joined two other commissioners in voting to rescind the city's agreement with Brightline for a downtown train station, a position that put him at odds with O'Rourke throughout the campaign. See also: Martin, Giordano head to November runoff for PSL mayor The campaign also had a tense moment in its final week, when Collins accused a man named Jim Gallegos of stealing his campaign signs, posting a Facebook video with trail camera footage and Apple AirTag tracking he said showed Gallegos pulling one of his signs from the ground. Gallegos denied stealing anything, saying he removed roughly 30 signs for various candidates, including some of Collins', at a property owner's request. The dispute also drew in Derreck Ogden, a Stuart City Commission candidate, who publicly confronted Gallegos over the signs. Collins did not respond to CBS12's requests for an interview at any point during the campaign, and did not respond to a request for comment following the results. Collins will replace outgoing Commissioner Stacey Hetherington, who chose not to seek re-election. O'Rourke, a former traffic engineer who previously served on Stuart's Local Planning Agency, ran on managing growth and easing traffic congestion. Her candidacy became the subject of a legal dispute earlier this year after Collins filed a challenge seeking to have her removed from the ballot, arguing she was not legally a Martin County resident when she qualified. A judge dismissed that challenge in July. Wiley, an author, Realtor and chef, ran on affordability, pointing to rising housing costs and other everyday expenses facing county residents. The Brightline project remains a live issue for the incoming commission. Plans call for a roughly 10,200-square-foot station, a 660-foot platform, parking and other rail infrastructure, with completion targeted for 2029. Martin County has sought $69.3 million in federal funding for the project, and the commission is expected to keep playing a role in how it moves forward. Collins will also take office as the county braces for a possible November ballot measure, Amendment 3, which would expand the state's homestead exemption and cut into local government revenue. Commissioners previously voiced their concerns about the amendment during a public meeting in July, where the Martin County Fire Chief told the county about cuts he may have to make if the amendment passes in November.

Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. The Kings Academy made headlines last year when the school announced it would leave the Florida High School Athletic Association and enter the Sunshine State Athletic Association for the first time. The school says the move best fits its core values and beliefs.Head Coach Dan Burack said the team's mindset reflects that philosophy.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:"Really just grinding together and being selfless and selling out for each other and what's good for the team, not what is good for me," Burack said.The Kings Academy has talent on both sides of the ball, and the offensive line wasted no time proving it, opening holes and lanes that helped fuel a standout performance in week zero.Running back Roman Driggers, one of Palm Beach County's best-kept secrets, rushed for over 150 yards and two touchdowns in week zero."Honestly, it felt amazing. I couldn't have asked for anything better. Just being surrounded by teammates that really help me and pushed me through that game," Driggers said.Driggers said he knew early the game would be something special."I knew that game was going to be special after the first drive; we came out with intensity. First drive we scored, and honestly, I give props to my o-linemen for getting me the blocks and giving me those good reads, and no matter what it is all glory to God," Driggers said.Standing about 5'5" and 140 pounds, Driggers has been overlooked, but he is viewed as one of the biggest steals in the Sunshine State. Burack said he has taken notice of more than just what Driggers does on the field."Watching him lead, watching him battle through adversities that he's had, he's an amazing young man; he's got a great family," Burack said.Driggers said he and his brother are focused on letting their play speak for itself — and he is ready for what is ahead."I'm ready; there are no nerves whatsoever, just ready to bring the intensity on Fridays," Driggers said.

The Miami Dolphins wide receiver room could receive a boost soon with the return of rookie Chris Bell, who has been sidelined for much of training camp while recovering from a knee injury sustained in college.Bell has participated in two practices this week after being activated from the non-football injury list on Monday. The third-round draft pick out of Louisville — who at one point was projected to go late in the first round — was recovering from a torn anterior cruciate ligament suffered last November.WATCH BELOW: Chris Bell potentially adds another option for Dolphins' receiving corps"It feels great," Bell said Tuesday. "I haven't played football in a little minute. So my first practice, I was a little nervous. But I'm just out there getting my feet wet and getting back to the swing of things."Bell, wearing a red noncontact jersey, has participated in individual work the past two days and ran a few routes during the 11-on-11 team period on Tuesday. He said he doesn't know yet whether he'll be ready in time for Miami's season opener at Las Vegas on Sept. 13.The Dolphins have been careful not to rush him back into action. He’s been running and cutting while ramping up for his return but needs to be cleared for tackling.Coach Jeff Hafley said Bell will not participate in Thursday's joint practice with the New York Giants or play in Saturday's preseason game.“He worked really hard at it, but there's still a lot of steps to go, so let’s just see how he progresses," Hafley said Tuesday. "I mean, with any injury, could there be setbacks? I think everyone’s really excited that he’s back. He's got to get in football shape. He's got to get in some timing and rhythm with the quarterbacks, but it’s good to have him out there."Miami drafted three receivers in April — Bell, Caleb Douglas in the third round and Kevin Coleman Jr. in the fifth — after moving on from stars Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle.Douglas has been a standout during training camp and has emerged as a top target for new quarterback Malik Willis, and Coleman had a strong practice Tuesday with a pair of touchdown catches. Bell, a bigger-framed 228-pound receiver, could give Miami another solid option to build around in the future."I feel like we've got a good receiver room," Bell said. "The young guys are coming along, right with the vets. I would say we've got a good chance to be something special, so y'all just wait and see."Hafley said Bell's physicality stood out when watching his film from Louisville, where he had 2,166 yards receiving and 12 touchdowns.Bell said he uses his size to his advantage, knowing most defensive backs are smaller than him, adding that he takes as much pride in blocking as he does catching passes.That's the attitude Hafley wants each of his receivers to have."Our receivers are going to block," Hafley said.

Students at West Boca High School are chasing two goals at once: building careers through the School District of Palm Beach County's Choice Programs and becoming the first football team in Palm Beach County history to win three straight state championships.The Choice Programs allow students from pre-K through 12th grade to pursue a wide array of career and technical education programs. For three West Boca Bulls football players, those programs are shaping who they are both in and out of school.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Offensive lineman Gavin Ciagel is studying digital design. Defensive back Mario Davis is enrolled in culinary arts. Defensive end Ma'Karion Owens is pursuing computer science.Each student has his own reason for joining."When I come to school and do different things on the computers, like different projects and make different stuff, it just brings me back to my regular state," Owens said."You get to show yourself and be creative, and throughout the years, I just feel like I got so much better at just using my brain and being creative," Ciagel said."Just trying different foods, it helps you when you're older, going home, you know how to cook and take care of your body," Davis said.For Davis, a sophomore, that mindset of keeping his body intact through food and nutrition is also helping him stand out for the Bulls as they look to make history. West Boca is chasing its third straight state championship — something no Palm Beach County team has ever done."It feels good. I feel like we have the team to do that. We practice hard, and we are disciplined," Davis said.That discipline will be tested this season. West Boca faces one of the toughest schedules in the state, including matchups with fellow state champions Cardinal Newman, a state championship rematch with American Heritage, and an Adidas Football Classic showdown with Georgia powerhouse Grayson.Ciagel said he embraces the pressure that comes with leading the offensive line."I'm the leader of the o-line, and I like to lead the o-line to the next state championship, and yeah, it's a lot of pressure, but I just got to get it done," Ciagel said.Owens said the schedule is just another obstacle to overcome."Everything in life is going to be hard; nothing in life is easy, so with this schedule it's just another hump and adversity that we have to overcome," Owens said.When asked what his best meal is, Davis did not hesitate."I can make steak, alfredo, spaghetti. I don't know; I can make a lot of things at home," Davis said.

A 23-year-old Fort Pierce man is behind bars for firing a gun through a bathroom door during a domestic disturbance and fleeing before being taken into custody hours later, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said. Deputies said they responded to a home on the 1700 block of Wyoming Avenue at around 11:30 a.m. Sunday for a reported domestic disturbance. During the incident, the victim locked herself inside a bathroom. Hsu allegedly fired a round through the bathroom door before fleeing the residence in a car. Fort Pierce police later located the car near Porpoise Beach, prompting an extensive search of the area. While the search was underway, detectives with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators said they executed a search warrant at the residence. At around 2:30 p.m., Hsu's family located him and alerted a passing Fort Pierce police officer. Hsu was taken into custody without incident and a firearm was recovered. Hsu is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on no bond. He faces multiple felony charges, including attempted felony murder, kidnapping, tampering with a witness, simple battery and grand theft of a motor vehicle. Authorities said the incident was isolated and there is no ongoing threat to the public. The investigation remains active.

A Florida woman took a scam beyond the phone lines, showing up at a Martin County resident’s door pretending to represent a bank and demanding the victim’s credit card on Monday. According to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office , Monique Love Turnbull, of Miami, was seen at a victim’s doorstep claiming the victim’s bank account had been compromised. Turnbull asked for the victim’s credit card and said she would dispose of it. As law enforcement investigated, deputies were alerted to another call identifying Turnbull in a separate case. Body camera video shows deputies pulling Turnbull over and asking her to step out of the car. See also: Palm Beach County clerk arrested on 5 felonies involving child, suspended by DeSantis The arresting deputy then tells Turnbull she is under arrest for fraud before placing her in handcuffs. The sheriff’s office is warning residents never to allow someone into their home if the person was not scheduled to visit. Residents should also never hand over credit cards, cash, gold or other valuables to someone who shows up unexpectedly. MCSO says anyone who comes to a resident’s home claiming to represent a bank or financial institution and asking for valuables should be treated with suspicion. Residents are urged to call 911.

A Miami woman was arrested in Martin County after allegedly posing as a bank representative to scam residents out of thousands of dollars, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. Newly released aerial footage shows sheriff's deputies following the suspect, 32-year-old Monquie Turnbull, on I-95 before stopping her vehicle. Body camera footage captured Turnbull exiting her car and being questioned by deputies. "You’re going to be placed under arrest," a deputy said in the footage. Budensiek said Turnbull drove from Miami to Martin County, where she approached two residents, claiming their debit cards were compromised and needed to be turned in for replacement. "They stated that their card was compromised and they needed to turn their card in and they were going to replace their card for them," Budensiek said. One resident was scammed out of hundreds of dollars. "The victim notices pretty quick that not long after the suspect left, there’s $3,180 now missing from her account," Budensiek said. While investigators were handling that case, they received a second 911 call matching the suspect’s description and vehicle. Deputies began their search. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "She was located as she came eastbound on Bridge Road and then she turned around and was going westbound on Bridge Road, which is the video you saw her getting arrested," Budensiek said. Officials later discovered Turnbull had entered the jail with about $3,200 hidden in one of her body parts. "She took our first victim’s card, withdrew $3,180, and that’s the exact amount recovered from inside her person in the jail," Budensiek said. The sheriff urged residents to be cautious if someone comes to their home claiming to be from a bank and asking for credit cards. "This particular incidence, this was all the money that this lady had, this was her rent money, it was everything that she had, and she handed it over to a scammer," Budensiek said. The sheriff is asking anyone who may have been a victim to contact authorities. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

A former Fraternal Order of Eagles secretary allegedly spent nearly $419,000 of the group's money on everything from guns and liquor to DUI fees and a LEGOs. According to Indian River County Sheriff's Office , Robert John Davison served of Aerie 4374 Fraternal Order of Eagles from February 2015 until November 2024, when he stopped showing up. The investigation began after a representative was sent to the chapter by the Grand Aerie to examine why membership and the organization's finances were declining. After reviewing expenses, he told deputies that he discovered that Davison had been using the organization's debit card for personal purchases that had not been authorized. The organization later hired forensic accounting firm Clay Price & Associates, P.A. , to review its financial records. See also: Palm Beach County clerk arrested on 5 felonies involving child, suspended by DeSantis On Feb. 24, 2025, the firm reported that Davison had used $418,899.26 in organization funds for personal expenses dating back to 2017, according to the investigation. The alleged spending included: $4,463.52 in personal court payments, including child support and DUI-related fees. $8,791.14 on firearms, ammunition, personal purchases and an NRA membership. $55,175.40 on personal bills, including credit cards, vehicle payments, utilities and cellphone bills. $115,087.49 in ATM withdrawals and associated fees that investigators say were outside the secretary's authorized duties. $9,861.27 in transfers to Davison's personal Cash App account. At least $2,461.37 in purchases for Davison's personal LEGO business. $16,038.66 in unauthorized flights and lodging. $5,930.98 in rideshare expenses. $2,476.43 in personal fuel purchases. $35,094.53 in personal grocery and liquor store purchases. Investigators say the organization’s Constitution and Statutes did not authorize the ATM withdrawals, travel expenses or other personal purchases. The current trustee chairman, and the current secretary, reportedly verified that the debit card charges were outside Davison’s duties and were not authorized by the organization. Investigators say receipts and transaction records supporting the alleged criminal activity were collected as evidence. Davison is accused of embezzlement involving a value of $100,000 or more.

The sheriff’s office said its deputies are at the scene searching for the source of the gunfire, and at this time, there is no indication that a crime occurred, but that could change as the search continues. Before the report was received, the school had initiated preparations for its alternative rainy day dismissal procedure.
