Travelers flying in and out of Palm Beach County will now see a new three-letter code on their tickets and baggage tags.The airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport officially changed from PBI to DJT on Tuesday, according to the Palm Beach County Department of Airports.The airport's website is also transitioning to flydjt.org.The International Air Transport Association, or IATA, code is used by airlines and passengers for flight bookings, reservations, check-ins and baggage tracking. Travelers should now search for DJT when making travel arrangements involving the airport.The new code follows the airport's name change from Palm Beach International Airport to President Donald J. Trump International Airport, which took effect July 9.According to the county, the name change was required under state legislation signed into law on March 30.The Palm Beach County Department of Airports said it worked with federal agencies, airlines and other airport partners ahead of the code transition.Despite the new name and airport code, officials said travelers should not notice any changes to their experience. The transition does not impact flights, airport services or passenger operations.The change also does not affect the airport's ownership, governance or operational control. The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners will continue overseeing the airport's policies, finances and strategic decisions.Travelers with upcoming flights should look for the DJT airport code instead of PBI when booking flights, checking reservations or tracking baggage.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office has identified the woman shot and killed Sunday morning in Vero Beach as 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic. Kriskewic was found with an apparent gunshot wound in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street Sunday morning. Despite life-saving measures by deputies, she was pronounced dead at a trauma center.The sheriff's office said there was a delay in releasing the victim's name because several out-of-state next of kin needed to be located and notified.Detectives are treating the case as a domestic violence homicide and continue searching for 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian, who has been identified as a person of interest. Investigators believe Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship.Sheriff Eric Flowers said a nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle, who should be considered armed and dangerous and may have fled the area."If you encounter this person, don't approach him," Flowers warned. "It's possible that he could harm other people or himself."Close friends remembered Kriskewic as someone who was beautiful inside and out — a mother, hairdresser and author who was loved by many.The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

Lucie voters are deciding Tuesday who they want to lead one of Florida's largest cities, with growth, traffic, development and the future of the city among the major issues in the mayoral race. CBS12 News sat down with incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin and challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Strazzeri ahead of Election Day, asking them the same questions about some of the biggest concerns facing Port St. Lucie and what they would do if elected. Their answers reveal different approaches to managing a city that continues to grow. Lucie's growth Giordano said he believes the city needs to slow development and focus on whether existing infrastructure can handle what is already being built. "I want to slow down the growth and make sure that our infrastructure can handle what we already have," Giordano said. He said the city needs to make sure its drainage systems, roads and traffic infrastructure can keep up with development. Giordano also said he wants the city to focus more heavily on supporting local businesses and attracting higher-paying jobs. Martin said one challenge is that many development rights were granted decades ago and cannot simply be taken away by the current City Council. "What a lot of people don't realize still is that the developer rights were granted over 20 years ago," Martin said. "Where the developers do have those rights that were granted and those entitlements, we can't make that change." Martin pointed to Rosser Lakes Preserve as an example of an area where the city was able to prevent additional development. She said a developer wanted to build 86 homes on the property, but the city instead acquired the land to preserve it as green space. Lucie has acquired more than 280 acres of green space since January 2025. Strazzeri said he supports what he calls responsible growth but believes infrastructure should be in place before communities are developed. "Our roads, our schools, our utilities, our emergency services need to be in place prior to them developing in these communities because they're playing catch up right now," Strazzeri said. Traffic All three candidates acknowledged traffic as a major issue, but offered different approaches. Giordano called traffic in St. Lucie West a "nightmare" and said he wants a new traffic study examining roadways, traffic signals and signal timing. "It takes almost 30 minutes to get from one end to the other," Giordano said of St. "That's totally unacceptable." He said the city should examine where roads could be widened, whether medians need to be removed and where other changes could improve traffic flow. Martin pointed to projects already underway, including work on Floresta Drive and Port St. Lucie Boulevard South, roundabouts in Torino and planned intersection improvements at Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway, Savona Boulevard and Gatlin Boulevard. She said roundabouts can help move vehicles more efficiently and the city is extending turn lanes where possible. "We're going to continue to look at all of our areas and do those intersection improvements so that we can keep the flow of traffic going to reduce that traffic congestion," Martin said. Strazzeri said the city needs to be "proactive and not reactive," calling for better traffic signal coordination, adaptive signal technology and road expansion where possible. "We have to ensure that the infrastructure keeps pace with the development," Strazzeri said. Who should pay for growth? The candidates also addressed concerns over whether developers are paying enough toward the infrastructure needed to support new development. Giordano said developers should be held accountable for infrastructure needs associated with their projects. "They need to pay their fair share if they're going to be coming here and developing," Giordano said, adding that if a project requires sidewalks or lights, developers should be responsible for those needs. Martin pushed back on the idea that developers are not already paying toward infrastructure. "All the developers are required to pay mobility or impact fees for roads, for parks, for law enforcement and for civic space," Martin said. She said the city periodically reviews and increases those fees, but noted state law limits how much municipalities can levy through impact and mobility fees. Strazzeri said he also believes developers should carry more of the burden associated with growth. "The developers have to pay their fair share," Strazzeri said. "This should not be pushed off to the residents." He said roads, schools, emergency services and utilities should be addressed as part of the development process. Property taxes, CDDs and housing costs Martin also addressed a distinction she said residents should understand when looking at what they pay to live in Port St. She said the city does not control housing prices or interest rates, but does control its own property tax rate. Lucie has lowered its property tax rate each year for the past 11 years, reducing the rate by 25% over that period. She also said 22% of a resident's property tax bill goes to the city, with the remainder going to other taxing authorities. Martin also addressed Community Development District assessments, or CDDs, which are common in parts of Tradition. She said those assessments are determined by their respective CDD boards, not the Port St. On housing affordability, Giordano said higher-paying jobs are an important part of making it possible for residents to afford homes. "We need to bring the jobs," Giordano said. Strazzeri acknowledged the city does not control the housing market or interest rates but said it can work on affordable housing and ensuring housing options exist for everyday workers. "Everybody deserves the right to afford a home," Strazzeri said. Giordano also tied housing affordability to the need for higher-paying jobs. He said he wants to attract investors, medical centers and technology companies to Port St. We need those $100,000 jobs for our community, Giordano said. Why do we have to travel to West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale or Miami? Strazzeri also said attracting higher-paying jobs could help residents afford to stay in the city. He said he would like to see Port St. Lucie become a technology hub rather than having residents leave for higher-paying work elsewhere. Trash collection Trash service is another issue that has generated debate in Port St. The city currently provides garbage collection once a week. Lucie voters will also get a chance to weigh in on trash service in the November general election, when a nonbinding question will ask whether residents support twice-weekly garbage pickup. Giordano said he supports allowing residents to decide service frequency and proposed creating a city-run trash operation instead of outsourcing collection. He estimated the city currently spends roughly $61 million outsourcing trash service and said he believes a city operation could provide the service for around $55 million while creating jobs. Those cost estimates are Giordano's and were not independently verified by CBS12 News. Strazzeri said he remains frustrated with trash service and also believes voters should have a say in how often their trash is collected. "We're paying more for less service, whereas previously we were paying less and getting more service," Strazzeri said. He said he has heard from residents who want twice-a-week pickup and others who prefer different service levels. The city has previously said twice-weekly collection would require more equipment and workers and would cost residents approximately $130 more per household each year. Soccer stadium and a downtown for Port St. Lucie One of the clearest differences between the candidates involves the planned minor league soccer stadium and the broader effort to create a downtown-like destination. Martin supports the project and said the stadium is intended to serve as an anchor for redevelopment on the city's east side. She said the city is not paying for the stadium itself, its operations or maintenance, or debt associated with it. "It's supposed to be the anchor to start attracting all those different uses of the retail, the shopping, the hotels to really redevelop that entire area so that we can have that walkable downtown-like destination point," Martin said. Giordano opposes the stadium and said he would try to stop it if possible. "If I can stop the soccer stadium, I will stop it," Giordano said. However, he said that if the project cannot be stopped, he would work to make the venue as profitable as possible by using it for concerts, graduations and other community events. Giordano said he does support creating a downtown and floated attracting investors and even a Seminole Hard Rock casino as possibilities. Strazzeri said he is not opposed to a downtown but does not believe it or the soccer stadium should be the city's priority right now. "I would really like to improve the roads," Strazzeri said. "I would like to bring, you know, Trader Joe's, a Topgolf, higher-paying jobs." He said Port St. Lucie should first focus on quality of life and other needs. "I'm not saying that I'm against a downtown, but right now we need to focus on other things," Strazzeri said. Water quality Water quality also came up during the candidate interviews. Giordano said he wants the city to stop chemical spraying in lakes and waterways, pointing to a fish kill at Sawgrass Lakes as an example of his concern. He attributed the deaths to spraying and said the practice would stop if he becomes mayor. Strazzeri similarly said he would prefer natural approaches, including aeration or dredging, over what he described as harsh chemicals. "I would prefer to find natural ways to fix these issues rather than using these harsh chemicals and killing the fish," Strazzeri said. Martin pointed to the city's existing water-quality programs, including the McCarty Ranch Water Quality Project, stormwater baffle boxes and other projects aimed at reducing nutrients and pollution. "We constantly have projects going that are all about water quality," Martin said. What would they prioritize in office? Martin said her top priority if reelected would continue to be public safety, followed by infrastructure, reducing traffic congestion and maintaining quality of life. She also pointed to what she considers accomplishments during her time in office, including lowering the city's millage rate, reducing city debt by more than $400 million and adding parks. Giordano said that during his first 100 days, he would focus on Flock license plate readers and red-light cameras as well as traffic patterns and signal timing. He said he would seek new traffic data to determine where the city can reduce congestion. Strazzeri said his first year would focus on increasing transparency between City Hall and residents. He proposed creating a small-business owner committee and holding quarterly town halls where residents could hear about upcoming city plans and provide feedback before decisions are made. He said he would also focus on higher-paying jobs and additional entertainment and dining options. Martin has served as Port St. Lucie's mayor for the past five years and previously served on the City Council. She was first elected in 2010 and said she has lived in Port St. Before elected office, Martin worked as a paralegal. Giordano said he has lived in Port St. Lucie since 1989, grew up and attended school in the city and has nearly 20 years of public-service experience. He said he spent about a decade with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, later worked in security at the nuclear power plant and is a local business owner. Strazzeri said he moved to Port St. He served in the Army, deployed to Iraq as a combat engineer and later transitioned into information technology and cybersecurity. He said he decided to run after his son died from cancer and his experiences led him to believe residents needed a stronger voice in local government. Why should voters choose them? Martin points to her experience. "I have the knowledge, experience, and the results-driven leadership in order to continue to make that happen, to continue to make Port St. Lucie the best it possibly can be," Martin said. Giordano describes himself as an alternative to longtime political leadership. I'm a local business owner," Giordano said. "I want to bring a different style of leadership that works for the community." Strazzeri said his campaign is centered on transparency and accountability. Lucie deserves leadership that's transparent, accountable, and independent and is only responsible to the people and not special interests," Strazzeri said. Lucie voters will make that decision Tuesday. Election Day information The Port St. Lucie mayoral race is nonpartisan, meaning candidates do not run with a political party affiliation. Polls close Tuesday at 7 p.m. If one candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, that candidate wins the mayoral race outright. If no candidate receives more than 50%, the top two vote-getters will advance to the November general election. CBS12 News will be tracking the Port St. Lucie mayoral race and election results throughout the night.

Fort Pierce City Council, from left, Arnold Gaines, Chris Dzadovsky, Mayor Linda Hudson, Curtis Johnson and Michael Broderick. FORT PIERCE – Salary terms are set to be negotiated with former St. Lucie County attorney Daniel S. McIntyre selected Monday to serve as interim Fort Pierce city attorney when incumbent Sara Hedges is scheduled to end her tenure Sept. A last-minute motion from Commissioner Michael Broderick to keep Hedges on board until Dec. 31 failed Monday night, getting support only from Mayor Linda Hudson who temporarily relinquished the mayor’s gavel to second and vote for Broderick’s motion. However, the motion failed on a 2-3 vote, with Commissioners Chris Dzadovsky, Arnold Gaines and Curtis Johnson Jr. saying they would continue supporting seeking new leadership in the city attorney’s office. Hedges had been an assistant city attorney before being tapped to head the legal team in September 2023. Her tenure became an issue in May, following controversy over the handling of a wage garnishment for an unpaid credit card account owed by Johnna Morris, city finance director. City officials also had suggested friction existed between Hedges and City Manager Richard Chess over Chess’ wish to consult outside counsel in the matter and Hedges’ claim that Chess was excluding her from staff employment issues. McIntyre has 43 years of local government law experience, serving three years as assistant Marin County attorney from 1982-85, then the chief legal counsel for St. Lucie County from 1985-2025. He has a bachelor’s degree from University of Miami and a law degree from Wake Forest School of Law. City officials said McIntyre has stepped in multiple times over the years to act as Fort Pierce interim city attorney when a vacancy has occurred Broderick Monday proposed extending Hedges’ engagement through year’s end, saying the city faces several thorny development issues that would profit by having Hedges’ institutional experience available. But once Broderick’s motion failed, Mayor Hudson agreed to support McIntyre’s appointment, with only Broderick voting no. The city’s Human Resources Department had also offered the name of John J. Anastasio, one-time counsel for former Port Saint Lucie Mayor JoAnn Faiella, as another possible choice for the interim appointment. Your comment has been submitted. The City of Stuart has been awarded $79 million in federal funding to replace the aging St. Lucie River Railroad Bridge as part of a massive $5.3 billion nationwide investment in rail safety and infrastructure announced by U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy on Tuesday.The grant, part of the National Railroad Partnership Program, will fund the replacement of the 100-year-old single-track bridge with a modern double-track structure featuring dramatically improved clearances for boats and vessels navigating the Okeechobee Waterway. Florida received a total of $496 million from the program, with the Stuart bridge project representing the second-largest allocation in the state.The new bridge will increase horizontal clearance from 50 feet to approximately 90 feet, while vertical clearance will jump from just 6.5 feet to 17.75 feet when in the closed position. These improvements will allow more than 90% of vessels to pass without requiring the bridge to open, significantly reducing delays for marine traffic on the federal navigation channel."Anyone who's spent time on the St. Lucie River knows that century-old bridge is too low, sitting at 6 feet, too narrow, and stuck in the closed position more often than it should be," said Congressman Brian Mast. "It's a daily headache for boaters and a safety risk for everyone who shares that corridor."The bridge serves both Brightline passenger trains and Florida East Coast Railway freight operations, making it a critical piece of infrastructure for the region's transportation network. The replacement project is expected to improve safety, reduce vehicle collisions at grade crossings, and encourage more people to use passenger rail instead of driving.The Stuart project is part of what the Trump administration is calling the "Golden Age of Rail," with the $5.3 billion investment targeting rail safety upgrades nationwide. The funding will improve over 1,000 grade crossings across the country and close more than 30 dangerous crossings. Grade crossings are the second leading cause of rail-related deaths in the United States, with more than 2,000 incidents and 200 fatalities occurring annually at these intersections.Other Florida projects receiving funding include $356 million for the Florida Department of Transportation to upgrade up to 910 highway-rail grade crossings statewide, $57 million for a new Brightline station in Cocoa, and $4 million for Jacksonville's Amtrak station relocation project.The total cost of the Stuart bridge replacement is estimated at $262 million. Combined with a previous $130 million federal grant awarded in 2023, the project now has approximately $209 million in federal funding committed.Construction timelines and additional project details have not yet been announced by the City of Stuart.

A 17-year-old Boynton Beach teen has been arrested in connection with the fatal shooting of 19-year-old Nigel Beckford, police announced.The teen faces charges of first-degree murder with a firearm and discharging a firearm from a vehicle in the death of Beckford. The shooting occurred just before 5 p.m. on Saturday, August 8, in the area of 100 Northwest 8th Avenue. The Boynton Beach Police Department's shot detection system alerted officers to multiple gunshots in the area, while dispatch simultaneously received several 911 calls reporting that a man had been shot.Officers working an off-duty detail at nearby Sara Sims Park responded immediately and found Beckford suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. Though conscious at the scene, Beckford was able to provide only limited information to officers before being rushed to a local hospital for emergency surgery. He later became unresponsive and died from his injuries.Police say the preliminary investigation revealed the suspect fired multiple rounds from a vehicle before fleeing the scene. Using license plate readers, detectives quickly identified a suspect vehicle and located it on Quantum Lakes Drive, though it was found empty. No suspects were found after an extensive search of the area.Through additional investigative leads, detectives identified a second suspect vehicle and obtained multiple search warrants, which they executed with SWAT team assistance.The teen was arrested by U.S. He is currently being held at the Juvenile Assessment Center while the investigation continues.

Palm Beach County Clerk of Court Michael Caruso was arrested Tuesday morning and immediately suspended from office by Governor Ron DeSantis on five felony child sex abuse charges.According to the arrest warrant and affidavit filed in Orange County Circuit Court, Caruso, 67, faces charges of kidnapping, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious exhibition, luring or enticing a child, and child abuse causing mental injury.During a recorded interview with Orange County law enforcement, the victim detailed multiple incidents spanning nearly a year. The child disclosed that around November 2024, Caruso took him fishing alone at a pond, touching him inappropriately.The most serious allegations center on a seven-day Royal Caribbean cruise aboard the Icon of the Seas that Caruso purchased for at least 10 family members in August 2025. Court documents state that while the ship was in international waters, Caruso separated the victim from other adults and engaged in inappropriate acts with the child.When confronted by family members in December 2025, Caruso made several partial admissions while denying the most serious allegations.Court documents reveal Caruso made threatening statements to his family, saying: "If you tell anyone I will get arrested. You tell anyone I'm going to jail." He also offered not to return to Orange County and suggested the matter didn't need to be reported.During a February 2026 recorded conversation with law enforcement, Caruso claimed the allegations were "impossible" because sexual deviation is directed toward only one sex, and since he's attracted to women, he couldn't be a sex offender.The victim has been receiving therapeutic services since April 2026 due to trauma from the alleged incidents.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement conducted the investigation with assistance from other agencies. FDLE is now overseeing the immediate transition of Caruso from office and ensuring no files or records are removed from the clerk's office.Caruso's suspension prohibits him from performing any official duties, receiving pay, or accessing any privileges of public office.The Palm Beach County Clerk of Court's office sent WPTV this statement Tuesday morning: This morning, our office was notified that Clerk Mike Caruso was arrested on serious criminal charges. We are awaiting additional information from the Governor’s office on next steps.While this is surprising news for our entire team, it does not change who we are at the Clerk’s office or our commitment to the community and customers we serve.For decades, the Clerk’s office in Palm Beach County has consistently stood for professionalism and outstanding service for our customers. That focus remains for every one of our 650 employees.Caruso will be transported to the Orange County Jail and held without bond pending first appearance. According to Attorney General James Uthmeier, more charges are expected and the case is being prosecuted by Special Counsel Rita Peters and Senior Assistant Statewide Prosecutor Lauryn Day in the Ninth Judicial Circuit.Caruso was appointed to the position in August 2025 by Governor Ron DeSantis, following seven years of service in the Florida House of Representatives. He is running for election in November to retain his position, but his name is not on today's primary ballot since he is running uncontested.The investigation remains ongoing, and additional details will be provided when available.

Despite calls to eliminate most mail voting, President Donald Trump voted by mail in Tuesday’s Florida Republican primary, Scripps News has learned.White House spokesperson Olivia Wales defended Trump’s use of a mail ballot despite his broader opposition to voting outside of in-person polling places, calling it a “non-story.”Earlier this year, Trump signed an executive order that would require the U.S. Postal Service to send ballots only to addresses preauthorized by the government.RELATED STORY | Trump administration urges Supreme Court to allow order targeting mail-in voting before midtermsFederal courts have temporarily blocked the executive order.Trump also has pushed to eliminate no-excuse mail voting while allowing exemptions for some voters through the SAVE America Act. His proposal also would require voters to include a copy of their identification with their ballot.“As President Trump has said, the SAVE America Act has commonsense exceptions for Americans to use mail-in ballots for illness, disability, military, or travel — but universal mail-in voting should not be allowed because it’s highly susceptible to fraud,” Wales said. “As everyone knows, the president is a resident of Palm Beach and participates in Florida elections, but he obviously primarily lives at the White House in Washington.”Trump has not been to Florida in months.Tuesday’s election was not the first time Trump voted by mail in Florida. Earlier this year, he cast a mail ballot in a special election.Since losing the 2020 election, Trump has repeatedly questioned election results in states that allow mail voting and do not require voter identification. Multiple audits and reviews found no evidence of widespread fraud, though officials identified isolated cases of illegal voting.RELATED STORY | Mail-in ballots will keep their grace period under new Supreme Court rulingSeveral states expanded mail voting access in 2020, extending early voting periods and adopting other measures to make voting from home easier during the COVID-19 pandemic.The United States Democracy Center said 31% of voters cast ballots by mail in the 2024 election.

A Republican attempting to become Florida's first Black governor faces a crowded field Tuesday while Democrats wage primary battles for a reduced pool of left-leaning seats under redrawn congressional maps.U.S. Byron Donalds is banking on President Donald Trump ’s endorsement in hopes of securing the Republican nomination and advance to the fall election. Jay Collins and political newcomer James Fishback.Democrats' leading candidate for governor is David Jolly, a former Republican congressman who switched parties last year.Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a leading conservative figure who has clashed and collaborated with Trump over the years, is barred from running for a third consecutive term.RELATED STORY | Democrats score win in Florida district home to Mar-a-Lago, defying TrumpThe primaries are giving final form to a November ballot whose races will test Trump’s grip on his adopted state and Democrats' ability to resurrect Florida as a national political battleground. Florida has moved notably to the right since Trump won his first election in 2016, though Democrats hope to regain ground from his slumping popularity ratings.Two Democrats are battling for nomination in a U.S. Senate special election to complete Marco Rubio’s term after he became Trump's secretary of state last year. Progressive state lawmake r Angie Nixon matches up against retired Army Lt. Alex Vindman, a former National Security Council official who testified in Trump's first impeachment case in 2019.Meanwhile, Sen. Ashley Moody, the DeSantis appointee currently holding the seat, appears in a strong position as she seeks the Republican nomination with Trump's endorsement for the term's final two years.For Congress, Tuesday's biggest nominating fight involves longtime Democratic U.S. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, former U.S. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick and others in a redrawn south Florida district.Wasserman Schultz, who is white, wants voters in the new, plurality Black district to grant her a 12th term. Cherfilus-McCormick is seeking a comeback after resigning earlier this year under a pending federal indictment and threat of House ethics sanctions.Donalds is trying to make history — and Jolly, tooThere have been three elected Black governors in U.S. Yet the 47-year-old Donalds is more likely to tout his conservative credentials than the possibility of joining that select group.He promises to push tax cuts, overhaul Florida's insurance regulations to lower consumer costs and seek greater price transparency from health care providers.“The people of Florida want to make sure that the Florida dream is alive and well into the future,” he said recently. “Affordability is a problem for all Floridians. It doesn't matter what your politics are. It doesn't matter what the color of your skin is.”Trump has had an inconsistent record on picks for governor in primaries this year, and a strong showing by Donalds would leave him, and Republicans in general, in a more commanding position for November. Though DeSantis coasted to reelection in 2022, he squeaked into office in 2018 by little more of 32,000 ballots out of 8.1 million cast.Jolly is hoping ultimately to prove a party-switching former Republican can actually carry the Democratic banner in a state where that's failed before. Democrats nominated former Republican Gov. Charlie Crist in 2022 only to see him lose by nearly 20 percentage points to DeSantis.Can Democrats make the Senate race interesting?Moody, a former state attorney general tapped for Rubio's seat in 2025, is in a strong position seeking the GOP nomination. DeSantis, when he appointed her, praised her as a law-and-order prosecutor ready to help Trump “shut the border,” tame inflation, and overhaul a federal bureaucracy “run amok.”RELATED STORY | 'Because I'm president': Trump defends casting mail‑in ballot ahead of electionDemocrats face a familiar theme of 2026 primaries, with the progressive Nixon confronting Vindman from the party's center-left establishment. Vindman's testimony in 2019 was notable in the Democrat-led House impeachment case that led to Trump's acquittal in the Republican-led Senate. Trump ousted Vindman afterward.Floridians haven’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 2012.Wasserman Schultz runs in a new plurality Black districtServing in Congress since 2005 , she faces a new district — thanks to DeSantis' successful push for new congressional maps amid the national redistricting battle intended to boost Trump's midterm election prospects.It’s not the first time Wasserman Schultz has had to convince new voters after Republicans tinkered with boundaries. But this time she’s the only white candidate in a plurality Black district. The redrawn Florida 20th is concentrated in the most Democratic and diverse parts of Broward County, and doesn't include her hometown of Weston, west of Fort Lauderdale.Her four Black primary opponents — including Cherfilus-McCormick — have argued the district requires a Black representative. Wasserman Schultz disagrees.“Representation matters and lived experience matters. But experience and making sure that you have someone who has the seniority and the seasoning to be able to deliver for a district, it matters as well,” she said.Cherfilus-McCormick, meanwhile, wants to return to Congress despite a pending federal indictment that accuses her of stealing $5 million in federal disaster aid. She has plead not guilty and disputed alleged violations of House rules.Republican Rep. Cory Mills faces primary challengesDeSantis and other Republicans have bailed on Republican Rep. Cory Mills as he seeks a third term in Florida's 7th Congressional District at the same time he's denying domestic violence allegations. He faces three primary opponents.“I have not endorsed Cory Mills, and I do not support Cory Mills,” DeSantis said recently in Mills' district.Turnout could offer clues to NovemberRegistered Republicans now outnumber Democrats in Florida, a relatively recent flip. That puts the burden on Republicans to outperform Democrats comfortably in overall primary turnout. If it’s close – with Democrats coaxing a clearly larger percentage of their voters to the polls – then the party would be more optimistic heading into November, as Democrats witnessed with primary turnout in other states this year. If Republicans buck national trends and dominate, then Democrats could be facing another rough fall campaign.Miami-Dade will be especially notable. Democrats carried the county comfortably through 2016, when Trump lost it to Hillary Clinton by 30 percentage points. Four years later, Trump closed the gap to 7 points before carrying it in 2024 by more than 11 points.

A woman has died after she was found with an apparent gunshot wound in a Vero Beach roadway Sunday morning, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded around 8:41 a.m. to the area of 501 1st Street after receiving a 911 call about an adult woman in the roadway. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said responding deputies found the woman suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures. She was taken to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel remained on scene processing evidence, and the sheriff's office said the case is being investigated as a homicide. Investigators have identified Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, as a person of interest in the case and are actively searching for him. During a news conference Sunday afternoon, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said investigators believe Waggle has left the area and have expanded the search nationwide. "We do not believe he is in the Vero Beach area any longer," Flowers said. "We have put out a nationwide BOLO for him at this point." Flowers said investigators believe Waggle and the victim had some type of relationship. Investigators also believe Waggle may have been in the area around the time of the shooting and that the shooting happened near where the woman was found, in front of her residence. The sheriff's office has a domestic violence investigator working alongside homicide detectives. Flowers said investigators are looking into whether domestic violence may have played a role but stressed that it is still early in the investigation. Authorities are warning anyone who sees Waggle not to approach him. "If you encounter this suspect, this person of interest, don't approach him, call 911," Flowers said. Flowers said investigators are treating the search as a serious situation because they believe it is possible Waggle could harm himself or others. Authorities have not released the identity of the woman. Anyone who witnessed the incident, was in the area of 1st Street Sunday morning or has information that could help investigators is asked to contact the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Tips can also be submitted anonymously through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers. "We want to know what you heard and saw," Flowers said. The investigation remains active and ongoing.

Lucie County Sheriff's Office said deputies responded around 11:30 a.m. 16 to a home in the 1700 block of Wyoming Avenue for a domestic disturbance. Voters in Florida will cast their ballots in several local and statewide primary elections on Tuesday.The race to become the next governor of Florida is in the spotlight, along with the U.S. WATCH: Palm Beach County residents prepare to head to the polls>> RELATED: More election newsEarly voting concluded over the weekend.On Election Day, you must vote at the polling place that is assigned to your precinct, and your ballot will be there waiting for you.You can find your assigned precinct number and polling place address either on your Voter Information Card, sample ballot or by calling your Supervisor of Elections office.On Election Day, polls are open from 7 a.m. until 7 p.m.Please bring one or two forms of valid and current identification (ID) that include your signature and photo. If your photo ID does not include your signature, you will be asked to provide another ID that has your signature.Note: If you do not bring your ID, you may still vote; however, you will be required to vote a provisional ballot, which will later be evaluated by the Canvassing Board for eligibility.A primary election is held 11 weeks before the general election. The Palm Beach Zoo is shining a spotlight on one of Florida's most important — and often overlooked — animals: the gopher tortoise.I visited the zoo to meet Franklin, a resident gopher tortoise, and learn about the critical role these animals play in the wild.WATCH: Callie Carpenter, the zoo's Associate Curator and a conservation leader, said gopher tortoises are far more than just slow-moving reptiles."You can kind of think of them as the engineers of our ecosystem because they create elaborate burrow systems that help protect them from the elements," Carpenter said. Carpenter said those burrows do more than shelter the tortoise itself."It also provides habitat for 350 other species of animals."All this week, employees of the City of West Palm Beach and Palm Beach County can get into the zoo for free. They can also bring three guests at 50 percent off.A valid form of ID is required.

Lantana police are investigating vandalism at multiple locations across town, including a memorial honoring fallen officers that was spray-painted with derogatory messages over the weekend.WATCH BELOW: 'Completely disheartening. I wouldn't have expected it here,' Assistant Chief Daniel Navas tells Palm Beach County reporter Joel LopezThe vandalism was discovered Saturday morning at the Lantana Police Memorial, which honors officers killed in the line of duty and includes a bench dedicated to 9/11 victims, according to Assistant Chief Daniel Navas."It's to honor the men and women in this job," Navas told WPTV. "It sends a message to the families that they'll never be forgotten."Investigators believe the memorial was specifically targeted based on the nature of the damage and messages left behind, Navas said. The memorial features three pillars representing strength in community, the city and police working together."Completely disheartening. I wouldn't have expected it here," Navas said. "We have such a great relationship with our community and just to know that somebody went out of their way to specifically damage something that's positive for the community and our profession, it really hurt."Town crews had already cleaned the black spray paint from the memorial by Saturday afternoon. Officials said they had been preparing the area for upcoming 9/11 commemorations.At least three other Lantana locations were vandalized with similar black markings, police said. The sites include a dumpster at Burger King, an area behind a local business and Holy Guardian Angels Church.Mayor Karen Lythgoe said residents have been shaken by the vandalism spree."They're horrified. Why are people damaging the community? We want answers," Lythgoe said.Police are asking residents and business owners to review security cameras that may have captured suspicious activity overnight Friday into Saturday morning.Lythgoe posted about the crimes on Facebook to alert the community and encourage tips."I wanted to get the word out so that A, people could see what happened and B, you know, people brag, people talk and maybe somebody will know something," the mayor said.Police said the town's Flock cameras likely won't help in this case, because they primarily read license plates and investigators believe the suspect was on foot.In response to the vandalism, town officials are exploring installing security cameras at municipal buildings and local parks.The person responsible could face criminal mischief charges or potentially felony charges depending on the cost of damage, according to Lantana police."We are working diligently to find who you are and hopefully hold you accountable," Navas said when asked if he had a message for the vandal.Investigators said they are actively pursuing leads in the case and are asking anyone with information to call police.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is sounding the alarm after receiving more than 50 reports from people targeted by a scam involving callers impersonating law enforcement officers. Lucie County Sheriff's Office , scammers have been using the names of the Civil Judicial Services Bureau, Lt. Michael O'Brien and retired Sgt. Jeff Buchanan when making fraudulent calls. See also: Palm Beach County School District employee arrested by WPBPD in prostitution operation Deputies said the scam follows a repeated pattern. A caller claims the victim missed court or jury duty and that there is a warrant for their arrest. SLCSO warned that scammers may use official-sounding language and personal information to make the call appear legitimate. The sheriff's office said scammers use fear, urgency and threats of arrest to pressure victims into taking immediate action. Deputies said residents who receive one of these calls should: Hang up. Do not provide personal or financial information. Do not send money or make any payments. Do not trust the caller ID or the name provided by the caller. If you have questions about a legitimate court matter, contact the appropriate agency using a verified phone number.

LUCIE – A recent request by the pastor of a Tulip Boulevard church for a larger LED sign than currently permitted by the city’s Sign Code has reopened a conversation and controversy that City Council members here thought they’d finally settled two years ago. Not too many years back, city officials found themselves embroiled in a controversy between two Prima Vista Boulevard churches, one of which had purportedly erected an LED sign without a city permit, followed by the other requesting permission for just such a sign. That propelled Council members and staff into action, who also worried about compliance with a U.S. Supreme Court decision related to church signs and free speech. They thought the dust had finally settled on that issue in 2024 when they amended the Sign Code to limit LED signs to 20 square feet in diameter broadcasting text only. Pastor Manzie’s email, however, led to an Aug. 10 discussion launched by Councilman Anthony Bonna. “The request was quite reasonable to me, so I just wanted to bring it to Council to see what the temperature of Council was,” he said. “Essentially, he’s not asking for the monument to be any larger; it’s just these LED panels are constructed in such a way that he would have to reduce the LED portion significantly, which would reduce the impact of his sign. The LED portion is currently allowed to be 20 square feet, so simply by increasing that to 24 square feet we can address that. There may be similar requests in the future, and it might make sense to make the code compatible with how these panels are constructed.” Councilman Bonna was referring to part of Manzie’s email that spoke of a significant size limitation in current LED sign choices. The pastor insisted he needed more space to advertise the churches annual events since the city forced him to stop using large banners for that purpose. “Our church has been seeking quotes for various LED signs,” he wrote. “We were told that – according to the statute – we could only have a 20-square-foot LED sign displaying text only. The LED screen we would like to purchase is 88.2 inches by 37.7 inches, or 23.09 square feet. To comply with the code, we would need to select the next smaller size, which would be 15.44 square feet. I would loose a dramatic amount of space all because of how LED signs are made. I respectfully request that we adjust the code to allow 25 square feet and permit pictures.” City Attorney Richard Berrios then provided the Council his initial legal guidance on that request. “Upon first review, it looks like it would be a comprehensive amendment to the code to allow for a larger square footage,” he said. “Alternatively, there might be some other paths from staff they might have.” Councilman David Pickett initially thought Central Baptist might proceed with the larger sign in the interim, but the city attorney shot that idea down. “We would have to change the code first,” Berrios explained. “What is the pastor’s ETA on putting the sign in?” Councilman Pickett asked. Councilman Bonna tackled that question. “I think they’re looking to do it soon, but they’ve been a part of the community for a long time and they want to work through our processes,” he said. “My preference would be to change the code and not look for a work-around and do it as soon as possible. The other thing he would like to do – which may be more controversial – is have some imagery in his LED display.” Mayor Martin, who was vice-mayor during those earlier conversations immediately hit the brakes. “There were reasons why that was done that way,” she said. “We need to go back and relook at that, especially as it related to the Reed v. “I think this is a two-prong thing, but I believe there are distinct reasons why we didn’t allow the imagery portion of it.” Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo also took part in that earlier LED discussion. “There was a lot more than just imagery,” she said. “There was also concern with light pollution, but LEDs have changed. We even utilize LED in some of our signage, so I think there is an opportunity to relook at where technology is and Reed vs Gilbert. I would like a comprehensive discussion and then make the changes on the Sign Code that we can come up with.” Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan, in turn, described the prior church controversy that led to the earlier Sign Code changes. “This came up because the Methodist Church on Prima Vista placed an LED sign without a permit,” she recalled. Andrews across the street wanted to construct one but was told they couldn’t. So, it was like, how do we fix this? It was not even two years ago that we changed it to allow for that, and it was for messaging only.” Councilman Bonna still sought a timetable from staff, with Berrios acknowledging he would need input from Planning Zoning officials as well. “I would definitely need to coordinate with staff and have an understanding of what the appetite is,” he said. “Square footage seems simple in concept, but I don’t want to rummage around in the code without talking to them first and understanding the background.” Assistant Planning Zoning Director Anne Cox then provided the formal framework. “You said you’d like to workshop it first,” she said. “Then, if the language is agreed to, it’s a zoning text amendment. It would have to go to the Planning Zoning Board and then two readings at Council.” “So, it’s going to take a few months then,” Mayor Martin responded. Councilman Bonna, in turn, insisting on separating the discussions on size and images so as not to logjam the pastor’s request. Vice-Mayor Caraballo agreed. “I think the second piece of it’s going to be more complicated,” she said. “The way I see it in Reed v. Gilbert, once we allow images, we won’t be able to discriminate against additional images. So, I think that’s going to be the challenge. I agree with separating the issues, but I would like to see where we’re currently at with best practices looking at the top largest cities and the size of signs with LEDs as well.” Council members and staff then suggested holding the workshop that same month, but the Aug. 17 workshop was subsequently canceled. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office is investigating a death. The Sheriff’s Office announced that on Sunday, Aug. 16, at 8:41 a.m., Indian River County Sheriff’s Office 911 dispatch received a call reporting a woman was in a roadway. When deputies arrived at 501 First Street in Vero Beach, the woman was found with an apparent gunshot wound. Deputies began life-saving measures. The woman was transported to a hospital where she was later pronounced dead. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The death was designated as a homicide, and a person of interest was identified as 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the victim and Waggle were in some sort of a relationship. “That’s what we know at this point, is that they have some sort of relationship. We do have our domestic violence investigator out here,” Flowers said. “Oftentimes in these cases, domestic violence is always a root cause in deaths, and we’re treating it as though because of their relationship it may be domestic violence, but we don’t know.” Authorities said Waggle’s last known address was in Sebastian, but investigators believe he is no longer in the area and is traveling by vehicle. “Based on our investigative techniques at this point, our team used a variety of different things. We have our flock cameras. We got a variety of resources available to us based on that. At this point, I can say we believe that he has left Indian River County, and so that’s why we’ve issued the ‘Be on the lookout,’” Flowers said. VIDEO BELOW: INDIAN RIVER COUNTY SHERIFF PRESS CONFERENCE If you have seen Matthew Allen Waggle or know his whereabouts, the sheriff's office asks to not approach him. This is a developing story and will be updated as information becomes available.

Authorities in Indian River County are investigating a homicide in Vero Beach that left one woman dead over the weekend, with 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle identified as a person of interest. Investigators believe Waggle is no longer in the area and are working to determine a motive. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the victim and Waggle "had some sort of relationship." “Oftentimes in these cases, domestic violence is always a root cause in deaths, and we're treating it as though because of their relationship it may be domestic violence, but we don't know,” Flowers said. Next-door neighbor Jaiquan Parks described the victim and Waggle as a quiet couple who lived together. “I probably ran into them a couple of times. I see them out here walking together with their dog, you know, a regular quiet couple,” Parks said. He added that he never heard anything alarming from their apartment. “The only thing you would hear from their apartment is their dog barking,” Parks said. “You never know what's going on right next door to you. It's pretty wild that your neighbor would do something like that, especially a neighbor who you think is relatively quiet and a nice couple.” State Rep. Debra Tendrich, who sponsored House Bill 277 to strengthen protections for domestic violence survivors, emphasized the importance of addressing domestic violence. “We really need to make sure that we're strengthening protections to make sure victims can become survivors,” Tendrich said. “It does add victim relocation allowance; it does protection for military families and pets. It does add for those strong protections for victims, but we're nowhere close to being done.” The bill, signed into law by Gov. Ron DeSantis in July, aims to prevent tragedies like this one. “I do have full confidence in our law enforcement that they will be able to apprehend him,” Tendrich said. “I do think that we also have to realize domestic violence is not contained in a specific area, which is also why it's so dangerous. What happens is we don't have a continuum of care where we can actually follow that trail to make sure that those victims are safe. We've seen quite a few times where a victim will stay here and the person who abused them will move across state lines; it's very hard to track someone if they don't live in the same city, county, or state as you. It's not really contained." Authorities have not released the victim’s identity. Flowers warned that Waggle is considered armed and dangerous. Anyone with information about the case is urged to contact the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

A Florida lawmaker wants to ban elective cat declawing statewide, calling the procedure painful, outdated and unnecessary.State Rep. Rob Long said he plans to introduce legislation during the 2027 Legislative Session that would prohibit elective cat declawing across Florida while still allowing veterinarians to perform the procedure when medically necessary."Declawing is still widely misunderstood," Long said. "It is not simply removing a cat's claws; it involves amputating the last bone of the toes."Long said the proposal would revive and update a bill first introduced by former State Sen. Lauren Book in 2020."The basic framework is simple: prohibit declawing for cosmetic or convenience reasons while preserving a veterinarian's ability to perform the procedure when it is genuinely medically necessary," Long said.Long said the issue hits close to home."My wife and I have three rescue cats, we care for community cats and regularly foster rescues, and my mother-in-law fosters as well," Long said. "We have volunteered with Peggy Adams and worked with Animal Rescue Force."Long said a recent visit to Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control during the height of "cat season" reinforced his concerns about animal welfare and overcrowded shelters."The rising cost of living is making an already difficult situation worse, with more animals being abandoned or surrendered because families simply cannot afford to keep them," Long said.Long said he learned about a cat that was recently adopted from Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control and later returned after being declawed, which he said led to behavioral issues he believes are commonly associated with the procedure.Supporters of the proposal argue declawing can leave cats with long-term physical and behavioral issues, including pain, biting and litter box problems.Janet Steele, director of Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control, said declawed cats that come through the shelter often need extra accommodations."We ensure that they have litter that doesn't irritate their sensitive paws, give them plenty of spaces to retreat to that don't require large distance leaps, and work with local adopters and rescues that focus on 'special needs' animals," Steele said.Steele said the procedure can also affect how cats interact with people and other animals."The behavioral impacts of declawing can cause pain redirecting actions (biting or swatting) towards people or other pets, difficulties using certain litters resulting in urinating/defecating outside the litter box, and an overall pulling back from social activities," Steele said.Long pointed to a growing shift within the veterinary industry."Banfield and VCA, two of the largest veterinary systems in the country, no longer support elective declawing," Long said, adding that organizations including the American Veterinary Medical Association and the American Animal Hospital Association also discourage medically unnecessary declawing.Animal advocacy group The Paw Project said Florida would not be the first state to act."Five states (New York, Maryland, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and California) have banned declawing within the past 9 years, as have all ten Canadian provinces," the group said.The Paw Project also pushed back on concerns that a ban could lead to more cats being surrendered to shelters."There is no evidence that declaw bans result in cats losing their homes," the group said. "To the contrary, shelter intake numbers declined in every jurisdiction where data is available."The group highlighted Los Angeles as one example, saying shelter intake of cats dropped by 43.5% in the years after the city banned declawing.For Long, the debate comes down to necessity versus convenience."An irreversible amputation should be performed because the animal medically needs it, not simply for human convenience," Long said. "Senator Book started this conversation in 2020, and my goal next session is to update that work and get it across the finish line."

A 52-year-old woman is dead after being shot Sunday morning in Vero Beach, and the Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching for a person of interest in what investigators are treating as a domestic violence homicide. At approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday, the sheriff's office received a 911 call reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street. Deputies located the woman with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home. Sheriff Eric Flowers identified the person of interest as 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian. Investigators believe Waggle and the victim were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle. "We have put out a nationwide BOLO for him at this point — be on the look out. Our team is working with real time crime center. Our detectives have been working on this all day and its our goal to ultimately locate him," Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle should be considered armed and dangerous. "If you encounter this person, don't approach him," Flowers said. "It's possible that he could harm other people or himself. We don't know those details so at this point we should treat it as a very serious situation," Flowers said. Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home. "My brother actually heard the shot," Cardenas said. "So he went inside to check on my sister." Cardenas said the neighborhood is typically quiet. "Nothing like this should happen, like especially in quiet neighborhoods," Cardenas said. He said he hopes an arrest comes soon. "I just hope that they find the suspect," Cardenas said. Flowers called the incident a tragedy and says detectives are using resources such as flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts. "At this point we're not sure but this could be a domestic violence incident. It's a loss of life that's so unnecessary," Flowers said. "So our team is committed to work on that." Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org , or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

Kevin Burns, a US history and civics teacher at Jupiter Middle School for more than 20 years, died Friday evening after being caught in a current while snorkeling off the Jupiter coast.According to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, Burns and a friend paddleboarded approximately half a mile offshore to a reef in the 3000 block of S. The two secured their paddleboards at the reef and entered the water to snorkel. While snorkeling, the current became increasingly strong and carried both men away from their paddleboards. After determining they were unable to swim against the current to return, they decided to swim toward shore.WATCH BELOW:Burns' friend made it to shore, but realized Burns had not made it back and was no longer visible in the water. He called 911, and Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office deputies and Palm Beach County Fire Rescue arrived. A PBSO helicopter located Burns in the water north of where the paddleboards had been secured at the reef. Burns was transported to Jupiter Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.His parents, Diana and Parker Burns, said the news was difficult to process."We just really couldn't believe that," Diana and Parker Burns said.Jupiter Middle School Principal Lisa Hastey shared the news with families and staff over the weekend."Mr. Burns was a beloved member of our Mariner family and taught U.S. History and Civics for more than twenty years. He maintained an unwavering commitment to education and will be deeply missed by all who knew him," Hastey said.Two of Burns' fellow teachers described the impact he had on everyone around him."He was the sunshine," one colleague said."He was just the most positive person probably that I ever met, just always looking for the bright side. A kind word for everybody," another colleague said.Burns' love for the ocean was as much a part of his life as his classroom. His colleagues said he made a daily ritual of early morning paddles."He would go out at 5:30 in the morning, just paddle out, and then he'd send us pictures of the sunrise and just say it's going to be a sublime day. He loved that word sublime," a colleague said.The night his death was confirmed, about 70 teachers and parents gathered to remember him. Tributes have continued since."One of the kids the other night wrote a note saying that because of Mr. Burns, she's now a history teacher," a colleague said."He helped us out. He touched a lot of lives. He did," Diana and Parker Burns said.School counselors are on campus this week to support students and staff. Additional counselors from the District's Department of Behavioral and Mental Health are also present. School Police are also on campus with a therapy dog.Hastey encouraged families to reach out if students need support."If a student expresses the need to speak with someone, please encourage them to do so," Hastey said.For assistance outside of school hours, families may contact the 211 HelpLine, a free, confidential crisis hotline available by dialing 2-1-1."We showed up and we're going to keep moving forward and taking his sunshine with us," a colleague said.Burns' family is planning a celebration of life near the water."We are going to have a celebration of life, probably down by the beach where he would want to be in Jupiter," Diana and Parker Burns said.

A new nonprofit launched by the Economic Council of Indiantown will seek private local business investment to support youth athletics and recreation in the community.The Youth Athletics Foundation of Indiantown was announced at a Thursday night meeting of the Economic Council of Indiantown. The organization aims to raise money from local businesses to fund new and existing youth sports programs, as well as upgrades to aging facilities.WATCH BELOW: New nonprofit aims to fund youth sports programs At Big Mound Park in Indiantown, Deborah Resos, Director of Parks and Recreation for Indiantown, pointed to some of the challenges facing local fields."It's an 80-yard field, so it's not an official-sized football field," Resos said. "We need 100 yards for it to be an official-sized field."Beyond field dimensions, Resos described the broader condition of facilities, including rusted fences and compacted turf."Our fields are safe to play on, but they're old, and they're compacted," Resos said.Scott Watson, who has worked with youth sports in Indiantown for decades, said current programming falls short of what the community needs."We do have some things going on, but not to the magnitude or not to the quality that we need," Watson said.Watson said sports like football require significant financial support to operate properly."To keep that going, we need all new equipment, the organization, the insurance, the standard operating procedures, everything that we need to put in place," Watson said.With the 800-acre Terra Lago community under construction and more families expected to move to Indiantown, Watson said the demand for space will only grow."We need more fields. We're actually absolutely going to need more fields and better quality stuff as time goes on," Watson said.Watson said reaching young people early is at the heart of the effort."You have to capture the hearts and minds of kids before they're 15 years old," Watson said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A months-long investigation dubbed "Operation Beneath the Surface" has resulted in the arrest of 17 people and the seizure of four kilograms of cocaine, marking one of the most significant drug busts in the Booker Park area of Indiantown in Martin County's history.Watch the full press conference below: Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek announced the results of the multi-agency operation at a press conference, flanked by federal partners from the FBI, DEA, and Homeland Security Investigations. The investigation targeted a cocaine trafficking organization led by Cecil Trimble, a career criminal who was operating under the guise of a car detailing business in Indiantown."Four kilos of cocaine might not sound like a lot to you, but that's one of the most significant amounts of drugs we've ever gotten out of the Booker Park area in Martin County's history," Budensiek said.The investigation began when Martin County Sheriff's Office narcotics detectives started working with informants and conducting undercover purchases. They initially focused on two younger suspects, Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson, who appeared to have an unlimited supply of cocaine. The investigation quickly led detectives to Trimble, who was identified as the main supplier.Trimble, who was on federal probation for a previous cocaine trafficking conviction, was running his operation from a car detailing business that served as a front. Through surveillance and undercover operations, investigators obtained court-ordered wiretaps on Trimble, Thompson, Wilson, and Janarie Jones.The wiretaps revealed that Trimble was supplying cocaine throughout Martin County and beyond, including dealers in Stuart, Port St. Lucie, and using "mules" to transport drugs to Daytona Beach. During the investigation, authorities intercepted Antonio Honor on I-95 with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol, seizing one kilogram of cocaine. A 52-year-old woman is dead after being shot Sunday morning in Vero Beach, and the Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching for a person of interest in what investigators are treating as a domestic violence homicide. At approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday, the sheriff's office received a 911 call reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street. Deputies located the woman with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home. Sheriff Eric Flowers identified the person of interest as 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian. Investigators believe Waggle and the victim were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle. "We have put out a nationwide BOLO for him at this point — be on the look out. Our team is working with real time crime center. Our detectives have been working on this all day and its our goal to ultimately locate him," Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle should be considered armed and dangerous. "If you encounter this person, don't approach him," Flowers said. "It's possible that he could harm other people or himself. We don't know those details so at this point we should treat it as a very serious situation," Flowers said. Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home. "My brother actually heard the shot," Cardenas said. "So he went inside to check on my sister." Cardenas said the neighborhood is typically quiet. "Nothing like this should happen, like especially in quiet neighborhoods," Cardenas said. He said he hopes an arrest comes soon. "I just hope that they find the suspect," Cardenas said. Flowers called the incident a tragedy and says detectives are using resources such as flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts. "At this point we're not sure but this could be a domestic violence incident. It's a loss of life that's so unnecessary," Flowers said. "So our team is committed to work on that." Lucie Nuclear Power Plant was manually shut down last week after three control rods fell into the reactor's core.Florida Power & Light says Unit 1 at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant is back at 100% power after being manually shut down Wednesday following what the company called "an equipment issue."WATCH BELOW: 'No cause for worry': Professor shares thoughts on nuclear reactor shutdownAccording to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, three control rods dropped into the reactor's core, prompting crews to shut the unit down for repairs. "Our normal procedure under such circumstances is to just shut down."Wall also noted the plant has multiple layers of protection built in."There's backup after backup after backup," Wall said.However, Wall pointed to an NRC report of a similar incident in November 2024, in which Unit 1 was also manually shut down after three rods dropped during rod control maintenance. Incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin is seeking another term and faces challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Strazzeri. All three candidates spoke with WPBF 25 News on Monday about their priorities for the city, with issues ranging from infrastructure and public safety to government spending and quality of life. The latest: WPBF 25 News coverage on Politics Martin said one of her top priorities is continuing to invest in the city while protecting the quality-of-life residents have come to expect. “My main goal is to continue to move the city forward, while protecting our quality of life that our residents expect, and that means we’re going to continue to invest in roads and infrastructure. Giordano said he wants to bring a different approach to city hall, with a focus on spending, transparency and adding more amenities for families. “We currently don’t have a downtown area. According to Florida's Insurance Commissioner, new data show decreasing property insurance premiums in the first six months of 2026 in 51 of 67 counties, including all five counties in the WPTV viewing area.WATCH BELOW: Decreasing homeowners insurance? Jay Collins has chosen Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie as his running mate in the Republican race for governor.Collins announced the pick just hours before the primary, as he tries to close a significant polling gap with frontrunner Byron Donalds. Donalds has held a commanding lead in many polls, although surveys have varied on the size of that advantage.Guthrie, who leads the state's hurricane response agency, is entering a statewide political campaign with the Republican primary just hours away.Collins said he spent weeks considering who could serve as his second-in-command. He said he wasn't looking for a political name or someone chosen for demographic or geographic reasons.Instead, he said he wanted competence, leadership, character and someone who could step in and lead on day one.With Collins trailing Donalds by a wide margin in many polls and primary day just hours away, Guthrie has little time to change the trajectory of the race.“I’m either going to be a political hero tomorrow or a political zero tomorrow,” he said.Guthrie said he accepted the offer out of principle, saying he could have taken the easier way out but believed Florida deserved someone willing to step forward.Guthrie said he has spent nearly 37 years in public safety, including more than two decades with the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office, before moving into emergency management. He eventually became director of the state's emergency management agency under Gov. Ron DeSantis.But his move into politics creates an immediate question about his current job.Guthrie is still leading the Florida Division of Emergency Management, and Florida is in the middle of hurricane season.Asked whether he would have to resign, Guthrie said he had not yet spoken with DeSantis. He said that conversation with the governor's office would happen Tuesday.If he is required to resign, Guthrie said he will do so and focus fully on the campaign. He said his second-in-command, Ben Fairbrother, is prepared to take over the agency if necessary.Guthrie also addressed concerns about moving from a public-safety role into a partisan campaign.“I've never been accused of being a politician,” he said, adding that he intends to remain a “statesman” and represent all Floridians.Guthrie said his experience has required him to work with both Republicans and Democrats and that he intends to continue serving everyone in the state.Collins said he wants the lieutenant governor to have a more active role than a traditional ceremonial position, focusing on “safety, security, readiness, and response.”The pick also reinforces Collins' effort to position himself as a continuation of the DeSantis administration.Both Collins and Guthrie praised DeSantis during the announcement. Guthrie called DeSantis the best governor he has worked for and said the governor had empowered him throughout his career.Whether that message, or Guthrie's addition to the ticket, can significantly change the race remains to be seen.Republican voters will decide Tuesday whether Collins can overcome Donalds' lead and win the nomination.

Kevin Keane is the founder of FortPierceWatch.org A local government may intervene through eminent domain when a privately proposed waterfront development would eliminate land or facilities the government determines are necessary for a continuing public use. Florida municipalities possess statutory authority to condemn property for recognized municipal purposes, including public parks. A Florida Attorney General opinion specifically concluded that the City of Maitland could exercise eminent domain to acquire land for a public park under its governing authority. For a waterfront parcel threatened by intensive private development, the strongest municipal record would state that the property is reasonably necessary for an identified public project such as: • Permanent waterfront green space; • Public shoreline access; • A municipal park; • Preservation of archaeological, historic, or cultural resources; • Storm-surge and flood-resilience infrastructure; • Conservation of environmentally sensitive habitat; or • A public waterfront trail and recreational corridor. Precedence has already been set: 1. Miami Circle — Miami-Dade County “This specific property is required for a legitimate public preservation purpose.” Stopping the private development was the practical result, but preservation was the legally stated public purpose. Fisher Island marine terminal — Miami-Dade County, 2026 The stated public purpose was preserving fuel infrastructure serving PortMiami. Nevertheless, it demonstrated the same operative principle: “A local government may intervene through eminent domain when a privately proposed waterfront development would eliminate land or facilities the government determines are necessary for a continuing public use.” 3. West Palm Beach waterfront-park proposal West Palm Beach recently considered a downtown waterfront-park expansion involving privately occupied or privately controlled property. Public concern arose that eminent domain could be used, although the mayor publicly denied that the city was threatening condemnation and later paused the proposal for further community discussion. “This therefore is not a completed Florida precedent, but it shows that eminent domain remains part of the public discussion when cities seek to assemble private waterfront property for park expansion.” Folks, can you imagine a 42-acre public park with new boat ramps, palm trees, white sand, day use covered pavilions, swimming area, kiddie pools, calypso music, grills, volleyball, corn hole, food trucks, boat slips, fishing docks, ice houses, etc? Keene is a fifth-generation Floridian and longtime Fort Pierce resident with more than 45 years of experience in contract management, project execution, and public accountability. He is the founder of FortPierceWatch.org , a community-based initiative dedicated to government transparency, responsible growth, and informed civic engagement. Through research, public records, and citizen involvement, he advocates for preserving Fort Pierce s historic waterfront and ensuring that public decisions reflect the interests of the community.
