A 2011 referendum set aside a two-acre commercial parcel near Haney Creek as a potential revenue source to help fund maintenance of the adjoining preserve. STUART — The City Commission voted Aug. 10 to have staff return with a resolution for a November referendum that would give Stuart voters the choice of undoing a 2011 referendum that set aside a two-acre commercial parcel near Haney Creek as a potential revenue source to help fund maintenance of the adjoining preserve. City Attorney Lee Baggett introduced the agenda item. The proposal was initially suggested in July 2025 by former Mayor Christopher Collins, who resigned April 30 to run for the District 2 Martin County Commission seat being vacated by Commissioner Stacey Hetherington. Since then, commissioners have struggled to move beyond 2-2 votes on several issues, postponing some matters until after the August primary election, when the commission will have a fifth member. Commissioners previously debated the Haney Creek referendum May 26 before postponing it until a deliberation and discussion item could be scheduled. “In 2011, the city went out to referendum on an approximately two-acre, commercially zoned parcel it had purchased,” Baggett said. “Instead of adding it to the Haney Creek preserve, they wanted to keep it separate so they could use income generated from leasing that parcel to help fund the maintenance of the park.” Earlier this year, the commission directed staff to begin the process of converting the parcel to conservation land and adding it to the Haney Creek Preserve. “Since in this instance we had to undo it, we needed to go back to the voters to undo that referendum,” Baggett said. The city also has an interlocal agreement with Martin County concerning the property. That agreement would have to be amended if the land’s status changes. “We had an interlocal agreement in which the county and the city agreed the property would be used to generate revenue to fund the maintenance of the park,” Baggett said. “So earlier this year, we had a resolution approving an amendment to that agreement. The county also passed a resolution agreeing to amend the interlocal, obviously conditional upon voter approval of the referendum.” Community Services Director Jim Chrulski provided commissioners with a history of the Haney Creek property, which was named for early Stuart-area physician Horace J. “The preserve protects part of the Haney Creek Watershed, which drains into the South Fork of the St. Lucie River,” Chrulski said. “The 157-acre preserve protects rare Florida habitats including coastal scrubland, pine flatwoods, wetlands and wet prairie.” The preserve is supported by community funding through a voter-approved half-cent sales tax dedicated to environmental improvements. It opened to the public in 2016. Chrulski said the city and Martin County purchased 51 acres of Haney Creek in 2011, the same year city voters approved setting aside the two acres of commercially zoned property as a potential funding source for maintaining preserve lands within the city limits. The city has never successfully leased the property. “The city explored several opportunities for the site,” Chrulski said. “Development plans included a restaurant, retail space, a hotel and even affordable housing. While several proposals were considered, none of them ultimately moved forward.” In 2025, the commission authorized a trailhead on the U.S. In 2026, after receiving an unsolicited proposal from RaceTrac, the commission decided to relocate the trailhead to Baker Road. At that point, commissioners began discussing whether commercial development was still the highest and best use of the property. The proposed resolution would establish ballot language asking voters to rescind the Nov. 8, 2011, referendum so the 1.97-acre parcel could be converted to conservation land and added to the Haney Creek Preserve. Baggett also clarified the difference between the Haney Creek proposal and a separate ballfield referendum approved by the commission on first reading Aug. “There’s a lot of confusion between the ballfields and Haney Creek since we’re doing it simultaneously,” he said. “In the ballfields, we’re amending the city charter to protect it in the future. That was already done in Haney Creek, and we’re just complying with our city charter.” After Mayor Sean Reed questioned staff and voiced his support for the resolution, Commissioner Campbell Rich argued that Stuart already has ample green space and could need potential income from the property if a property-tax referendum also on this year’s ballot passes. Chrulski previously told commissioners the city has nearly three times the parkland required by its comprehensive plan, with a total of 731 acres of green space. “We’re talking about one third of one percent of all the green space the city has,” Rich said. “Green space is a responsibility, [and] green space is an expense.” Rich said if the property-tax referendum passes, parks could face cuts because other essential services would be difficult to reduce. “The potential income from this property could be a million dollars over 10 years, and I do not want to deny the taxpayer the opportunity to earn that money,” he said. Reed, however, said 64% of Martin County voters want more green space. Commissioner Laura Giobbi agreed. “As the mayor said, in 2011 the citizens decided to approve this referendum, but a lot has changed over the last 15 years,” Giobbi said. “As more and more development happened, more green space was lost. We have an opportunity here. The people in the city — the taxpayers that own it — will be making the decision and not us.” After further debate, Reed passed the gavel to Commissioner Clarke and made a motion to have staff return Aug. 17 with a resolution containing the proposed ballot language for final approval. Giobbi seconded the motion, which passed 3-1, with Rich dissenting. Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. LUCIE — What began as a peaceful Sunday morning at church quickly turned into a potentially deadly confrontation when two men witnessed an armed man attempting to abduct his former girlfriend.. James “Jimmy” Mawhinney Jr. of Fort Pierce and Todd Moore of Port St. 12 with Community Hero Awards from the Port St. Lucie Police Department for their actions during the May 31 incident. The awards were presented during the department’s second-quarter awards ceremony at Port St. Lucie City Hall, which recognized law enforcement officers and members of the community. Police Chief Leo Niemezyk said Mawhinney and Moore demonstrated “extraordinary courage, selfless actions, and unwavering commitment” in protecting another person during the dangerous encounter. “Their actions undoubtedly prevented further violence and potentially saved a life,” Niemezyk wrote in his award letter. Mawhinney was outside of the First United Methodist Church on Southwest Prima Vista Boulevard after Sunday service. He was talking with Moore and his wife, Karen, who teaches Sunday school, when he heard his name being called and a car horn. Mawhinney walked around the building and saw a man later identified as Jose Tsu Zamora approaching a woman from behind and grabbing her by the arms. “As he grabbed the woman from the rear, a pistol fell from his pants,” Mawhinney said. Knowing Zamora was armed, Mawhinney went to his truck, retrieved his firearm and approached him from behind. “I asked him to politely leave the property,” Mawhinney said. At the same time, Moore saw the confrontation from the nearby playground, where he said there were at least six children and two adults. His wife moved the children inside as Moore jumped a fence and approached the scene. “I’m 280 pounds, so jumping over a fence, that’s not my first priority,” joked Moore. Within moments, Mawhinney and Moore were positioned on opposite sides of Zamora with their guns drawn. “We have the guy from two different directions,” Mawhinney said. “And we de-escalated the situation.” Another parishioner who received an award, George Webber, also approached Zamora and told him to stop. Moore said Zamora pointed the firearm at Webber, who backed away. Moore then attempted to move behind Zamora, but the suspect noticed him and turned with the firearm in his hand. “We’re all armed here,” Mawhinney recalled telling him. “You need to get out of here.” The goal, both men said, was to end the confrontation without anyone getting hurt. After several tense moments, Zamora eventually walked to his vehicle and drove away without any shots being fired. The men immediately provided police with information, including Zamora’s license plate number. Investigators obtained an arrest warrant, and Zamora was arrested later that evening in Hialeah. According to Chief Niemezyk, investigators determined Zamora was a convicted felon who was armed with a firearm and attempting to forcibly kidnap the woman while threatening her with the weapon. The victim later told investigators she feared she was going to die. For Mawhinney and Moore, the recognition came with little sense that they had done anything extraordinary. “Honestly, I was just doing what I believe was right,” Moore said. Moore, who grew up in Detroit, said he was accustomed to dangerous situations. “Somebody pointing a gun at you is like just another day,” he said. Mawhinney, who grew up in Fort Lauderdale in the 1980s, said he felt similarly. “This is Florida,” he said. “Don’t go waving guns around at people here. It’s probably not good for your health.” Both men said the incident could have ended much differently. “(Zamora) would have probably got the victim in the car, and she may have been found on the side of the road someplace,” Mawhinney said. Instead, the woman escaped, no one was shot — allowing police to take over the investigation and ultimately make an arrest. Your comment has been submitted. A network of license plate cameras facing growing privacy scrutiny across the country is now part of the search for a person of interest in a Vero Beach-area homicide. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers took CBS12 News Reporter Katie Bente inside the agency's Real Time Crime Center on Monday, where analysts are using Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for 33-year-old Matthew Waggle. Waggle has not been charged in the killing. Deputies identified him as a person of interest after a 52-year-old woman was found shot near her home Sunday morning in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach. Deputies performed lifesaving measures before the woman was taken to a trauma center, where she later died. Flowers said investigators believe the woman had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the killing as a domestic violence homicide. "One of the first places that we go, Real Time Crime Center gets activated," Flowers said. "They're looking at all the Flock cameras. They're looking at the traffic in the area." How Flock plays a role Flock's automated license plate readers capture information about vehicles as they pass, including license plates, locations and timestamps. That allows investigators to search for vehicles connected to crimes and potentially piece together where they traveled. Indian River County has previously said it operates 140 license plate readers. Flowers pointed to a deadly hit-and-run investigated by the Florida Highway Patrol last week as one recent example. He said analysts in the Real Time Crime Center used Flock data to help build a case that otherwise had no leads. He said the technology can also work in reverse helping investigators eliminate someone as a suspect. "If we're able to show that that person's vehicle was nowhere near the homicide," Flowers said, "that's a great way for us to show that somebody is innocent as well." A crime-fighting tool and a privacy fight The ability to reconstruct where vehicles have traveled is also at the heart of a growing national debate over Flock. Privacy and civil liberties advocates have questioned how extensively law enforcement should be able to track drivers, how information is shared between agencies and what safeguards exist to prevent misuse. More than 50 jurisdictions have reportedly ended relationships with Flock. The company announced new safeguards last week, including plans to reduce its recommended default data retention period from 30 days to seven days and require searches to be connected to case numbers. Flowers strongly defended Indian River County's use of the cameras. "You're on camera every time you go to Walmart. You're on camera every time you go to Walgreens," Flowers said. "Everywhere you go, your bank transactions are being tracked." Flowers said law enforcement should be able to use available technology to protect the public. "Don't you want your law enforcement protecting your community and making it safer by leveraging technology?" he said. Flowers said Indian River County has largely avoided the public backlash seen elsewhere because the Sheriff's Office explained its use of the technology early and, he argues, residents have seen results. He pointed to auto burglaries as an example, saying the county recorded more than 800 in 2015 compared with roughly 250 last year. Flowers attributed at least part of that decline to the camera network and proactive policing. Now, the technology is being used in an active homicide investigation. See also: 12 pounds of meth, 12,000 rounds,12 guns, and fentanyl found in Boynton Beach SWAT raid Flowers said investigators spent Monday speaking with the victim's coworkers and examining her relationship with Waggle as they work to determine what led to the shooting. "It really looks like she was trying to break up with him," Flowers said. He wasn't ready for it to be over." A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle. Investigators have said he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

FORT PIERCE – The members of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency here voted unanimously Aug. 11 to approve an interlocal funding agreement with the city for the cost of a yearlong pilot program employing two new code-enforcement officers to work solely in the community redevelopment areas of Fort Pierce. Community and Economic Development Director Shyanne Harnage introduced the resolution to the Board that evening, whose members are made up of city commissioners wearing different hats. “We have outlined this pilot program to provide enhanced code-enforcement services within the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency boundaries only,” she said. “These will go above and beyond the baseline code enforcement services that are currently offered through the City of Fort Pierce. If you read through the redevelopment plan, you’ll see multiple goals that talk about elimination of slum and blight, vehicles, litter [and] illegal dumping. We think this is a very creative way to eliminate those issues, be more proactive and have relationships with our residents that maybe our code-enforcement officers don’t have the time to do.” Harnage then provided clarification on the pilot program oversight. “There are quarterly reporting requirements,” she continued. “They would come to you all and discuss how it’s going [and] what’s happening. Then on an annual basis, we’ll decide if we want to renew this program. I will say that other CRAs are implementing similar programs, and they have been very successful. I don’t think this should be looked at negatively in terms of double enforcement for the residents who live in the CRA, but more so of additional beautification and how we can work together and engage.” Community Response Director Shaun Coss also provided his input on the program, whose first year will cost up to $183,200. “Shyanne hit the nail on the head,” he said. “We’re definitely looking at very focused, supplemental enforcement [of] non-operable vehicles, illegal dumping, the trash and litter. There will be daily sign sweeps on the main corridors within the FPRA boundaries and we’ll potentially deal with the noise complaints once we revise the noise ordinance. These are issues the typical code-enforcement officers are not going to be addressing. This is all proactive in nature and supplemental to what code enforcement typically does.” Mayor Linda Hudson immediately expressed her satisfaction with the parameters of the new code-enforcement service. “So, this is not necessarily complaint driven, but it is going to be aggressive and people are going to be looking out,” she said. “I think we need eyes on our streets and our properties and identifying it rather than somebody having to call it in. I am pleased about that.” Commissioner Arnold Gaines, however, expressed concerns about potential misunderstandings by CRA residents directly impacted by the work of the two new code-enforcement officers. “Let’s be very clear that we get the word out that certain neighborhoods are not getting picked on doubly because of this new program,” he said. “If we’re going to look for cars, you need to let people understand what they can and can’t do. If you have a car that might have a flat tire, but the car is registered, has insurance and is parked on their property, a homeowner’s saying, why are you messing with me when my car has a tag on it? Another thing is to make sure with the different cultures that we get the right information out with the language they can understand. Because what somebody things looks bad to us, their culture might think think is beautiful. Let’s be proactive and get the word out instead of getting all these emails after you guys start.” Commissioner Curtis Johnson Jr. agreed, hoping the new officers will solve the issue of illegal signs in the city’s rights of way. “I think we should do a campaign to let people know who they are and what their assignments will be,” he said of the new officers. “I think it’s a really good program and I’m really interested to get the community to understand we’ve got to change the behaviors here to clean our city up. One of the things I want to talk to you about is trash cans. That’s becoming a problem because they’re in the street now, and people are hitting them causing damage not only to their cars but to the cans.” Mayor Hudson posed a final clarification question related to the renewed enforcement of non-operable vehicle in the community redevelopment areas. “So, you’re talking about on private property if somebody leaves a vehicle and it’s parked there forever and it doesn’t move and grass grows around it,” she asked. “Is that the kind of code enforcement you’re talking about in terms of the vehicles?” Coss tackled that inquiry. “Vehicles parked there with flat tires and clearly not operable, have expired tags or no tags on private property. The Police Department will continue to handle vehicles within the right of way or on the streets. The key component to this campaign is public education. A very big focus for these officers is going out and speaking with the residents and business owners and educating the public.” The FPRA Board then voted unanimously for approval. This poster of Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, was put on the Indian River County Sheriff's Office Facebook page as a means to enlist the public's help in search for Waggle, described as a "person of interest" in the homicide case of a woman who was fatally shot outside her home in the 500 block of 1st Street, Vero Beach on Aug. Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching for Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, who is a "person of interest" in the homicide case of a woman who was fatally shot outside her home in the 500 block of 1st Street, Vero Beach on Aug. VERO BEACH – Indian River County Sheriff's Office is actively looking for a "person of interest" who may have been involved in the homicide of a woman who was killed on Aug. 16 outside her home in the 500 block of 1st Street, Vero Beach, Sheriff Eric Flowers said. 16, deputies responded to a 911 call about a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street, Vero Beach, according to sheriff's office reports. 1 in unincorporated Indian River County, south of Vero Beach. Deputies located the victim suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures. She was transported to a local trauma center, where she was later pronounced deceased, Flowers confirmed in press briefing at the scene. The death was confirmed as a homicide and a "person of interest" was identified as Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, described as having brown hair and blue eyes, about 6-feet, one-inch tall and weighing about 200 pounds. Indian River County Sheriff's Office posted on its Facebook page a photo of Waggle and a poster asking the public for its help in locating Waggle. Flowers said at the press briefing that investigators believe that Waggle may have left Indian River County in a vehicle of some kind. "We believe he's in a vehicle, we don't have the specifics right now," Flowers said. The sheriff's office has issued a BOLO for Waggle. The sheriff's office is not releasing the name of the victim as yet, pending notification of next of kin. "They're out of state, so that may take some time," he said. It is believed that Waggle and the woman may have had some kind of a relationship but investigators "don't know the extent of the relationship," he said. "It's very early in the investigation. At this point, we're not sure, but it could be a domestic violence incident." Investigators were still at the scene as of Aug. 16, processing information and speaking to witnesses who may have heard gunshots, Flowers said. Anyone who encounters Waggle should not approach him but immediately call 911, Flowers said. Anyone who may have information on the case is urged to contact the sheriff's office, Flowers said. A routine call for service turned into a rescue mission for two Port St. Lucie police officers after a group of ducklings became trapped in a storm drain. Lucie Police Department said Officers Ortiz and Garcia responded Friday to the area of Southeast Oakridge Drive and Southeast Oaklyn Street, where the young ducks had fallen into the drain. Body camera video released by the department shows officers working around the storm drain and reaching inside to retrieve the ducklings one by one. Their mother remained nearby as officers worked to free her babies. See also: Can Flock find him? License plate cameras aid search after Vero Beach homicide After carefully removing the ducklings from the drain, officers reunited them with their mother, bringing the unusual call to a happy ending. It may have been a small rescue, but it made for a pretty great start to the weekend, the department wrote in a Facebook post. Police used the rescue as a reminder that protecting the community can sometimes include its smallest residents. At PSLPD, we’re always here to lend a helping hand especially when our smallest community members need us, the department said.

A Florida couple who had both flood and homeowners insurance before the 2024 hurricane season says the money they received from their insurer and FEMA was nowhere close to enough to rebuild. They shared their story, still standing on an empty lot nearly two years later.'IT JUST CAME IN TOO FAST'Jen and RJ Garbowicz lost their home first to flooding during Hurricane Helene, then had roof damage in Hurricane Milton."It was coming in through the floor, coming in through the walls. I actually got electrocuted a couple of times," RJ said.He said he ultimately had no choice but to stop trying to save the home."So I called it quits. I can't keep up," he said.Then 13 days later, water poured in again through the roof as Hurricane Milton took force.RELATED STORY | Is your home covered? Why summer is peak season for insurance claims 'WE DID ALL THE RIGHT THINGS'The couple paid between $18,000 and $20,000 a year for both flood and homeowners insurance. They are still in legal discussions with their homeowners insurance company over one claim.Their flood insurance, through FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program, paid out the maximum of $250,000."Which is great," Jennifer said.But RJ added that the couple is only getting $50,000 of that to rebuild, "Because we had a mortgage, they took the money, and they're holding it."FEMA also required the couple to rebuild under the 50% rule. The $250,000 payout was nowhere near enough to cover demolition and rebuilding. They turned to FEMA for additional help."I appealed four times by sending the same documentation over and over, and finally, after the fourth time, I got an approval, so we got a total of 33,000," Jennifer said.That FEMA disaster grant approval was not nearly enough. So the couple turned to an SBA loan. But the money there is being withheld too."Well, you have to first cover the difference between what insurance monies you received and the total cost of the build and subtract out the loan. So you have to cover the gap with your own cash," RJ said.And then the couple said that before they could receive an SBA disaster loan they had qualified for, they now had to repay that $33,000 grant to FEMA."It's really unfortunate that we did all the right things. We took all the right steps. We had insurance, we did everything as homeowners that we were supposed to do, and at the end of the day when we were counting on it, it didn't work like we thought that it would," Jennifer said.AVERAGE FEMA PAYOUTIn June, the Scripps News Group's Nadeen Yanes traveled to an insurance workshop where Florida Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie spoke as a guest. Guthrie also served on the President's FEMA Review Council. He nearly urged insurance companies to make sure policyholders understand that FEMA will not make homeowners whole."Let's just be very, very candid. The average person is going to get a $4,500 payout from this, from FEMA," Guthrie said.FIGHTING FOR FEMA REFORMThe Garbowicz traveled to Washington, D.C., as part of the Extreme Weather Survivors group to push for both FEMA and insurance reform."Everyone here today knows that disasters don't end when the news coverage does," a speaker at the event said."The important thing for us was just to get the conversation going, get the message out there," RJ said.The couple met with lawmakers to advocate for the FEMA Act, a House proposal that would completely reform the agency. Key provisions of the bill include:Makes FEMA and independent agency by removing FEMA from under the Department of Homeland SecurityCreating a universal application process for disaster recoveryProcessing FEMA grants faster, providing money to homeowners before recovery rather than as reimbursementFacilitates investment, mitigation efforts, and damage prevention before a storm hitsRELATED STORY | The hidden risk in your insurance policy: Why state minimums may not save you'WE NEED LONG-TERM SOLUTIONS'"Long-term disaster recovery, as you can see, doesn't end a day, a week, a month, or even in this case a year after the storm. It's many, many years of recovery, and we need long-term solutions," said one of the speakers at the Extreme Weather Survivors group in DC.The couple says those reforms would have helped them rebuild sooner, instead of still standing on an empty lot nearly two years after the storms. They estimate they have another 18 to 24 months of rebuilding ahead."It's been a long time coming, two years, and we probably still have another 18 to 24 months still left," RJ said."The important thing for us was just to get the conversation going, get the message out there," Jennifer added. "Just tell our story as much as possible because I think that's what it's going to take. It's going to take interviews like this, getting out there and really putting pressure."This story was originally published by Nadeen Yanes with the Scripps News Group in Tampa.

The memory of 16-year-old Roylynn Scott was front and center Friday night as students, family members and friends gathered at Billy Livings Field during Vero Beach High School's season opener to honor her life. Members of the Vero Beach High School band took the field wearing purple ribbons, Roylynn's favorite color, as classmates, teachers, teammates and loved ones filled the stands before kickoff. At her parents' request, the stadium announcer addressed the crowd, sharing details about Roylynn's life, including her love of football games, her passion for art and the impact she had on those around her. The remarks were followed by a moment of silence. As the tribute unfolded, Roylynn's family stood in the bleachers wearing purple in her honor. Moments later, the game began. The tribute came less than a week after Roylynn died following a fall at an abandoned condominium property in Sebastian. Investigators with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Roylynn fell nearly 30 feet through a hole in the roof of an abandoned building where a group of teenagers had been trespassing. Detectives said evidence indicates the fall was accidental. The tribute also came one day after Roylynn's family spoke exclusively with CBS12 News, describing a vibrant teenager whose loss has devastated loved ones. "She was my baby girl," her grandmother, Carole Melasi, told CBS12 News. Also read: Family remembers teen, pushes for safety changes after fatal fall at abandoned condo Family members say they hope Roylynn's story leads to changes that could help prevent similar tragedies in the future. CBS12 News has reached out to Indian River County officials seeking information about the abandoned condominium property where the fatal fall occurred, including whether the site had a history of safety concerns and what actions, if any, may have been taken regarding the property over the years. CBS12 News has also requested records from the Indian River County Sheriff's Office regarding trespassing incidents and calls for service at the site. In addition, CBS12 News has attempted to contact the property's owner, who is based in New Jersey, but has not received a response. County officials said they are working on those requests. A memorial service honoring Roylynn is scheduled for next Saturday at Periwinkle Park, one of her favorite places, according to her family. Through a GoFundMe campaign , loved ones are raising money for a memorial bench at one of her favorite parks and donations to animal charities she cared about.

Tommy John, who won 288 games during a 26-year big league career and became the first pitcher to successfully return following groundbreaking elbow surgery that later was named after him, has died. He was 83.He died at his home in Bradenton, Florida, on Saturday night, agent Mike Maguire said Sunday. He had been in hospice care.On Aug. 8, the New York Yankees released a social media post in which John wrote that he wanted to say goodbye to everyone, including friends and fans who followed him throughout his career, saying, “I will never forget you.”The Yankees called John “a bedrock of our rotation during his time in pinstripes and a longtime favorite of Yankees fans.”John was a four-time All-Star with a record of 288-231 and a 3.34 ERA during a career that stretched from 1963 to 1989. He pitched for Cleveland, the Chicago White Sox, the Los Angeles Dodgers, the Yankees, the California Angels and the Oakland Athletics.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Bryan Braman, former NFL linebacker, dies at 38 from 'very rare form of cancer'“Tommy was an exceptional pitcher throughout his career in Major League Baseball, and his courageous role in becoming the first to have surgery that would go on to bear his name can’t be overstated,” Stan Kasten, Dodgers president and CEO, said in a statement. "His impact both on and off the field has been felt by ballplayers of all ages and will be for generations to come.”The left-hander was 31 years old when he tore the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow in 1974, a death knell for pitchers' careers to that point.John allowed Dr. Frank Jobe, the Dodgers’ team physician, to replace the ligament with a tendon from his right forearm. Jobe gave the surgery 100-to-1 odds of being successful.John was a great pitcher, but his elbow surgery made him a baseball legendThe procedure had been done on others before, although it was usually performed on wrists and hands. John was the first pitcher to have it done on his elbow.More than 2,600 big leaguers and thousands more amateurs have since had UCL reconstructions, better known as Tommy John surgery. It’s been a godsend for many of baseball’s greatest stars, including two-way sensation Shohei Ohtani, three-time Cy Young Award winner Justin Verlander and even Philadelphia Phillies slugger Bryce Harper.“If you put it in dollars and cents, I think there’s no question that Tommy John is the most valuable reconstructive procedure there is,” Dodgers team physician Dr. Neal ElAttrache told The Associated Press in 2024.Born Thomas Edward John Jr. on May 22, 1943, in Terre Haute, Indiana, he was a top baseball and basketball player at the city’s Gerstmeyer High. He graduated in 1961 as valedictorian but did not give the commencement speech because of a stutter. Despite being recruited by the University of Kentucky to play basketball, John chose baseball and signed with Cleveland.“The day I left for my first job as a pitcher, my father looked at me & said: ‘Good luck, Tommy. Just remember one thing: Whether you make it big in the big leagues or you don’t, you’ll always just be Tommy John from Terre Haute, Indiana.’ I’ve never forgotten those words,” John wrote in his Aug. 8 post.John recorded 2,245 strikeouts but never led either league in wins or strikeouts. He had the second-most wins of any pitcher since 1900 not to be elected to the Hall of Fame. From 1995 through 2009, John was on the Hall of Fame ballot, but he never received more than 31.7% of the votes, falling well short of the 75% required for election.John won more games after his eponymous surgeryKnown for his longevity, John was the opening day starter for both the 1966 Chicago White Sox and the 1989 New York Yankees. He won 124 games before his UCL repair and 164 after. His final appearance came days after his 46th birthday.“While his incredible longevity and post-surgery achievements changed the fortunes and trajectory of countless athletes around the world, it also overshadowed his excellence as a pitcher,” the Yankees said in a statement. “We pause to remember the totality of his legacy — his competitiveness and skill, his penchant for conversation, his kind and gracious nature, and his stature as an athletic and medical pioneer.”IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 2-time NASCAR champion Kyle Busch dead at 41 after battling severe illnessJohn made his major league debut on Sept. 6, 1963, pitching one inning in relief for Cleveland.He was traded to the White Sox in 1965 and worked his way into the starting rotation. The following year, he tied for the American League lead with five shutouts and in 1967, his six shutouts led the AL.In 1971, he was traded to the Dodgers.In 1974, John had a 13-3 record and led the National League in victories going into the All-Star break. He was pitching against the Montreal Expos when he permanently damaged the UCL in his left arm. After a month, the injury had not improved.During the four-hour surgery on Sept. 25, 1974, Jobe made holes in the humerus and ulna bones of John’s left arm and used anchors to insert the tendon in a figure-eight pattern.At first, John’s left hand was shriveled and he lacked feeling in several of his fingers because of damage to the ulnar nerve. Jobe performed a second procedure to reroute the nerve that was necessary to John’s full recovery.John’s arm was in a cast for four months. He had recovered the full range of motion in his left arm by spring training of 1975, and spent that season resting, healing and rebuilding strength in his arm. John worked with fellow Dodgers pitcher Mike Marshall, who had a doctorate in kinesiology, on learning a different grip.That September he made five appearances during an offseason instructional league, working his way up to seven innings by his final game.John resumed pitching for the Dodgers in 1976 as the fourth starter in their rotation. He allowed three runs in five innings and took the loss in his first start against Atlanta, the first time any pitcher had started a game following UCL reconstructive surgery.John donated the original cast from his surgery to the Smithsonian Institution in June 2022. His teammates on the 1974 Dodgers signed it, as well as Jobe and the team’s Hall of Fame announcer Vin Scully.The procedure has become so widely known that in 2019, Merriam-Webster added the term to its dictionary.John made 31 starts for the Dodgers in 1976, posting a 10-10 record, a 3.09 ERA, 91 strikeouts, 61 walks and 207 hits allowed in 207 innings.In 1977, he won 20 games for the first time in his career, finishing with a 20-7 record. He finished second behind Philadelphia’s Steve Carlton in voting for the NL Cy Young Award.John and his family had mixed feelings about the legacy of his operationOver 50 years later, Tommy John surgery is as much a part of baseball as peanuts and hot dogs. Advanced training methods are helping pitchers of all ages throw harder than ever. They take comfort knowing a torn UCL won’t necessarily end their careers.“I am sick my name is attached to a surgery happening in kids more than pros,” John tweeted in July 2018.John’s oldest son, Tommy III, became a chiropractor who wrote a book suggesting ways to prevent young athletes from having to undergo major sports-related surgery similar to what his father endured.After his pitching career ended, John worked as a broadcaster for the Minnesota Twins and Yankees in the 1990s. He managed the Bridgeport (Connecticut) Bluefish from 2007-09.John was hospitalized in December 2020 because of COVID-19 and later had Guillain-Barré syndrome, in which a person’s immune system attacks their nerves. John told the New York Post in May 2022 that he was paralyzed in his lower extremities for several months.John and his wife Sally Simmons had four children: Tamara, Tommy III, Travis and Taylor, who died of a prescription drug overdose at 28 in 2010. The couple divorced in 2013.Besides his children, he is survived by his second wife, Cheryl, and son-in-law Patrick Mannelly, a retired NFL long snapper who played 16 years for the Chicago Bears.

The memory of 16-year-old Roylynn Scott was front and center Friday night as students, family members and friends gathered at Billy Livings Field during Vero Beach High School's season opener to honor her life. Members of the Vero Beach High School band took the field wearing purple ribbons, Roylynn's favorite color, as classmates, teachers, teammates and loved ones filled the stands before kickoff. At her parents' request, the stadium announcer addressed the crowd, sharing details about Roylynn's life, including her love of football games, her passion for art and the impact she had on those around her. The remarks were followed by a moment of silence. As the tribute unfolded, Roylynn's family stood in the bleachers wearing purple in her honor. Moments later, the game began. The tribute came less than a week after Roylynn died following a fall at an abandoned condominium property in Sebastian. Investigators with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Roylynn fell nearly 30 feet through a hole in the roof of an abandoned building where a group of teenagers had been trespassing. Detectives said evidence indicates the fall was accidental. The tribute also came one day after Roylynn's family spoke exclusively with CBS12 News, describing a vibrant teenager whose loss has devastated loved ones. "She was my baby girl," her grandmother, Carole Melasi, told CBS12 News. Also read: Family remembers teen, pushes for safety changes after fatal fall at abandoned condo Family members say they hope Roylynn's story leads to changes that could help prevent similar tragedies in the future. CBS12 News has reached out to Indian River County officials seeking information about the abandoned condominium property where the fatal fall occurred, including whether the site had a history of safety concerns and what actions, if any, may have been taken regarding the property over the years. CBS12 News has also requested records from the Indian River County Sheriff's Office regarding trespassing incidents and calls for service at the site. In addition, CBS12 News has attempted to contact the property's owner, who is based in New Jersey, but has not received a response. County officials said they are working on those requests. A memorial service honoring Roylynn is scheduled for next Saturday at Periwinkle Park, one of her favorite places, according to her family. Through a GoFundMe campaign , loved ones are raising money for a memorial bench at one of her favorite parks and donations to animal charities she cared about.

Lucie Nuclear Power Plant was manually shut down Wednesday morning after 3 control rods dropped into the reactor core, according to a notification filed with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).The manual reactor trip occurred at 9:47 a.m. 13, 2026, while Unit 1 was operating at 100% power. Decay heat is being removed by discharging steam to the main condenser using the turbine bypass valves and main feedwater. Thirty-six dogs are now safe and beginning a long road to recovery after being rescued from what officials are calling a "house of horror" in Palm City. The animals were discovered living in filth, covered in matted fur and their own feces. The horrific discovery has prompted state lawmakers and the Martin County Sheriff's Office to call for new laws to prevent this from happening again.The dogs were rushed to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which is now dealing with its second massive hoarding case in the last month.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Staff at the humane society are working around the clock to provide medical care and grooming for the traumatized animals. According to officials, the condition of the dogs was shocking."We're averaging about six pounds of mat per dog," one staff member said.Crews performing emergency grooming have found 4-inch shards of glass and metal hidden in the dense, matted fur. The shelter is using every available space to house and treat the animals, with 20 of the 36 dogs having been groomed so far.The severity of the situation drew a swift response from local leaders. State Representatives Meg Weinberger and John Snyder, State Senator Gayle Harrell, and Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek toured the facility to see the dogs' condition firsthand."It's time to really roll up our sleeves, get up to Tallahassee this session, and to try and make sure we're doing everything we can to make sure this never happens again," Rep. Snyder said."We need to work with our sheriffs in particular to really gain that experience as to what they are seeing out there," said Senator Harrell. "We need to empower our sheriffs to be able to take the steps that they are that they need to take from our conversations today. We need to empower them to do what's necessary to protect the animals."Rep. Weinberger added, "Sadly, I've seen cases like this, but this was really bad... the fact that nobody could get in to check on these dogs, it was horrific."The officials agreed that current laws are not enough. Sheriff Budensiek said the owner of the dogs had been a breeder years ago and called for more stringent regulations."We need some teeth in the breeder law where we can inspect them," Sheriff Budensiek stated. "And then, oh, by the way, after the fact, we're still going to come back and inspect to make sure you're following the parameters that we put forward."Despite the monstrous ordeal, some of the dogs are already showing signs of recovery. They are slowly learning what it is like to experience love, clean food, and water.For these 36 dogs, the journey is just beginning, but for the first time, they are safe.

Lucie Police Department officers have been placed on paid administrative leave as investigations continue into two separate incidents involving political campaign signs that occurred last week on Southwest Airoso Boulevard.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: 'I'm disappointed that she doesn't take accountability for her and her husband's actions,' Candidate Steven Giordano tells WPTV's Tyler HatfieldThe officers placed on leave effective Tuesday, are Lieutenant Aaron Martin, Lieutenant Jason Vega and Detective Sergeant Joseph Alves. Chief Leo Niemczyk made the decision following a review of the initial facts and timeline surrounding the incidents. Lucie Police Department released more information regarding the incidents over the weekend.The first incident occurred on Aug. 5 near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.WATCH BELOW: WPTV's Tyler Hatfield speaks with Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin after husband placed on administrative leaveDetectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on Aug. 7 near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Lt. Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Aaron Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Port St. Lucie police release details on 2 separate political campaign sign investigationsThe Port St. Lucie Police Department says it remains committed to ensuring all investigations are conducted fairly and impartially, maintaining its longstanding commitment to integrity, professionalism and accountability.Lt. Aaron Martin's wife is Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin, who is currently running for re-election.WPTV's Tyler Hatfield spoke with the mayor on Thursday, following the news that her husband is on paid administrative leave with the Port St. Lucie Police Department following the investigation."Whenever there's a criminal investigation of any kind, it's standard operating procedure for the police department to place people on administrative leave pending the outcome of an investigation," she said.She said she hopes the incident will not impact her campaign and Tuesday's primary election."This issue about signage and campaign signs has nothing to do with my campaign in terms of how I have been leading the city and how I will continue to lead the city and the important issues that we're facing here in Port St. Lucie," Mayor Shannon Martin said.When asked what she wanted to tell voters learning about her husband's leave in real time, the mayor pushed back on the framing of the situation."It was blown way out of proportion, but the process has to work the way that the process has to work in order to ensure fairness and transparency," she said. "So that process will go forward, but that has nothing to do with the elections. It has nothing to do with my campaign, whatsoever."The mayor said she intends to press forward despite the circumstances."It's a disappointing situation. However, I'm going to continue to move forward and making sure that I am continuing my campaign. And continuing to work to earn residents' votes," Shannon Martin said.When asked to comment on the investigation itself, the mayor declined."I cannot comment on that. It has nothing to do with me. I'm not part of that process whatsoever. I've never been part of that process as a mayor. That is not my role, and it will never be part of part of my process," she said.

A 52-year-old woman is dead after being shot Sunday morning in Vero Beach, and the Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching for a person of interest in what investigators are treating as a domestic violence homicide. At approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday, the sheriff's office received a 911 call reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street. Deputies located the woman with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home. Sheriff Eric Flowers identified the person of interest as 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian. Investigators believe Waggle and the victim were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle. "We have put out a nationwide BOLO for him at this point — be on the look out. Our team is working with real time crime center. Our detectives have been working on this all day and its our goal to ultimately locate him," Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle should be considered armed and dangerous. "If you encounter this person, don't approach him," Flowers said. "It's possible that he could harm other people or himself. We don't know those details so at this point we should treat it as a very serious situation," Flowers said. Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home. "My brother actually heard the shot," Cardenas said. "So he went inside to check on my sister." Cardenas said the neighborhood is typically quiet. "Nothing like this should happen, like especially in quiet neighborhoods," Cardenas said. He said he hopes an arrest comes soon. "I just hope that they find the suspect," Cardenas said. Flowers called the incident a tragedy and says detectives are using resources such as flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts. "At this point we're not sure but this could be a domestic violence incident. It's a loss of life that's so unnecessary," Flowers said. "So our team is committed to work on that." Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org , or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

A 99-year-old Boca Raton woman who lives on the fourth floor of her building has been left largely trapped in her home during elevator outages — and her family says building management has offered little help.Norma Schweitzer lives in Guildford-D, a building in Century Village Boca Raton. Her children reached out to WPTV toward the end of a three-week elevator outage caused by a part that needed to be replaced. The repair was made, but now the building is preparing for a separate six-week outage for a full elevator replacement.WATCH BELOW: 99-year-old trapped in 4th-floor home during elevator outagesAsked what the three-week outage felt like, Schweitzer replied, "Murder!" "It's boring because nobody's there, but yourself," she added.Her son, Neal Schweitzer, said the impact on his mother's daily life was immediate and severe."Your life stops. You know, a simple thing of my mom going down to the pool and visiting her friends, or going to the doctor, or getting her nails done —she couldn't do it," Neal Schweitzer said. "So it was not good, and there was no place to call, nobody to help. The management was not there for us."Neal Schweitzer said he and his siblings asked building management for help during the outage, but were told navigating the situation was their responsibility."The management said that this is a 55-and-over community. You could walk downstairs," Neal Schweitzer said.Norma Schweitzer relies on a wheelchair and a home health aide to get around."I can't walk! Can't put my foot down," Norma Schweitzer said.He said management's proposed solution for getting Norma out of her home was to call the fire department."We had to call the fire department for her to go to the doctor to get Palm Tran to take her," Neal Schweitzer said.Norma Schweitzer described the physical toll of that process on her fragile body."That's why I'm all black and blue, because they had to hold me under my arms," Norma Schweitzer said, showing dark bruises under her arms.With the six-week elevator replacement now approaching, the family says they still don't have a plan because they don't know when the project will start.Leigh Markowitz, an attorney with Disability Rights Florida, said the issue of elevator outages leaving seniors stranded in 55-and-older communities is widespread in South Florida."It's a really big issue, and we have been seeing a lot of people calling in about it," Markowitz said.Markowitz said residents in situations like Norma Schweitzer's have legal rights, and can formally request accommodations from building management."You can always request a reasonable accommodation, and that can take a lot of different forms," Markowitz said.She said accommodations could include a hotel stay or grocery delivery service, but in a 55-and-older community — where more residents may have mobility issues — even basic communication from management can make a significant difference."It's about giving notice and what can the residents do to prepare and how can management be as accommodating as possible," Markowitz said.The Schweitzer family said communication is exactly what they're asking for."I'd like them to at least let us know really what's going on," Neal Schweitzer said.The Century Village Boca Raton website currently shows no upcoming projects. WPTV tried calling FirstService Residential, the company that manages the community. A customer service agent said there was no way to reach corporate by phone, so I visited their Dania Beach headquarters and reached a spokesperson.A spokesperson for the Century Village board provided the written statement below:In response to follow-up questions, the board said it does not provide temporary housing or delivery accommodations during an elevator outage. However, it said it will provide residents with advance notice of the elevator replacement once more information is available and will continue to update residents on progress.If you are stuck at home because of an elevator outage, Disability Rights Florida has resources that can help.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A car crash occurred before the interview even started. Video footage captured heart-stopping moments— a child nearly being struck by a passing car, families desperately dodging traffic and children on e-bikes and scooters attempting the risky crossing."This road right here is a dangerous road," Pote said. "If the kids are going to school or not going to school, they speed up and down this road 24/7."The family is calling for immediate action before tragedy strikes, specifically requesting a crosswalk and school zone designation at Haverhill and Carver."Try to put a crosswalk in right here, and make it a school zone before someone gets hurt or killed," Pote urged.Neighbor Omar Trevino shares these safety concerns and explained why the existing crosswalk near Greenacres Christian Academy isn't a realistic solution– it's simply too far from Greenacres Elementary for families to use regularly."We need a crosswalk and a stoplight. You can't cross," Trevino said. "Cars can't cross, much less children."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County is set to welcome students Monday morning after construction delays postponed its opening by a week, according to school district officials. During a rescheduled open house on Friday, parents and students toured the new campus and shared their impressions. Eighth-grade student Isabella Conde is excited. "You saw the new school; what do you think? It's really nice; it's a lot bigger than my old school," Conde said. TRADITION LAKES K-8: ‘Could we have started Monday? Yes’: Superintendent explains decision to delay opening of Tradition Lakes K-8 Orlando Reyes helped his daughter set up a classroom earlier in the day. "Looks like it's ready to go? Yeah, it is; it is pretty much ready to go. I was here early this morning with my daughter to set up her room, and the room is really pretty nice," Reyes said. Kenneth Rozier, a worker who helped install the flooring, shared positive feedback. "Ah, it looks beautiful; everything looks beautiful. Yeah, everything looks wonderful. The school’s opening was delayed due to construction and final preparations taking longer than expected. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "Part of it was occupancy, but a lot of it was just the fact that there were a lot of things like textbooks, furniture, things weren’t put together. You know, you don’t want parents coming into empty classrooms or unfinished classrooms," said St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Jon Prince. Although some construction is still ongoing, the school is ready to begin the academic year. "So, it’s a phase construction. When the school is fully completed, it will have 1,800 students. But we capped it at 1,100. There’s one academic wing and the gym that will be finished in mid-September, and the last academic wing will probably be finished between September and October," Prince said. Crews are expected to continue working over the weekend, with much of the remaining work being cosmetic. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

The Port St Lucie mayor’s race is one of the races we are watching closely this week. And if you’ve been following of our coverage of the WastePro Settlement and the public’s frustration with trash pickup, you know, that is likely top of mind for voters. The current mayor, Shannon Martin, is fighting to hold on to that office. She’s facing two challengers, and both have been downright boisterous in their attacks on her leadership. They say she and other officials have botched the situation with garbage collection so badly that it’s time to overhaul City Hall. Dating back to the pandemic, trash has been a very serious matter in the city and now many residents say it's why the mayor’s race is in the balance. On the set of ARC Florida, the three candidates talked about the Waste Pro Settlement decision. They are Shannon Martin , Steve Giordano and Eric Strazzeri . The city told residents they would be getting a tax credit , not a refund check in the mail, after the city won $24 million; essentially, the prize money for suing WastePro for years of shoddy service. And not only would there be no cash back, sometime later, the cost of trash collection went up. Now, the question of how many times a week should trash be collected will be a ballot issue in November. Marco Ortiz is a small business owner. His Top Notch barbershop is a place where men talk about what's happening in the community, he says the conversation often turns to trash pickup, the hot topic as it were, going into this election. Lucie beautiful," Ortiz said. "Of course trash collection is important. It's hot, trash brings flies and it smells, we need more reliable service." The mayor’s race has also been overshadowed in recent days by a dispute over campaign signs that has led to a state investigation. Lucie police officers, including Mayor Shannon Martin’s husband, Lt. Aaron Martin, were placed on paid administrative leave as the Florida Department of Law Enforcement took over a criminal investigation into two campaign-sign incidents involving mayoral challenger Steve Giordano. One of those incidents involved a confrontation between Giordano and Aaron Martin over signs placed at a home, while another involved questions about whether a Martin campaign sign had been removed or replaced without the homeowner’s permission. We could know who the next mayor is this week, if there’s a clear majority winner, but if it's close, two finalists will advance to the General Election in November.

A longtime and "beloved" middle school teacher in Jupiter has died, the School District of Palm Beach County confirmed Monday. Jupiter Middle School principal Lisa Hastey said that Kevin Burns, a U.S. History and Civics teacher at the school for 20 years, passed away. Hastey's statement to families and staff over the weekend did not outline the cause of his death. "He maintained an unwavering commitment to education and will be deeply missed by all who knew him," said Hastey. "On behalf of the entire school, I have extended our sympathy and support to his family during this difficult time."According to the Jupiter Middle School website, Burns was the leader of the school's paddleboard club.Hastey said that school counselors will be available on campus to provide assistance. Additional counselors from the District's Department of Behavioral and Mental Health will also be at the school to provide support.School police will also be at school on Monday with a therapy dog to provide extra comfort and support.On Friday, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said crews responded to an open water incident in Jupiter at 7:15 p.m.When they arrived, fire rescue said that two individuals had been paddleboarding and were separated from their boards. One of the individuals made it to shore, but the other person was unable to. Fire Rescue said a search involving multiple agencies was then conducted, and the other paddleboarder was later located. Fire Rescue said both patients were taken to a local hospital but did not share any other details about the incident.Stay with WPTV and WPTV News for updates on this story.

A 52-year-old woman is dead after being shot Sunday morning in Vero Beach, and the Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching for a person of interest in what investigators are treating as a domestic violence homicide.At approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday, the sheriff's office received a 911 call reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street. Deputies located the woman with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead.Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home.Sheriff Eric Flowers identified the person of interest as 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian. Investigators believe Waggle and the victim were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle."We have put out a nationwide BOLO for him at this point — be on the look out. Our team is working with real time crime center. Our detectives have been working on this all day and its our goal to ultimately locate him," Flowers said.The sheriff said Waggle should be considered armed and dangerous."If you encounter this person, don't approach him," Flowers said. "It's possible that he could harm other people or himself. We don't know those details so at this point we should treat it as a very serious situation," Flowers said.Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home."My brother actually heard the shot," Cardenas said. "So he went inside to check on my sister."Cardenas said the neighborhood is typically quiet. "Nothing like this should happen, like especially in quiet neighborhoods," Cardenas said.He said he hopes an arrest comes soon. "I just hope that they find the suspect," Cardenas said.Flowers called the incident a tragedy and says detectives are using resources such as flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts. "At this point we're not sure but this could be a domestic violence incident. It's a loss of life that's so unnecessary," Flowers said. "So our team is committed to work on that."Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org, or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

This artist made a very realistic-looking toadstool. This artist crafted a beautiful pony. The children enjoyed a summer of creativity. VERO BEACH — The 90-year-old Vero Beach Art Club filled the summer with creativity, learning and plenty of smiles during its annual Summer Art Camp. Over the course of 10 weeks, 91 students from the Vero Beach area — along with a few children visiting their grandparents — took part in the popular program. Each week gave young artists an opportunity to explore their creativity while learning new skills and making new friends. Campers learned how to work cooperatively, listen to instructions and express themselves through art. They practiced drawing, experimented with mixing colors and created projects using paper, glue and other art materials. While the campers were busy creating, they also learned important lessons about patience, teamwork and following directions. Most importantly, they had fun and left camp smiling each day. This year’s Summer Art Camp was sponsored by Quail Valley Charities, whose support helped the Art Club provide the program to local children and families. The Vero Beach Art Club offers youth art camps three times a year, giving children opportunities to participate during school breaks. Camps are offered during the week following the Christmas holiday break, during spring break and throughout summer break. The programs are designed to introduce children to art in a welcoming, hands-on environment where they can explore different materials and techniques while building confidence and friendships. Parents interested in learning more about upcoming youth art camps can call the Vero Beach Art Club at 772-231-0303 or visit the club at 1903 14th Ave. The club is open Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m. More information about the Vero Beach Art Club and its youth programs is available at www.verobeachartclub.org . Monday’s city commission meeting begins at 5:05 p.m. in the Fort Pierce City Hall commission chambers. FORT PIERCE–Mayor Linda Hudson Monday urged city staff to begin an immediate search for a successor to City Attorney Sara Hedges whose employment contract was not renewed by a 3-2 vote of city commissioners June 8. “We need to make sure we have a city attorney as soon as possible,” said Hudson, who voted with Commissioner Michael Broderick June 8 against a motion to not renew Hedges contract for another year. “We don’t have a lot of time and we need a city attorney.” Deputy City Manager DeVoshay Johnson said the city’s human resources department had already been activated to begin the search, saying most of the city’s top lawyers have been hired from outside existing ranks. Hedges had been an assistant city attorney before being tapped to head the legal team in September 2023. Under terms of Hedges’ existing contract, the city was required to give her notice by June 15 if commissioners planned not to renew it. The existing contract now officially ends in mid-September, although officials hinted that departure negotiations could see Hedges leave sooner. Before the vote June 8 not to renew Hedges’ contract, she had offered her resignation, effective Dec. Under terms of the existing contrast, the city has the right to terminate her employment “with or without cause” at any time. Severance provisions can be invoked in some circumstances if the city ends the contract before its Sept. Hedges’ tenure became an issue in May, following controversy over the handling of a wage garnishment for an unpaid credit card account owed by Johnna Morris, city finance director. Morris was originally suspended after the garnishment order was received and there were allegations that Hedges had ordered Morris to be terminated as a result. Internal city communications obtained by Hometown News have not substantiated that. City officials also have suggested there has been friction between Hedges and City Manager Richard Chess over Chess’ wish to consult outside counsel in the matter and Hedges’ claim that Chess was excluding her from staff employment issues. Both Hedges and Commissioner Broderick had suggested there could be other issues involved in the friction that city leaders don’t want aired publicly. They did not elaborate on what those might be. The city may hire an outside recruiter to help with the attorney search and consult with the Florida League of Cities and the Florida Association of Counties for assistance. A person died after being shot Wednesday night at a residence in the Seminole Mobile Home Park community, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies with the Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau and personnel from the St. Lucie County Fire District responded to the 3300 block of Orange Avenue at approximately 9:11 p.m. 12 following reports of a shooting. According to investigators, the initial caller reported that an individual had been shot while allegedly attempting to enter a residence. When deputies arrived, they found the victim suffering from a gunshot wound. The individual was transported to a local hospital, where they were later pronounced dead. Detectives with the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators responded to both the scene and the hospital as the investigation unfolded. Authorities later obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, where they recovered a firearm believed to have been used in the shooting. Investigators remained at the scene overnight, processing evidence and conducting interviews. Detectives and crime scene personnel completed their work and cleared the residence at approximately 6:11 a.m. The circumstances leading up to the shooting remain under investigation. At this time, authorities believe the incident was isolated and say there is no known immediate threat to the surrounding community. Anyone with information about the shooting, including possible witnesses or those with relevant video footage, is asked to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-3230. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-TIPS (8477). Continental Shooting Center in Stuart is rallying behind the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, collecting hundreds of donations just one day into a fundraiser for rescued border collies involved in a recent animal hoarding case.WATCH: Donations pour in to help hoarded dogsThe shooting center is raffling off an exclusive membership with higher-level perks for every $5 donation, can of dog food, or blanket brought in to the range. All donations go to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which is caring for 36 border collies and over 100 other animals from another animal hoarding case a few weeks ago.Matthew Olivo, vice president of Continental Shooting Center, said the conditions the dogs endured motivated the business to act."These dogs just the deplorable conditions that they had to survive in—we figured they deserve a chance and we're in a position to be able to offer them some help," Olivo said.The fundraiser launched Thursday, and the response from the community was immediate. Daniel Martelle, a customer service representative at Continental Shooting Center, described the turnout."So surprising. I mean we opened the doors at 10 am and we had people outside at 9 o'clock looking for carts to bring stuff in. We took in over 125 cans today over 25 blankets," Martelle said.The shooting range has also accepted a number of monetary donations.The shelter says staff are working around the clock to nurse all of the dogs back to health, but treatment has become costly. Sarah Fisher, communications manager for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said financial support is the most urgent need."Our biggest need right now is monetary donations towards our emergency medical fund. I think we're going through that fund just daily by the minute," Fisher said.Olivo said the effort reflects a broader responsibility to those who cannot speak for themselves."We've got to stand up for the weakest among us and somebody's got to be their voice and bring them the help they need when they need it," Olivo said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. For Delores Roundtree, a fresh coat of paint turned into something much more.Roundtree has lived in her house since 1973 and has been part of the neighborhood for about 65 years. Two years ago, her home became the focus of a community project when local police officers and volunteers repainted the exterior.WATCH BELOW: Fresh coat of paint spark lasting bond between resident, policeWhat began as a one-day effort has since grown into a deep, family-like relationship between Roundtree and Officer Cherrise Knight."Oh, it was a blessing. First from God above, next from the city," Roundtree said. "I was just over-blessed, overwhelmed. I was so happy, and everybody was so kind and so good, so loving, and I look at it; it was a blessing from the sky."As officers worked on the house, they noticed her address was posted above the carport but hard to see from the street. That raised concerns about how easily paramedics or firefighters could find her home in an emergency.One of the officers, Officer Borum, called his station for permission to go to Lowe's and buy new house numbers. He later installed them himself."He said that he wanted to go to Lowe's to buy some numbers for my house," Roundtree said. "When he brought the numbers, he said, 'Now I'm going to put them up there …' and he placed the numbers up there, and I thought that was so wonderful, a blessing."The paint job itself was a major effort. About 50 people came to help, finishing the work in roughly four hours."I thought it was going to take two or three days," Roundtree said. "They were finished within about four hours. It was just that many."Borumlater introduced her to Knight. Roundtree, who describes herself as someone who "just loves people," said she quickly grew attached to the officers, in part because they showed such concern for her."They were concerned about me. That made me feel so wonderful, and we've just been friends ever since," she said.Knight said the relationship is the deepest community connection she has made through such a project. "It's a really good relationship," Knight said. Roundtree, I consider her to be my grandma. I always have to come and check on her."Knight visits about every one to two months, depending on her workload. If too much time passes, she knows she will hear about it."If we don't check on her … when we come, we know we're gonna be in trouble," Knight said. "She was gonna put a warrant out for your arrest if you didn't come see me."During the visits, Roundtree fills Knight in on family reunions, visitors and neighborhood activity. When she spots patrol cars outside, she often checks to see whether it is Knight or another officer she knows.The friendship stands out at a time when relationships between police and residents are often strained.Knight said being welcomed into someone's home on a positive note is a powerful reminder of why many officers join the profession."It means everything to me," Knight said. "It's a great feeling knowing that we're wanted, not just when a crime happens or like a traffic stop or something like that. She wants to see us on a good note. So that means everything."Roundtree said she still remembers the day multiple officers came to her door unexpectedly."I said, 'Now I didn't call the policeman. I haven't done anything,'" she said. "And when I looked and saw who they were, oh, I came to the door. They just came to see how I was doing, and that made me feel so wonderful."Now, when Roundtree looks at her freshly painted home and the clearly visible house numbers, she sees more than an upgraded exterior."Everybody come out here, I tell them what happened to me and my painting, and the people," Roundtree said. "When they finished, I said, 'Oh, we got to take a picture,' and I got right on in front of it. I'm telling you, I was so happy."For Roundtree and Knight, a simple act of service — repainting a house — has grown into a lasting example of what can happen when police and community members meet not over a crisis, but over kindness.In simple terms, "I love her. She loves me," Knight said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
