Amendment 3 has new wording, but the same policy.Attorney General James Uthmeier released a court-ordered rewrite Thursday, 10 days after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank ruled that the original title and summary were biased, misleading and inaccurate.WATCH BELOW: Florida releases court-ordered rewrite of Amendment 3 First reported by the Tampa Bay Times, the new title, "Increased Homestead Exemption; Lower Cap on Increases in Non-Homestead Property Assessments," replaces "Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes," which Frank called more of a political slogan than a neutral description.The rewrite also removes claims that the amendment "benefits" taxpayers, "protects small businesses," "ensures" core services and guarantees "fairness" for Florida residents.Instead, it spells out the mechanics.The measure would raise the homestead exemption for non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments after that. The old language only mentioned the $250,000 exemption, even though it would not take effect until the second year.The rewrite also makes clear there is no required schedule to eliminate non-school homestead property taxes. Lawmakers would instead create a process allowing local governments to raise the exemption further, potentially up to a home's full assessed value.It also says the annual assessment-growth cap would drop from 10% to 5% for all non-homestead property, including rentals, vacation homes and commercial buildings, not just small businesses.New Florida residents would receive the existing exemption after qualifying for homestead, but would not receive the larger exemption until their fifth year of claiming it.Former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes, a plaintiff in one of the consolidated challenges, welcomed the rewrite."Finally, the practicing attorneys took control of the language," Brandes said in a text. "The text is honest about what the amendment does. I hope Florida voters will dig deeper, ask hard questions, and understand the consequences before they decide the outcome."Opponents say the clearer language does not fix what they consider a flawed proposal."The revised ballot language in response to the court's ruling more accurately represents the underlying policy for voters," Florida Policy Institute CEO Sadaf Knight said. "However, the amendment’s harmful potential impacts remain the same."State analysts estimate the measure would eventually reduce recurring local property-tax revenue by nearly $12 billion annually. Opponents warn that could mean service cuts or higher taxes and fees elsewhere."The language on voters' ballots may have changed, but Amendment 3 is still a scam and a tax shift," said Jackson Peel, communications director for Save Our Services–No on 3.Gov. Ron DeSantis, who pushed the proposal, argues homeowners need relief from rapidly rising local property-tax collections and local governments can rein in spending.Amendment 3 needs at least 60% support to pass in November. If approved, it would take effect Jan.

A Riviera Beach woman who survived a brutal domestic violence attack that left her hospitalized with possible brain injuries is now receiving protections under a new Florida law that includes pets as part of domestic violence cases, according to state Rep. Debra Tendrich.WATCH BELOW: 'If you're going through a domestic violence situation, there are ways to get out,' Rep. Debra Tendrich tells WPTV's Kayla McDermottThe attack occurred around midnight when the suspect repeatedly struck the victim with his fists, a cell phone and a flat iron, according to a probable cause affidavit. Police say the man choked the woman until she may have briefly lost consciousness, prevented her from calling for help and dragged her back inside when she tried to escape.The suspect also choked the victim's small dog and attempted to drown it in a sink while threatening the woman, telling her the animal's injuries served as a warning of what would happen if she contacted law enforcement, investigators said.The woman was taken to St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach with severe head and ear injuries. Medical personnel warned of a possible brain bleed, according to police reports. Officers found blood spatter on the walls inside the Riviera Beach home.The suspect now faces multiple charges including aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, felony domestic battery by strangulation, false imprisonment, tampering with a 911 device and animal cruelty.The case has drawn attention from Tendrich, D-Lake Worth Beach, who said it demonstrates why Florida expanded domestic violence protections under legislation that took effect July 1, 2024."This was a horrible case. Every case of domestic violence is bad, but this one truly highlights multiple components in one," Tendrich told WPTV. "Not only what she went through was awful, but to know that your pet and the place that you lay your head at night is not your safe place … it's a pretty devastating situation."Tendrich, who has publicly described herself as a domestic violence survivor, authored the legislation after hearing from victims and law enforcement that abusers frequently use pets to manipulate partners and prevent them from leaving relationships.Previously, Florida law largely focused on pets only after they had been harmed or killed. The updated law expands injunction protections to include pets, service animals and emotional support animals, recognizing threats against animals as part of a broader pattern of abuse."One of the biggest things that pops out … was that pets were used as manipulation tools and pawns to keep the victims there," Tendrich said. "A lot of times the victim will not leave, because they know that their pet will be harmed or killed in the process."The Riviera Beach attack underscores the critical importance of recognizing strangulation as one of the strongest predictors of escalating domestic violence, according to Tendrich."If someone is willing to wrap their hands around someone's neck and stop them from breathing, they are able to kill that person," she said. "When we see someone who's willing to take that to strangulation, next time they might not end up breathing."Research cited by domestic violence experts shows victims who have been strangled by an intimate partner face significantly increased odds of later being killed by that partner.The new legislation also increases relocation assistance available through a state trust fund for victims attempting to leave abusive situations.Tendrich described domestic violence as "one of our largest public safety crises" in Florida, noting many cases remain hidden because abuse often extends beyond visible physical injuries."There's also other types of domestic violence that don't even cause physical bruises," she said. "Controlling finances, withholding medications, withholding basic needs, isolation, surveillance."She emphasized that leaving an abusive relationship often represents the most dangerous period for victims."A lot of people don't realize that leaving is the dangerous part for many people," Tendrich said. "When you leave, when you get law enforcement involved or the courts involved, that is when it becomes the most dangerous time for the victim."Victim advocates in Palm Beach County are now helping the Riviera Beach woman navigate medical care, mental health support and housing safety options, according to Tendrich."Walking back into that house, she's going to be walking into that memory of what happened yesterday," she said. "There's also going to be a lot of fear to make sure that he is held accountable for his actions."Tendrich encouraged anyone experiencing domestic violence to seek help and develop a safety plan with local agencies or advocates."If you are in a situation and you're going through a domestic violence situation, there are ways for you to get out," she said. You don't have to endure."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The owner of a beloved West Palm Beach tea house says she was asked to vacate her location, leaving customers heartbroken and the future of the 28-year-old business uncertain.Audrey Farrelly has owned Serenity Garden Tea House & Cafe, located at Dixie Highway and Vallette Way, for 13 years. She said the eviction notice came suddenly.WATCH BELOW: Beloved West Palm Beach tea house faces eviction after 28 years "Honestly, I was asked to vacate, and that's like the bottom line," Farrelly said.When Farrelly posted the news on the Serenity Tea House Facebook page, customers responded with words like "sad news," "so sorry," and "great memories.""Emotional, and I have a full heart with the love and appreciation," Farrelly said.Some customers have been coming to the tea house for as long as Farrelly has owned it, and the connection runs deep. Much of the china and teacups inside the café were donated by guests over the years."The majority of all of this is donations by guests that have come in here, either they had a passing or are moving out, there's people I can say hello to when I come in the morning, I know they gave me a cup, I know they gave me this," Farrelly said.For regulars, the loss feels personal."For me, it was heartbreaking; it was like a family member was moving away, and we weren't going to see them anymore, so," customer Lorianne Porcelain told WPTV on Friday. "This place has always been so dear to our hearts because it's like a sweet place where you can come and just enjoy your family."She worries the closure is another sign of rapid development reshaping West Palm Beach."Are they just going to knock it down and build something here?" Porcelain said. "How heartbreaking to take such a tradition, something so rooted in our community, and take it away from us when it brings such joy to all the people who live here," Porcelain said.The teahouse is inside a structure built in 1919 as a home when pineapple groves surrounded the city.Farrelly, a native of Dublin, Ireland, who has lived in West Palm Beach for 16 years, said she does not know why she is being evicted. WPTV tried contacting the property owner on Friday and did not hear back.Despite the uncertainty, Farrelly is not giving up on the tea house."I'm switching this over to a positive thing. I'm going to find a good home for the tea house; this happened for a reason, and we're just going to find a location," Farrelly said.The last high tea at the current South Dixie location will be held on Aug. 23.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Indian River County works to extradite murder suspect arrested in West Virginia
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's Office is working to bring Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, back to Florida to face a first-degree murder charge in the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, outside her Vero Beach home in the 500 block of 1st Street on Aug. 16. U.S. Marshals deputies arrested Waggle on Aug. 19 at a motel in Dunbar, West Virginia, about six miles west of Charleston. Sheriff Eric Flowers announced at a press conference on Aug. 21 that the gun found near the scene belonged to the ex-wife of Waggle, who was also at the same motel where he was arrested.

Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewicz and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation. Kriskewicz, a hairdresser, had expressed concerns about Waggle to her coworkers at a hair salon. She had told her coworkers that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him and asked them to tell him she was not there.

Sheriff Flowers credited the Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle. He said without the Flock system, the office would not have been able to announce Waggle's arrest four days after the homicide. The sheriff said the system helped investigators piece together Waggle's movements after the shooting.

Waggle's ex-wife is still being questioned by detectives. Sheriff Flowers said investigators do not know the extent of her communication with Waggle or whether she knew his plans. She is not currently facing any charges. Indian River County detectives responded to a 911 call on Aug. 16 about a woman lying in the roadway at the 1st Street address.

cards.headline: Sheriff credits license plate readers in Vero Beach murder case
cards.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said automated license plate readers helped investigators track Matthew Waggle after the Aug. 16 fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewicz in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Sheriff Eric Flowers credited the agency's Real Time Crime Center and a network of license plate readers with helping investigators piece together Matthew Waggle's movements and locate him after the Aug. 16 fatal shooting in Vero Beach. Waggle was arrested on Aug. 19 at a motel in West Virginia in connection with the death of Dawn Kriskewicz.

Flowers said the Flock automated license plate reader system was crucial to the investigation. He said the agency has made many cases and protected the community as a result of the system. The sheriff addressed critics of the technology, saying the murder suspect was captured because of the system.

Flowers clarified that Flock is one brand of automated license plate reader used by law enforcement. The system helped investigators track Waggle's movements from the scene of the shooting in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach.

cards.headline: Vero Beach hairdresser killed outside home, ex-boyfriend charged
cards.teaser: Matthew Waggle, 32, of Sebastian was arrested in West Virginia in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, outside her home on First Street in Vero Beach on Aug. 16.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced the arrest of Matthew Waggle in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewicz on First Street in Vero Beach early Sunday morning, Aug. 16. Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewicz and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said Kriskewicz had expressed concerns about Waggle to her coworkers at a hair salon. She had told her coworkers that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him and asked them to tell him she was not here. Flowers said Waggle was at the scene for 10 to 15 minutes at most and murdered Kriskewicz in cold blood in the street.

Waggle was found at a motel in West Virginia. Officials said the gun used in the shooting belonged to Waggle's ex-wife, who was at the same hotel where Waggle was arrested. Sheriff Flowers said investigators do not know the extent of their communication or whether she knew Waggle's plans. The ex-wife is still being questioned and is not currently facing any charges.

hero.headline: Disciplined St. Lucie County firefighters challenge district investigation at public meeting
hero.teaser: Three terminated firefighters are questioning the integrity of an investigation into alleged hazing incidents at the St. Lucie County Fire District.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District faced community pressure Wednesday to reinstate five disciplined firefighters, with the terminated employees alleging the investigation into hazing incidents was limited and mischaracterized. Three firefighters were terminated and two were suspended following an independent investigation into alleged hazing incidents. Videos surfaced that appeared to show the firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees.

Jordon Hutchinson, one of the terminated firefighters, told the meeting that the disciplinary action was retaliation for filing complaints against district leadership. Many residents at the meeting argued that the investigation produced a limited report, with some allegations reviewed internally and others by independent investigators.

A motion was made to suspend the district chief and attorney, but the vote failed 4-1. The dispute has now moved to arbitration. Hutchinson said the firefighters are still trying to fix the process even after being fired.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office searches for missing man last seen Thursday morning
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is searching for Benton Doyle Tomlin, who was last seen at 2 a.m. Thursday. Authorities believe Tomlin may be endangered.

Tomlin is described as being 6 feet 1 inch tall, weighing 200 pounds, and having brown hair and brown eyes. The sheriff's office did not disclose where Tomlin was last seen.

Anyone who has seen Tomlin is asked to call 911 or contact Detective Corporal Drawdy at 772-462-3230. The sheriff's office released the missing person alert Friday morning.

The search for Tomlin comes as law enforcement agencies across the Treasure Coast continue to respond to missing person cases. The sheriff's office is asking the public for help locating Tomlin as quickly as possible.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Fire District board rejects motion to suspend chief and attorney
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District board voted down a motion to suspend the fire chief and district attorney after more than two hours of discussion about hazing allegations.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District board met Wednesday to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation.

After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it. The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing.

Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying it was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate. Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Stuart's Bathtub Beach
hero.teaser: Deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man who had swum more than 300 yards into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon.
hero.body:
Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life.

Deputy John Wilkes said the man was probably more than 300 yards from shore when he arrived on scene. Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was in a very distressed emotional state and advised that he was having relationship issues and issues with his direct family. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted.

Castoro said he built a rapport with the man and encouraged him to keep living. Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made.
hero.article_text: Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man faces five sexual activity with minor charges after SWAT operation
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz on Thursday morning after executing a search warrant at a residence in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. Vinz faces five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. Officers arrested Vinz without incident during the operation. The response drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Authorities said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry into the home.

Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024.

Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation and say they are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. Martinez said officers take cases involving children very seriously.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce brewery to host Sunday church services starting in September
cards.teaser: The Sailfish Brewery in downtown Fort Pierce will host Sunrise City Chapel church services on Sunday mornings, combining a relaxed atmosphere with a new place for worship.
cards.body:
The Sailfish Brewery in downtown Fort Pierce will soon host Sunrise City Chapel church services on Sunday mornings. Pastor Thomas Neiman, a longtime Fort Pierce resident and former firefighter, paramedic, and chaplain with the St. Lucie County Fire District, shared his gratitude for the brewery owners' support in welcoming the church. When Tommy came by, he was like, 'Hey, man, what do you think about a church and a brewery?' And I was like, 'Yeah, let's do this. Because, you know, taprooms and breweries are more family friendly than most other places that you go to,' said Gabe Atkinson, production manager at Sailfish Brewery.

The sermons will take place outside and be broadcast on indoor television screens. A kids zone will also be available for parents to drop off their children during the service. Acknowledging the unusual concept of a church inside a brewery, the organizers plan to embrace the fun side of the idea by encouraging people to share family friendly riddles and jokes on the church website. The church will hold its first service at the brewery starting in September.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County fire district board debates hazing allegations and leadership suspension
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District board met Wednesday to discuss hazing allegations and the termination of three firefighters during a contentious meeting.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District board met Wednesday to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation. After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it.

The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing. Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying it was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate. Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on 5 sexual activity with minor charges after SWAT operation
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz early Thursday morning on five counts of sexual activity with a minor and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child after executing a search warrant at a home in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. Thursday and arrested Vinz without incident.

The SWAT operation drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry. Martinez said the devices are used for the safety of both officers and the individual during high-risk operations.

Vinz faces five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024.

Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation. Martinez said police take cases involving children very seriously. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending.

Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewic and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle to her co-workers at a hair salon. She had actually told her co-workers out at the hair salon, If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I'm not here, Flowers said during a news conference Thursday. He was there for 10, 15 minutes tops. He murdered her in cold blood in the street, Flowers said.

The sheriff credited the Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle at a motel in West Virginia. Without Flock, I'm not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia. So for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system, Flowers said.

hero.headline: Brightline station in downtown Stuart unlikely after Martin County denied federal funding
hero.body:
Martin County will not receive federal funding for a proposed Brightline station in downtown Stuart through the Intercity Passenger Rail Program, making the future of the project uncertain. The railroad bridge project in Stuart, a replacement for the century-old St.

U.S. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., who represents District 21 in the U.S. House of Representatives, said additional federal funding for a station is unlikely. Mast raised concerns about the structure of the proposed project, saying it is extremely problematic that the potential Brightline station would be entirely taxpayer-funded at the various levels, from federal all the way down to the local municipalities, with Brightline not putting anything into it. He said the company had no interest in examining whether they should build something less expensive.

John Dial, a mariner and owner of At the Helm Training, welcomed the bridge funding but expressed reservations about using public money for a private company's station. Christopher Vitale, the manager at the Old Colorado Inn, said a Brightline station would benefit the local economy and expressed hope that community leaders find another path forward. Jenna McGrew, a local resident, said federal tax dollars should go to things that help better the community, and a Brightline station would definitely help better the community.

Martin County released a statement saying it is pleased to see the announcement of federal funding for a Brightline station in Cocoa Beach, as well as additional federal funding awarded to the City of Stuart for the St. Lucie River Railroad Bridge. The county said it recognizes the importance of supporting and investment in transportation projects that benefit residents, strengthen local businesses and contribute to the continued economic vitality of the state. Tony Scozzafava, a resident, said he hopes the county can find an alternative approach to secure funding for the station.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Bathtub Beach in Stuart
cards.teaser: Martin County deputies, lifeguards and marine units saved a man who was attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon.
cards.body:
Martin County deputies, lifeguards and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning and was probably 300-plus yards from the shore, according to Deputy John Wilkes.

Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was obviously in a very distressed emotional state and was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues and issues with his direct family. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living, relating over being fathers and discussing that it can be tough being a man and having emotions.

Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him and that there were a lot of people out there trying to help him, which changed his demeanor. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made.

Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. hero.headline: Donalds pledges 20% insurance cut, backs data centers as Florida governor's race pivots to general election
hero.body:
Republican nominee Byron Donalds promised to reduce Florida property insurance costs by another 20% to 25% through regulatory changes and defended data center development as the governor's race shifts from the August primary to a November contest against Democratic nominee David Jolly. In a recent interview, Donalds outlined positions on property taxes, insurance, school vaccine requirements and data centers that now define the campaign.

Donalds supports Amendment 3, which would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for Floridians who establish permanent residency by the end of 2026. The measure would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. New residents would face a five-year phase-in before qualifying for the full exemption. A legislative financial analysis estimates the amendment would reduce local non-school property-tax revenue by nearly $5 billion in its first full fiscal year, with the recurring impact projected to approach $11.9 billion by the 2031-32 fiscal year. Donalds called the amendment a first step and suggested Florida should eventually consider a multi-tiered taxing system that treats counties differently based on property values and economic output. He did not spell out how the tiers would work or how local governments would replace lost revenue.

On insurance, Donalds said regulatory changes could push costs down another 20% to 25%. His ideas include changing the Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund, lowering reinsurance costs and making home-hardening grants more efficient. Donalds specifically pointed to the catastrophe fund's 25% cash buildup factor, which insurers pay on top of actuarially calculated premiums. He said the state could eliminate the charge or create a formula that turns it down when the fund has healthy reserves and raises it when the balance falls. Donalds did not provide an independent analysis showing how the changes would produce the promised savings or how quickly homeowners would see them.

Data center development has become the main division with Jolly. Donalds supports building the facilities with safeguards including closed-loop water-cooling systems, protections for residential utility customers and restrictions keeping large centers away from homes. Jolly has proposed a statewide moratorium while Florida studies environmental protections, long-term economic effects and privacy and security concerns connected to AI. A Seeking Rents analysis of state campaign-finance records estimated that roughly $5.8 million in donations and outside spending connected to AI investors, utilities and data-center interests had benefited Donalds. A Gallup survey released in May found 71% of Americans opposed building an AI data center in their local area, including 48% who strongly opposed it.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on 5 sexual activity with minor charges after SWAT operation
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested a 48-year-old man Thursday morning on multiple charges involving a minor after the department's SWAT team served a search warrant at a home in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. Officers took Virgil Jason Vinz into custody without incident around 6 a.m. He faces five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor.

Neighbors reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry. He said the devices are used for the safety of both officers and individuals during high-risk operations. Martinez said officers take any case involving a child very seriously but are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active.

Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024.

Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation.

hero.headline: Sebastian man arrested in West Virginia for Vero Beach homicide after Flock license plate readers track multi-state flight
hero.body:
Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel and faces a first-degree murder charge in the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, a Vero Beach hairdresser, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. The arrest ended a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that Kriskewic had recently ended things with him. Kriskewic had told her co-workers that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him. Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from West Virginia to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence after being dropped off around the corner, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area.

After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators. The sheriff's office real-time crime center tracked Waggle's movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. U.S. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife.

Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic's body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night. Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges in Indian River County.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County fire board meeting draws calls to reinstate three fired firefighters over hazing allegations
cards.teaser: Community members packed a Wednesday board meeting to support three firefighters fired following a hazing investigation. Nearly every public speaker urged the St. Lucie County Fire District board to bring the men back.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting Wednesday turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations. The packed meeting lasted about three hours, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them.

The St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others last month over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired.

Fire Chief Jeff Lee told the crowd he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. Lee acknowledged the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. The dispute is now in arbitration. A motion to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney failed during the meeting. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting.

The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

hero.headline: SUV driver hospitalized after collision with Brightline train in Hobe Sound
hero.body:
An SUV collided with a northbound Brightline train Thursday morning in Hobe Sound, sending the driver to the hospital with traumatic injuries. The crash occurred just before 11 a.m. near the intersection of Southeast Dixie Highway and Southeast Crossrip Street.

Martin County Fire Rescue crews transported the man to a local hospital. Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to the scene and are working to determine the cause of the collision.

All train tracks in the area have been reopened following the incident. Martin County Fire Rescue and the Martin County Sheriff's Office handled the emergency response.

The proper investigative agencies have been notified of the collision. The incident marks another collision between a vehicle and Brightline trains that run through Martin County communities.

The crash occurred just before 11 a.m. when an SUV collided with a northbound Brightline train near the intersection of Southeast Dixie Highway and Southeast Crossrip Street. The man driving the SUV sustained traumatic injuries and was taken to a local hospital. Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies also responded to the scene, and are working to determine the cause of the collision. All train tracks in the area have since been reopened following the incident.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Bathtub Beach in Stuart
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and marine units rescued a man who swam hundreds of yards into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon after he called a suicide hotline saying he intended to end his life.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, lifeguards, and marine units rescued a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life.

The man had already swum approximately 300 yards from shore when Deputy John Wilkes arrived on scene. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was in a very distressed emotional state and advised that he was having relationship issues and issues with his direct family. The man told deputies the ocean was peaceful for him and he wanted to swim out until he got tired.

Castoro built a rapport with the man and encouraged him to keep living, relating over being fathers. Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him and changed his demeanor, deciding not to end his life that day. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made.
cards.article_text: Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. hero.headline: Florida school camera lawsuits face dismissals as judges side with automated enforcement systems
hero.body:
Legal challenges to automated school bus and school zone cameras that have generated more than 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in fines across Florida are hitting roadblocks as judges dismiss cases and rule against drivers contesting tickets. Miami-based Attorney Gino Moreno filed three lawsuits last year after drivers hit with $225 school bus camera fines had no way to challenge their citations because the cameras started operating without proper due process in place. Since then, a judge dismissed his federal case in Polk County, a revised complaint remains pending in Miami-Dade, and a Hillsborough County case filed on behalf of client Stanley Shultz awaits a decision on whether it will move forward.

Shultz, who lives in Plant City, was fined for illegally passing a school bus even though video from his citation shows the bus warning lights never flashed. Shultz appealed the fine, but a judge in Tallahassee upheld it despite state law requiring appeals must be heard by local hearing officers. Shultz is now accusing the county of not following state rules for appeal hearings. Legal questions extend beyond school buses to school speed zone cameras, with drivers fined when school was not in session or when signs directing them to slow down when flashing never flashed.

Questions have also emerged about the camera devices themselves. The radar inside the cameras, which state law requires to be approved by the state, is not approved. The state maintains it is exempt. Attorney Ira Karmelin with The Ticket Clinic has successfully used that argument to get school speed zone tickets thrown out, but judges are now starting to side with the state claim of exemption, even though the exemption refers to a radar design, not the device itself.

Since the cameras began operating in Florida, they have generated well over 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in paid fines as of earlier this year. While these legal challenges continue to hit roadblocks, judges have left the door open for appeals or new legal arguments. Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp have been tracking the problems with these automated school cameras for nearly three years.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg investor cuts $41,000 in annual costs by replacing contractors with AI
cards.teaser: A Florida real estate investor says artificial intelligence handles nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation, from marketing to bookkeeping.
cards.body:
Alex Jandick, owner of 131 Cash Home Buyers in St. Petersburg, now relies on an AI agent called Claude to handle nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation, saving him more than $41,000 a year. Before making the switch, Jandick was paying $2,500 a month for marketing and nearly $1,000 a month for a bookkeeper. Claude currently handles both for $100 a month. After spending about two weeks setting up and fine-tuning the system, Jandick said the results were immediate.

Jandick says he and Claude essentially split the workload. A human still has to verify the information and input the correct prompts. Jandick is the sole employee of his company, meaning no workers were displaced when he made the switch. After posting online about his AI-driven savings, he faced criticism. According to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report, AI will displace 92 million jobs globally by 2030. However, the same report projects 170 million new roles will open up, a net gain of 78 million jobs worldwide. A separate 2026 Goldman Sachs study estimates 300 million jobs globally are exposed to automation by AI.
cards.article_text: A Florida investor tells Scripps News Group Tampa Bay reporter Michael Paluska that artificial intelligence has become his most valuable business partner — one that never takes a day off, never calls in sick, and never asks for a paycheck.Alex Jandick, owner of 131 Cash Home Buyers in St. Petersburg, says he now relies on an AI agent called Claude to handle nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation — from marketing to bookkeeping — saving him more than $41,000 a year.Before making the switch, Jandick was paying $2,500 a month for marketing and nearly $1,000 a month for a bookkeeper."Did you tell them that you replaced them with AI?" Paluska asked."Nope. I just let them go," Jandick said.Claude currently handles both for $100 a month."So what does Claude do now for the marketing side?" Paluska asked."Everything, everything that I tell it to," Jandick said. "I sit in my office, and I tell a robot, Claude, what to do."After spending about two weeks setting up and fine-tuning the system, Jandick said the results were immediate."It's like holy smokes! This is — it was everything that I had wanted to get done at a cheaper rate for a year," Jandick said.Now, Jandick says he and Claude essentially split the workload. A human still has to verify the information and input the correct prompts. But the AI takes it from there."I put in 25 to 30 hours a week, and I have Claude probably putting in 25 to 30 hours a week," Jandick said.Jandick is the sole employee of his company, meaning no workers were displaced when he made the switch. Still, after posting online about his AI-driven savings, he faced criticism."I get that there's going to be haters out there," Jandick said.He pushed back directly."I'm saving $41,000 per year; for me, that is an incredible amount of money. That's my kids' college savings funds."The broader question of how many jobs AI could eliminate remains unsettled. According to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report, AI will displace 92 million jobs globally by 2030. However, the same report projects 170 million new roles will open up — a net gain of 78 million jobs worldwide. A separate 2026 Goldman Sachs study estimates 300 million jobs globally are exposed to automation by AI, though that research did not cite specific numbers for job gains.For Jandick, the technology has changed more than just his bottom line. He said he used to feel isolated working alone. Now, he tells Paluska, that has changed."Before Claude, I did get lonely," Jandick said. Now, I wake up in the morning with a bit more energy. I'm more excited because it's like I don't have to work so hard to break even each month. You know, it does take a little bit of legwork to get all set up and everything, but I have not found anything that is a better cost cutter than AI at this point," Jandick said.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on sexual activity with minor charges after SWAT operation
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie police arrested Virgil Jason Vinz early Thursday after executing a search warrant at a home on SW Jaslo Avenue.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested Virgil Jason Vinz early Thursday morning after executing a search warrant at a residence in the 900 block of SW Jaslo Avenue. During the operation, Vinz was taken into custody on an arrest warrant without injury. Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor.

The police response drew attention from nearby residents, some of whom reported hearing sounds they believed were gunfire. According to the department, the noises were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices, commonly used by SWAT teams during certain tactical operations. Authorities said the devices were deployed by the Port St. Lucie Police Department SWAT Team while officers carried out the warrant.

The department emphasized that the case remains an active and ongoing investigation. Additional information is expected to be released when authorities determine it is appropriate.

Police said Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. The police response drew attention from nearby residents, some of whom reported hearing sounds they believed were gunfire. According to the department, the noises were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices, commonly used by SWAT teams during certain tactical operations. Authorities said the devices were deployed by the Port St. Lucie Police Department SWAT Team while officers carried out the warrant. cards.headline: Sebastian man arrested in West Virginia for Vero Beach homicide after license plate readers track multi-state flight
cards.body:
Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia and faces a first-degree murder charge in the shooting death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, in Vero Beach on Sunday morning, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally.

Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide. Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. She had told her co-workers that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him.

According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from West Virginia to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife.

The sheriff's office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle's movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. U.S. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement.

The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife, according to the sheriff's office.Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest."I'm not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia," Flowers said. "So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this."The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic's body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night — a timeline Flowers called "unbelievable police work."Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement. Waggle will be extradited back to Indian River County to face the first-degree murder charge.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.body:
The incident happened Aug. 19 at St. Lucie Draft House, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Three women, later identified as 24-year-old Kamri Ashanti Reese and 25-year-old Kayla Reese, both of Fort Pierce, reportedly ordered food and drinks before one of them handed over a $100 bill that was marked FOR MOTION PICTURE PURPOSES. The women then left the restaurant in a dark blue Dodge Charger.

Deputies on patrol later located the vehicle. Criminal Investigations Division detectives assisted with the investigation, leading to the arrest of both Reese and Ashanti Reese. Both were arrested for counts of larceny, possession of a forged bank bill or note, and fraud for uttering a false bank bill. The duo was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County fire board refuses to suspend chief as residents demand fired firefighters be reinstated
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board of Commissioners voted against suspending Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the district attorney Wednesday during a three-hour meeting where nearly every public speaker urged leaders to reinstate three firefighters terminated over hazing allegations. The motion to suspend both Lee and the district attorney failed with four out of six commissioners voting against it. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from the meeting.

Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to their terminations and alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. The St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others last month after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper.

Fire Chief Jeff Lee told the crowd he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. Lee also acknowledged the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief.

The dispute is now in arbitration. Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September. Several speakers at Wednesday's meeting questioned the district's handling of the investigation, with one telling the board they had made a mockery of the three men and another accusing leadership of retaliation.
cards.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board meeting turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." See also: Deputies arrest man, 27, accused of traveling to meet 14-year-old in Hallandale Beach Another commenter said to the chief, "I don't know how you sleep at night." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

cards.headline: Al's Family Farms in Fort Pierce celebrates 50 years of family citrus business
cards.teaser: Al's Family Farms in Fort Pierce has been run by the Schorner family since 1977, offering fresh Florida citrus and produce directly from a packinghouse owned by the farm itself.
cards.body:
Al's Family Farms on the St. Lucie County and Fort Pierce area is a generational family farm now in its third generation and 50 years of serving fresh Florida produce. The farm has been run by the Schorner family since 1977. The farm picks, packs and ships citrus directly from the family.

The farm operates a packinghouse, which distinguishes it from many gift fruit companies. Nine out of 10 so-called gift fruit companies don't own a packinghouse. Al's Family Farms is located at 101 Melody Lane in Fort Pierce and offers products including fresh citrus, Georgia peaches, and its Sunshine Shake.
cards.article_text: This week, I found myself somewhere that's all about agriculture, family, and lots of Florida oranges. Let me tell you about my incredible day at Al's Family Farms in Fort Pierce!I was with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau, who knows this area like the back of her hand. Lucie County at Al's Family Farms right here in Fort Pierce," she explained. "This is a generational family farm, three generations now, 50 years of serving up just the freshest Florida produce. The reason why I brought you here is because I cover this area. Lucie County is home to me. It is so special."WATCH: What I learned during my visit really stuck with me. Al's Family Farm has been run by the same family since 1977 – the Schorner family – which means you're guaranteed fresh and real produce. In fact, I discovered that 9 out of 10 so-called gift fruit companies don't even own a packinghouse! But you can trust Al's to pick, pack and ship your citrus from the family itself.Now, Brooke had something special planned for me— indulging in a Sunshine Shake.But before I could get my hands on that famous Sunshine Shake, Brooke had other plans: Trying a Georgia peach.And let me tell you, I didn't even wait for permission. That peach was incredible, but I was getting excited about the shake that everyone was talking about.This hot and humid day was perfect for a Sunshine Shake. "Oh my goodness, that is so fresh," I exclaimed after my first sip.But here's what made this visit even more meaningful. Brooke reminded me of something important- "If you ate today, thank a farmer." Farmers play such an important role in all of our lives, and we don't always think about the people who worked hard to produce the food we enjoy.I was so thankful for my trip to Al's Family Farm. It reminded me that some of the best experiences happen when you slow down, appreciate where your food comes from, and connect with the hardworking families who make it all possible.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Stuart's Bathtub Beach
hero.body:
Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life. The man was approximately 300 yards from shore when Deputy John Wilkes arrived.

Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was in a very distressed emotional state and advised that he was having relationship issues and issues with his direct family. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. Castoro said the man told rescuers that the ocean was peaceful for him and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired.

Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. Castoro said they were able to relate over being fathers and that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking help. Deputy Wilkes said crisis intervention training, which helps deputies learn how to deal with somebody dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse, definitely helped them all that day.

Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. The man would kind of look back at Wilkes and realize there were a lot of people out there trying to help him right now, and Wilkes thinks that is what really changed his demeanor and made him say this was the wrong decision. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made.

Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. Detectives from the Indian River County Sheriff's Office are working to return Waggle to Indian River County. The sheriff's office is treating the death as a domestic violence homicide.

Deputies received a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. Deputies located Kriskewic with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside Kriskewic's home.

Sheriff Eric Flowers identified Waggle as a person of interest and said investigators believe Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship. Waggle fled the area in a vehicle following the shooting. Flowers said detectives used resources such as Flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts.
