cards.headline: St. Lucie County deputy found guilty of DUI, remains on unpaid leave during internal review
cards.teaser: Arthur Alfaro was found guilty Wednesday of Driving Under the Influence Unlawful Breath Alcohol Level .08 or More. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is conducting a separate Internal Affairs investigation to determine whether Alfaro violated agency policies.
cards.body:
Arthur Alfaro, a St. Lucie County deputy, was found guilty of Driving Under the Influence Unlawful Breath Alcohol Level .08 or More on Wednesday, ending the criminal case against him. Alfaro remains on unpaid administrative leave while the sheriff's office reviews whether his conduct violated agency policy. Initial reports indicate he also fled from deputies at a high rate of speed, but no criminal charges were filed regarding those actions.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard R. Del Toro said accountability applies to everyone, regardless of rank or position. The sheriff's office will wait for the administrative process to conclude before deciding whether disciplinary action is warranted.

Alfaro, 47, was arrested after Sebastian police spotted him driving 80 mph in a 30 mph zone on Indian River Drive. Officers initially tried to stop the black sedan, but Alfaro fled. Officers did not immediately pursue because of heavy traffic. Police later spotted the vehicle heading toward U.S. 1 and said Alfaro struggled to stay in his lane and crossed the fog line several times. Officers conducted a high-risk traffic stop after the sedan entered a dead-end cul-de-sac. A passenger allegedly told police Alfaro had been drinking. Alfaro declined a field sobriety exercise but consented to a breath test at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. The results showed blood alcohol levels of .120 and .129.

Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said its Internal Affairs investigation will continue separately through an administrative process. That review will determine whether Alfaro violated agency policies or other standards expected of sheriff’s office employees. hero.headline: Fort Pierce commission rejects third settlement offer in Little Jim lawsuit
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce City Commission on Monday unanimously rejected a third settlement proposal in a citizen lawsuit over the Little Jim Bait and Tackle property and instead countered with an offer to drop the city's claim for legal costs if plaintiff Kevin Keene withdraws his case. Commissioner Arnold Gaines said the settlement demand that Little Jim's current operator be given the right to match the outcome of any future bids to lease the city-owned property would violate state law. Public entities are required to competitively bid the awarding of things like property leases to get the best outcome for taxpayers. Gaines suggested giving Little Jim's current operator an automatic right of first refusal would violate the principle of competitive bidding.

Commissioners decided to offer a counter settlement saying they will forgo a claim for the city's legal costs involved in defending the lawsuit, a minimum $3,600, if Keene drops his action. Keene, a Fort Pierce resident, filed suit against the city in October as an attempt to give citizens more authority in determining how city-owned waterfront property is used. A St. Lucie County judge has twice dismissed Keene's lawsuit but gave him an opportunity to refile.

Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. The current operator, Salty Baitshack 3, has continued business there on a month-to-month lease for more than a year.

Keene's latest settlement offer would require the city to suspend any new Requests for Proposals for awarding the next long-term Little Jim lease until all issues with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection have been resolved. It would also require the city to agree to put any future sale or long-term lease of publicly owned waterfront property to a citywide vote and give Little Jim's current operator the right to match the highest bid resulting from an RFP process. A new lease would be for no more than nine years and the property would be leased in its existing condition, without requiring or conditioning the new lease upon any additional improvements, alterations, redevelopment, or other changes to the property.

hero.headline: Indian River County school superintendent Dr. Moore to step down in June 2027
hero.teaser: School District of Indian River County Superintendent Dr. Moore announced he will conclude his tenure with the district effective June 30, 2027, after nearly seven years of service.
hero.body:
School District of Indian River County Superintendent Dr. Moore announced Wednesday he will conclude his tenure with the district effective June 30, 2027, after nearly seven years of service. Moore shared his decision with school board members and his Cabinet Leadership Team before informing district and school leaders and broader SDIRC staff. His tenure currently ranks as the second longest among Florida's appointed district school superintendents.

During Moore's time leading the district, SDIRC advanced from 38th to 5th among Florida's 67 school districts based on District Grade and earned 4 consecutive A district grades. The district grew the share of schools earning an A or B from 47 percent to 100 percent. The district also achieved a 96 percent high school graduation rate and was named the No. 1 Best Place to Teach in Florida by Niche for 2026. Moore was named the 2025 Florida Superintendent of the Year and a national finalist.

As Moore enters his final school year, he identified two priorities: ensuring every SDIRC school earns an A grade and positioning the district to become the No. 1 school district in Florida. Following his departure, Moore said he intends to explore opportunities to help other leaders and school systems create conditions for exceptional student outcomes.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County fire board hears pleas to reinstate three firefighters fired over hazing allegations
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting Wednesday drew a packed crowd urging district leaders to reinstate three firefighters fired following an investigation into hazing allegations. The three-hour meeting featured nearly every public speaker calling on the board to bring back the terminated firefighters, with many criticizing Fire Chief Jeff Lee and questioning the district's investigation process.

Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings last month. The St. Lucie County Fire District fired the three senior firefighters and suspended two others after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Both Hutchinson and Baldwin questioned the integrity of the investigation and alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired.

Fire Chief Jeff Lee told the crowd he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. Lee acknowledged the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. A motion to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney was made during the meeting but failed.

The dispute is now in arbitration. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting, and board members did not provide a reason for her absence.

Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." hero.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Stuart's Bathtub Beach
hero.body:
Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life. The man was already 300 yards from shore when Deputy John Wilkes arrived on scene.

Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was in a very distressed emotional state and advised that he was having relationship issues and issues with his direct family. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. Castoro said the man told them that the ocean was peaceful for him and he just wanted to swim out until he got tired.

Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. Castoro related to the man over being fathers and discussed how it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need. Deputy Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him and said the man would kind of look back at him and realize there were a lot of people out there trying to help him right now. Wilkes said that's what really changed his demeanor and made him realize this was the wrong decision.

After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. Wilkes explained how the crisis intervention training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue, which teaches them how to deal with somebody dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse.
hero.article_text: Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. hero.headline: Environmental Learning Center in Vero Beach hosts mosquito and insect lecture Saturday
hero.teaser: Jeff Summersill with Indian River Mosquito Control District and two UF professors will discuss insects during a Double Feature Lecture at the Environmental Learning Center in Vero Beach on Saturday.
hero.body:
Jeff Summersill, agricultural pilot and with Indian River Mosquito Control District, and Eva Buckner, UF/IFAS associate professor and medical entomology specialist, along with Panpim Thongsripong, UF/IFAS assistant professor of vector-borne disease ecology, will discuss insects during a Double Feature Lecture at the Environmental Learning Center in Vero Beach on Saturday, Aug. 22, from 12:30 to 2:30 p.m. The Environmental Learning Center is located at 255 Live Oak Drive in Vero Beach.

The lecture is part of the Currents Connections series at the Environmental Learning Center. Additional events this weekend at the center include a Nourish Flourish knife skills class with Chef Stacy Maple on Saturday at a cost of $20 for ages 12 and older, with those under 12 required to be accompanied by a paying adult.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff identifies Vero Beach homicide victim as Dawn Kriskewic
hero.teaser: Dawn Kriskewic, 52, was identified Tuesday as the woman found shot near her Vero Beach home Sunday. Investigators delayed releasing her name while they worked to locate and notify several out-of-state next of kin.
hero.body:
The woman found shot near her Vero Beach home Sunday has been identified as 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office confirmed Tuesday. Investigators delayed releasing her name while they worked to locate and notify several out-of-state next of kin. Kriskewic was found in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach, Sunday morning.

Deputies performed lifesaving measures before she was taken to a trauma center, where she later died. Investigators have identified 33-year-old Matthew Waggle as a person of interest in the homicide. A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle. Investigators say he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

The Sheriff's Office previously said investigators believe Kriskewic had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the shooting as a domestic violence homicide. The agency has also been using its Real Time Crime Center and a network of Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for Waggle and work to piece together what happened.

Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian, was arrested Wednesday night at a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, in connection with the shooting death of 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic in Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced. Marshals took Waggle into custody and detectives are working to return him to Indian River County. Investigators are treating the death as a domestic violence homicide.

Deputies found Kriskewic with an apparent gunshot wound in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday after receiving a 911 call. Deputies began life-saving measures and transported Kriskewic to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home.

Sheriff Eric Flowers identified Waggle as the person of interest and said investigators believe Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle following the shooting. Flowers said detectives used resources such as Flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts. Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home. His brother heard the shot and went inside to check on his sister.

The Sheriff's Office scheduled a news conference for Thursday at 1:30 p.m. to share more details on the arrest. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org, or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: Indian River County schools superintendent to step down June 2027
hero.body:
School District of Indian River County Superintendent Dr. Moore announced Wednesday he will conclude his tenure with the district effective June 30, 2027, after nearly seven years of service. Moore, whose tenure currently ranks as the second longest among Florida's appointed district school superintendents, shared his decision with school board members and his Cabinet Leadership Team before informing district and school leaders and broader staff.

During Moore's time leading the district, the School District of Indian River County advanced from 38th to 5th among Florida's 67 school districts based on District Grade and earned 4 consecutive A district grades. The district grew the share of schools earning an A or B from 47 percent to 100 percent and achieved a 96 percent high school graduation rate. The district was named the No. 1 Best Place to Teach in Florida by Niche for 2026. Moore was named the 2025 Florida Superintendent of the Year and a national finalist.

Moore said serving as Superintendent of Schools has been one of the greatest privileges of his professional life. He said his belief in the power of public education to transform lives is stronger than ever. Moore said the accomplishments are evidence of what happens when beliefs become behaviors, behaviors become habits, and habits become coherent systems of work.

As Moore enters his final school year, he identified two priorities: ensuring every School District of Indian River County school earns an A grade and positioning the district to become the No. 1 school district in Florida. Following his departure, Moore said he intends to explore opportunities to help other leaders and school systems create conditions for exceptional student outcomes.

cards.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office uses Flock license plate cameras in search for homicide suspect
cards.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers showed how the agency's Real Time Crime Center is using Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for Matthew Waggle, a person of interest in a Vero Beach homicide.
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers showed how the agency's Real Time Crime Center is using Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for 33-year-old Matthew Waggle. Waggle has not been charged in the killing. Deputies identified him as a person of interest after a 52-year-old woman was found shot near her home Sunday morning in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach.

Flowers said analysts in the Real Time Crime Center used Flock data to help build a case in a deadly hit-and-run investigated by the Florida Highway Patrol last week that otherwise had no leads. Flock's automated license plate readers capture information about vehicles as they pass, including license plates, locations and timestamps. That allows investigators to search for vehicles connected to crimes and potentially piece together where they traveled. Indian River County has previously said it operates 140 license plate readers.

Flowers defended Indian River County's use of the cameras. Flowers said Indian River County has largely avoided the public backlash seen elsewhere because the Sheriff's Office explained its use of the technology early and residents have seen results. He pointed to auto burglaries as an example, saying the county recorded more than 800 in 2015 compared with roughly 250 last year. Flowers attributed at least part of that decline to the camera network and proactive policing.
cards.article_text: A network of license plate cameras facing growing privacy scrutiny across the country is now part of the search for a person of interest in a Vero Beach-area homicide. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers took CBS12 News Reporter Katie Bente inside the agency's Real Time Crime Center on Monday, where analysts are using Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for 33-year-old Matthew Waggle. Waggle has not been charged in the killing. Deputies identified him as a person of interest after a 52-year-old woman was found shot near her home Sunday morning in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach. Deputies performed lifesaving measures before the woman was taken to a trauma center, where she later died. Flowers said investigators believe the woman had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the killing as a domestic violence homicide. On Monday, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office released 911 calls made after a bystander found the woman's body. "Is there anyone else around this female?" the 911 dispatcher can be heard asking. I didn't see nothing, because I was in my house," the caller responded. The dispatcher then asked the caller how long the woman had been there. The caller said she did not know. "One of the first places that we go, Real Time Crime Center gets activated," Flowers said. "They're looking at all the Flock cameras. They're looking at the traffic in the area." How Flock plays a role Flock's automated license plate readers capture information about vehicles as they pass, including license plates, locations and timestamps. That allows investigators to search for vehicles connected to crimes and potentially piece together where they traveled. Indian River County has previously said it operates 140 license plate readers. Flowers pointed to a deadly hit-and-run investigated by the Florida Highway Patrol last week as one recent example. He said analysts in the Real Time Crime Center used Flock data to help build a case that otherwise had no leads. He said the technology can also work in reverse helping investigators eliminate someone as a suspect. "If we're able to show that that person's vehicle was nowhere near the homicide," Flowers said, "that's a great way for us to show that somebody is innocent as well." A crime-fighting tool and a privacy fight The ability to reconstruct where vehicles have traveled is also at the heart of a growing national debate over Flock. Privacy and civil liberties advocates have questioned how extensively law enforcement should be able to track drivers, how information is shared between agencies and what safeguards exist to prevent misuse. More than 50 jurisdictions have reportedly ended relationships with Flock. The company announced new safeguards last week, including plans to reduce its recommended default data retention period from 30 days to seven days and require searches to be connected to case numbers. Flowers strongly defended Indian River County's use of the cameras. "You're on camera every time you go to Walmart. You're on camera every time you go to Walgreens," Flowers said. "Everywhere you go, your bank transactions are being tracked." Flowers said law enforcement should be able to use available technology to protect the public. "Don't you want your law enforcement protecting your community and making it safer by leveraging technology?" he said. Flowers said Indian River County has largely avoided the public backlash seen elsewhere because the Sheriff's Office explained its use of the technology early and, he argues, residents have seen results. He pointed to auto burglaries as an example, saying the county recorded more than 800 in 2015 compared with roughly 250 last year. Flowers attributed at least part of that decline to the camera network and proactive policing. Now, the technology is being used in an active homicide investigation. See also: 12 pounds of meth, 12,000 rounds,12 guns, and fentanyl found in Boynton Beach SWAT raid Flowers said investigators spent Monday speaking with the victim's coworkers and examining her relationship with Waggle as they work to determine what led to the shooting. "It really looks like she was trying to break up with him," Flowers said. He wasn't ready for it to be over." A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle. Investigators have said he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County fire board declines to suspend fire chief amid firefighter termination dispute
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board of Commissioners voted Wednesday to keep Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the district attorney in their positions after a motion to suspend both officials failed. Four of six commissioners voted against the motion during a three-hour meeting focused on hazing allegations and the termination of three firefighters.

Nearly every public speaker at the meeting urged the board to reinstate the three senior firefighters who were fired last month after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two other firefighters were suspended in connection with the investigation. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their terminations. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation and alleged the district retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired.

Fire Chief Jeff Lee told the crowd he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. Lee also acknowledged the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief.

The dispute is now in arbitration. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting. Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September.
hero.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board meeting turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." See also: Deputies arrest man, 27, accused of traveling to meet 14-year-old in Hallandale Beach Another commenter said to the chief, "I don't know how you sleep at night." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Stuart's Bathtub Beach
hero.body:
Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units saved a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life.

Deputy John Wilkes said the man and lifeguards were already about 300 yards from shore when he arrived on scene. Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was in a very distressed emotional state and advised that he was having relationship issues and issues with his direct family. The man told deputies the ocean was peaceful for him and he wanted to swim out until he got tired. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted.

Castoro said he built a rapport with the man and encouraged him to keep living. The two related over being fathers and discussed how it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking help. Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him and changed his demeanor, deciding not to go through with his plan.

After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. Wilkes said crisis intervention training, which helps deputies learn how to deal with someone in a mental health crisis or substance abuse situation, helped during the rescue.
hero.article_text: Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. cards.headline: Miami woman arrested in Martin County for posing as bank representative, hiding $3,200 in body
cards.teaser: Monquie Turnbull, 32, of Miami drove to Martin County and scammed two residents by claiming their debit cards were compromised. Deputies recovered $3,200 hidden in one of her body parts at the jail.
cards.body:
A Miami woman was arrested in Martin County after allegedly posing as a bank representative to scam residents out of thousands of dollars. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said 32-year-old Monquie Turnbull drove from Miami to Martin County, where she approached two residents, claiming their debit cards were compromised and needed to be turned in for replacement. One resident was scammed out of $3,180. The victim noticed shortly after the suspect left that the money was missing from her account.

While investigators were handling that case, they received a second 911 call matching the suspect's description and vehicle. Deputies began their search and located Turnbull as she came eastbound on Bridge Road, then turned around and was going westbound on Bridge Road. Newly released aerial footage shows sheriff's deputies following Turnbull on I-95 before stopping her vehicle. Body camera footage captured Turnbull exiting her car and being questioned by deputies before being placed under arrest.

Officials later discovered Turnbull had entered the jail with about $3,200 hidden in one of her body parts. Budensiek said she took the first victim's card, withdrew $3,180, and that was the exact amount recovered from inside her person in the jail. The sheriff said this was all the money that the victim had, including her rent money. Budensiek is asking anyone who may have been a victim to contact authorities.

cards.headline: Hallandale man arrested in Indian River County for traveling to meet 14-year-old
cards.teaser: A 27-year-old Hallandale Beach man was arrested Aug. 8 in Vero Beach after allegedly traveling to Indian River County to meet a 14-year-old.
cards.body:
Emaad Mir, 27, of Hallandale Beach was arrested after he allegedly traveled to Indian River County to meet a 14-year-old, according to Indian River County Sheriff's Office reports. Mir was communicating with undercover detectives, working alongside the juvenile's parents, for some time, with Mir believing that the person was 14, according to reports.

Deputies were able to locate Mir's vehicle in a residential neighborhood as Mir made his way to the meeting location, allowing deputies to intercept him before he could reach the intended victim, according to reports. He was arrested in the 1300 block of 29th Avenue, Vero Beach and taken to Indian River County Jail.

Mir is in jail on charges of traveling to meet after use of a computer to lure a child, transmit information harmful to minors, and unlawful use of a two-way communications device. He is being held in the jail on a $1.75 million bond on those charges.

hero.headline: Indian River County school superintendent to step down in June 2027 after nearly seven years
hero.body:
School District of Indian River County Superintendent Dr. David K. Moore announced Wednesday he will conclude his tenure with the district effective June 30, 2027, after nearly seven years of service. Moore shared his decision with school board members and his Cabinet Leadership Team before informing district and school leaders and broader SDIRC staff.

During Moore's time leading the district, SDIRC advanced from 38th to fifth among Florida's 67 school districts based on District Grade, earned four consecutive A district grades, and grew the share of schools earning an A or B from 47 percent to 100 percent. The district also achieved a 96 percent high school graduation rate and was named the No. 1 Best Place to Teach in Florida by Niche for 2026. Moore was named the 2025 Florida Superintendent of the Year and a national finalist. His tenure currently ranks as the second longest among Florida's appointed district school superintendents.

As Moore enters his final school year, he identified two priorities: ensuring every SDIRC school earns an A grade and positioning the district to become the No. 1 school district in Florida. Moore said these accomplishments tell an extraordinary story of improvement, but they are the evidence of the story. The story is what happens when beliefs become behaviors, behaviors become habits, and habits become coherent systems of work.

Following his departure, Moore said he intends to explore opportunities to help other leaders and school systems create conditions for exceptional student outcomes. Moore said serving as Superintendent of Schools has been one of the greatest privileges of his professional life, and his belief in the power of public education to transform lives is stronger than ever.

cards.headline: Vero Beach homicide victim identified as Dawn Kriskewic, Matthew Waggle sought as person of interest
cards.teaser: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office identified the victim of a Sunday shooting in Vero Beach as 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic and named Matthew Allen Waggle as a person of interest in the case.
cards.body:
The woman found shot in the 500 block of First Street in Vero Beach on Sunday morning has been identified as 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office confirmed Tuesday. Kriskewic was found in a roadway at 501 First Street on Sunday, Aug. 16, by Indian River County Sheriff's Office deputies. She suffered an apparent gunshot wound. Deputies began life-saving measures on Kriskewic. She was transported to a local hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Investigators delayed releasing her name while they worked to locate and notify several out-of-state next of kin.

The sheriff's office named 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle as a person of interest. The sheriff's office said Kriskewic and Waggle were in some sort of a relationship. Investigators believe Kriskewic had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the shooting as a domestic violence homicide. A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle. Investigators say he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

As of Tuesday afternoon, law enforcement continues its investigation and search for Waggle. The Sheriff's Office has been using its Real Time Crime Center and a network of Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for Waggle and work to piece together what happened. Anyone with information about the case or Waggle's whereabouts is asked to contact the Indian River County Sheriff's Office or submit information anonymously to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: Former Vero Beach Eagles secretary accused of embezzling nearly $419,000 for guns, liquor and personal expenses
cards.teaser: Robert John Davison allegedly spent nearly $419,000 of Aerie 4374 Fraternal Order of Eagles money on unauthorized personal purchases between 2017 and 2024, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.
cards.body:
Robert John Davison served as secretary of Aerie 4374 Fraternal Order of Eagles in Vero Beach from February 2015 until November 2024, when he stopped showing up. The investigation began after a representative was sent to the chapter by the Grand Aerie to examine why membership and the organization's finances were declining. After reviewing expenses, he told deputies that he discovered that Davison had been using the organization's debit card for personal purchases that had not been authorized.

The organization later hired forensic accounting firm Clay Price & Associates, P.A., to review its financial records. On Feb. 24, 2025, the firm reported that Davison had used $418,899.26 in organization funds for personal expenses dating back to 2017. The alleged spending included $115,087.49 in ATM withdrawals and associated fees that investigators say were outside the secretary's authorized duties, $55,175.40 on personal bills including credit cards, vehicle payments, utilities and cellphone bills, $35,094.53 in personal grocery and liquor store purchases, $16,038.66 in unauthorized flights and lodging, $9,861.27 in transfers to Davison's personal Cash App account, $8,791.14 on firearms, ammunition, personal purchases and an NRA membership, $5,930.98 in rideshare expenses, $4,463.52 in personal court payments including child support and DUI-related fees, and at least $2,461.37 in purchases for Davison's personal LEGO business.

The current trustee chairman and the current secretary reportedly verified that the debit card charges were outside Davison's duties and were not authorized by the organization. Davison is accused of embezzlement involving a value of $100,000 or more.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie mayor race heads to November runoff between Shannon Martin and Steven Giordano
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin and challenger Steven Giordano will face off in the November general election after neither candidate secured the 50% threshold needed to win outright in Tuesday's primary race. Martin captured nearly 48% of the vote while Giordano received approximately 35%, forcing a runoff between the top two candidates. Third candidate Eric Strazzeri was eliminated from the race after receiving nearly 17% of the vote.

Both candidates addressed how an ongoing investigation into campaign signs may have affected Tuesday's results. The investigation has been a focal point in the mayoral campaign leading up to the primary. Giordano told WPTV at his election watch party at My Brother's BBQ that if the investigation would have happened earlier, he thinks the results would have swayed better to his race. Martin acknowledged the investigation's potential impact during a phone interview with WPTV, saying she thinks that had something to do with it but plans to keep focused on the issues important to residents.

Martin said she plans to let her track record with the city speak to voters as the campaign moves forward. The incumbent emphasized her experience leading the city and her commitment to continuing her work for residents. Giordano outlined his campaign priorities for the November race, focusing on supporting local youth programs and local businesses. Giordano said he is the people's mayor and the people's voice and is very excited to be in this position.

The November general election will determine who leads Port St. Lucie for the next four years. Voters will choose between Martin's experience as the current mayor and Giordano's vision for change in city leadership. Family and friends gathered at Giordano's election watch party to celebrate advancing to the general election.

cards.headline: Bicyclist critically injured in Port St. Lucie crash on Southwest Rosser Boulevard
cards.teaser: A bicyclist was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in critical condition after being struck by a driver with a suspended license Wednesday morning.
cards.body:
A bicyclist is in the hospital after he was struck by a woman who was allegedly driving with a suspended license on Wednesday. According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, the crash happened around 6:45 a.m. near Southwest Rosser Boulevard and Southwest Meridian Avenue. Police said the bicyclist was riding on Southwest Rosser Boulevard when the crash occurred.

Officers said the bicyclist was breathing but unconscious and was wearing a helmet. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he was listed in critical but stable condition and is expected to survive. The driver remained at the scene and was issued a notice to appear after officers determined she was driving with a suspended license. Her vehicle was later removed from the scene by her husband.

Traffic in both directions was shut down, with motorists diverted onto side streets. The investigation remains ongoing.

hero.headline: Miami woman accused of scamming Martin County seniors hid $3,200 in her body during jail intake
hero.body:
A 32-year-old Miami woman arrested in Martin County for posing as a bank representative to scam seniors faces an additional charge after deputies say she smuggled $3,180 in cash into jail concealed in her body. Monquie Love Turnbull never mentioned she was carrying the money when arrested, and it was not discovered until she was being processed into the Martin County jail. The Martin County Sheriff's Office confirmed the cash is the same money taken from one of her alleged victims.

The case began Monday when Turnbull showed up at an elderly victim's home in Martin County claiming the person's bank account had been compromised. Investigators say an unidentified male caller, posing as a Chase Bank fraud representative, told the victim her account had been compromised and that someone would come to her home to collect and destroy her card before a replacement arrived. Turnbull, using the alias Monica, arrived at the home, verified herself with a code relayed from the caller, and collected the card, cutting it in half in front of the victim and placing the pieces in a manila envelope. Minutes later, the victim's bank account was drained through a $3,000 withdrawal and a $180 ATM withdrawal.

Sheriff John Budensiek said Turnbull revealed she had the money inside her body when she complained of pain during a jail phone call to an unknown man. Deputies went back to the jail and interviewed her, and she admitted to having money inside of her. While deputies were investigating the first report, they were alerted to a second call identifying Turnbull as a possible suspect in a nearly identical incident targeting another victim the same day. That attempt was caught on a Ring doorbell camera, but the second victim's family member grew skeptical and refused to hand over the card.

Deputies located Turnbull's vehicle, a gray two-door Nissan Altima, on Bridge Road in Hobe Sound near the I-95 interchange and conducted a traffic stop. The first victim was brought to the scene and positively identified Turnbull as Monica from about 15 feet away. Turnbull now faces a charge of introducing contraband into a corrections facility on top of her original charges including scheme to defraud, grand theft, fraudulent use of a credit or debit card without consent involving a victim 60 or older, fraudulent use of ID without consent, and felony use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. She is being held on a $500,000 bond.

They interviewed her yet again. She admitted to having money inside of her. She said at that point it was only $400. This was everything that she had. And she handed it over to a scammer," said Budensiek. cards.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Bathtub Beach in Stuart
cards.teaser: Deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man who swam more than 300 yards into the ocean at Bathtub Beach on Sunday afternoon after calling a suicide hotline.
cards.body:
Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life. Deputy John Wilkes said the man and lifeguards were probably 300-plus yards from the shore when he arrived on scene.

Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was obviously in a very distressed emotional state and advised that he was having some relationship issues and issues with his direct family. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. Castoro said he built a rapport with the man and encouraged him to keep living. They were able to relate over being fathers, and Castoro discussed how it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking help.

Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. He would kind of look back and realize there were a lot of people out there trying to help him, and Wilkes said that is what really changed his demeanor and made him say this is the wrong decision. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made.

Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. hero.headline: Palm Beach County Clerk Michael Caruso extradited to Orange County jail on five felony child sex abuse charges
hero.body:
Suspended Palm Beach County Clerk of Court Michael Caruso was extradited to Orange County jail Wednesday after his arrest on five felony child sex abuse charges. Caruso, 67, faces charges of kidnapping, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious exhibition, luring or enticing a child, and child abuse causing mental injury, according to the arrest warrant and affidavit filed in Orange County Circuit Court. Gov. Ron DeSantis immediately suspended Caruso from office following his arrest Tuesday.

Caruso made his first appearance Wednesday morning at the Palm Beach County Criminal Justice Complex, where a judge issued a comprehensive no-contact order prohibiting any contact with the alleged victim, immediate family, witnesses, and any individual under the age of 18. When Caruso's defense attorney requested an extradition bond that would allow him to remain out of jail while awaiting transport, the judge denied the request, stating it was inappropriate based upon the nature and extent of the charges. The judge clarified that the Palm Beach County court was not making any probable cause findings, but was only facilitating Caruso's expedited transfer to Orange County, where the charges originated.

According to court documents, the charges stem from allegations involving multiple incidents with a child victim spanning nearly a year, including incidents during a family cruise in August 2025. The victim disclosed the abuse during a recorded interview with Orange County law enforcement and has been receiving therapeutic services since April 2026. When confronted by family members in December 2025, court documents state Caruso made partial admissions while making threatening statements about potential consequences if the allegations were reported.

Shannon Ramsey-Chessman, the chief of staff and chief deputy clerk, has been appointed as interim clerk following Caruso's suspension. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is overseeing the transition and ensuring no files or records are removed from the clerk's office. Questions remain about Caruso's status on the November ballot, where he was scheduled to face Democrat Yvette Drucker for the clerk position. The Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections is awaiting guidance from state officials on how to proceed with his candidacy.

cards.headline: Florida school bus and speed zone camera lawsuits face dismissals and legal setbacks
cards.teaser: Legal challenges to automated school bus and school zone cameras generating millions of citations across Florida are hitting roadblocks, with judges dismissing cases and ruling against drivers who contest tickets.
cards.body:
Miami-based Attorney Gino Moreno filed three lawsuits last year after drivers hit with $225 school bus camera fines had no way to challenge their fines because the cameras started rolling without the proper due process in place. His cases have since hit a wall. In Polk County, a judge dismissed his federal case. In Miami-Dade, a revised complaint is pending, and in Hillsborough County, his client Stanley Shultz is still waiting to see if his case will move forward.

Shultz, who lives in Plant City, was fined for illegally passing a school bus even though video from his citation shows the bus's warning lights never flashed. Shultz appealed the fine, but a judge in Tallahassee upheld it, despite state law requiring appeals must be heard by local hearing officers. Attorney Ira Karmelin with The Ticket Clinic has successfully used arguments about unapproved radar devices to get school speed zone tickets thrown out, but judges are now starting to side with the state's claim of exemption.

Since the cameras began operating in Florida, they have generated well over 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in paid fines as of earlier this year. Concerns have emerged over school speed zone cameras, with drivers fined when school was not in session or when signs directing them to slow down when flashing never flashed. Questions also emerged about the camera devices themselves, as the radar inside the cameras, which state law requires to be approved by the state, is not approved, though the state maintains it's exempt.

cards.headline: Angie Nixon wins Democratic nomination for Florida U.S. Senate special primary election
cards.teaser: State Rep. Angie Nixon won the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Florida's special primary election Tuesday, defeating Army veteran Alex Vindman.
cards.body:
Vindman gained national attention when he was serving on the National Security Council in 2019, when the Republican president pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to investigate Joe Biden, then a Democratic candidate. He and his brother, Eugene, a lawyer on the National Security Council, reported their concerns and sparked investigations.

Nixon will take on incumbent U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody in the November general election. Moody easily won the GOP primary on Tuesday, defeating three challengers. The winner of November's special election will finish the last two years of Marco Rubio's term after he left the Senate to become U.S. Secretary of State.

A Democrat has not won a Senate seat in Florida since 2012, when former U.S. Sen. Bill Nelson won his third term.

hero.headline: Miami woman arrested in Martin County for posing as bank representative, hiding stolen cash in body
hero.body:
A Miami woman was arrested in Martin County after allegedly posing as a bank representative to scam residents out of thousands of dollars, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. Monquie Love Turnbull, 32, drove from Miami to Martin County where she approached two residents, claiming their debit cards were compromised and needed to be turned in for replacement. One victim lost $3,180 from her account minutes after Turnbull left with the card.

Deputies located Turnbull on Bridge Road in Hobe Sound near the I-95 interchange and conducted a traffic stop. Aerial footage shows sheriff's deputies following Turnbull on I-95 before stopping her vehicle. The first victim was brought to the scene and positively identified Turnbull as the woman who had collected her card. A search of the vehicle turned up a surgical mask and multiple yellow envelopes matching witness descriptions.

Turnbull never mentioned she was carrying $3,180 in cash concealed in her body when she was arrested, and the money was not discovered until she was being processed into the jail. She revealed she had the money inside her body when she complained of pain during a jail phone call to an unknown man. The sheriff's office confirmed the cash is the same money taken from one of her alleged scam victims. Budensiek said the victim handed over all her rent money to the scammer.

The case began Monday when Turnbull, using the alias Monica, arrived at an elderly victim's home after an unidentified male caller posing as a Chase Bank fraud representative told the victim her account had been compromised. Turnbull verified herself with a code relayed from the caller and collected the card, cutting it in half in front of the victim and placing the pieces in a manila envelope. While deputies were investigating that report, they received a second call identifying Turnbull as a possible suspect in a nearly identical incident targeting another victim the same day. Turnbull now faces charges including scheme to defraud, grand theft, fraudulent use of a credit or debit card without consent involving a victim 60 or older, fraudulent use of ID without consent, felony use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and introducing contraband into a corrections facility. She is being held on a $500,000 bond.

cards.headline: Vero Beach homicide victim identified as Dawn Kriskewic, person of interest remains on the run
cards.teaser: The woman found shot near her Vero Beach-area home Sunday has been identified as 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office confirmed Tuesday.
cards.body:
Kriskewic was found in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach, Sunday morning. Deputies performed lifesaving measures before she was taken to a trauma center, where she later died. Investigators delayed releasing her name while they worked to locate and notify several out-of-state next of kin.

Investigators have identified 33-year-old Matthew Waggle as a person of interest in the homicide. He has yet to be located or charged. A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle. Investigators say he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

The Sheriff's Office said investigators believe Kriskewic had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the shooting as a domestic violence homicide. The agency has been using its Real Time Crime Center and a network of Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for Waggle and work to piece together what happened.

hero.headline: Indian River County school superintendent Dr. Moore to step down June 2027
hero.body:
School District of Indian River County Superintendent Dr. Moore announced Wednesday he will conclude his tenure with the district effective June 30, 2027, after nearly seven years of service. Moore shared his decision with school board members and his Cabinet Leadership Team before informing district and school leaders and broader SDIRC staff. His tenure currently ranks as the second longest among Florida's appointed district school superintendents.

Moore said during his time leading the district, SDIRC advanced from 38th to 5th among Florida's 67 school districts based on District Grade, earned 4 consecutive A district grades, and grew the share of schools earning an A or B from 47 percent to 100 percent. The district also achieved a 96 percent high school graduation rate and was named the No. 1 Best Place to Teach in Florida by Niche for 2026. Moore was named the 2025 Florida Superintendent of the Year and a national finalist.

As Moore enters his final school year, he identified two priorities: ensuring every SDIRC school earns an A grade and positioning the district to become the No. 1 school district in Florida. Moore said the district has spent close to seven years proving that dramatic improvement is possible, and this year he wants the district to demonstrate how far a mature, coherent, high-performing system can go.

Following his departure, Moore said he intends to explore opportunities to help other leaders and school systems create conditions for exceptional student outcomes. Moore said serving as Superintendent of Schools has been one of the greatest privileges of his professional life, and his belief in the power of public education to transform lives is stronger than ever.

hero.headline: Vero Beach shooting victim identified as Dawn Kriskewic, suspect Matthew Waggle remains at large
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office identified the woman shot and killed Sunday morning in Vero Beach as 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic. The Sheriff's Office announced the identification on Tuesday after locating and notifying several out-of-state next of kin. The victim's body was found in a roadway at 501 First Street in Vero Beach on Sunday at 8:41 a.m.

Deputies found Kriskewic with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a local hospital where she was pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home. The Sheriff's Office is treating the case as a domestic violence homicide.

The Sheriff's Office named 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian as a person of interest. Sheriff Eric Flowers said Kriskewic and Waggle were in some sort of relationship. Investigators believe the victim had been trying to end the relationship with Waggle. A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle, who authorities believe has left Indian River County and is traveling by vehicle.

Sheriff Flowers warned that Waggle should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached. Investigators are using resources including flock cameras and the Real Time Crime Center to search for Waggle. As of Tuesday afternoon, law enforcement continues its investigation and search. Anyone with information about the case or Waggle's whereabouts is asked to contact the Indian River County Sheriff's Office or submit information anonymously to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: Former Vero Beach Eagles secretary accused of spending $419,000 on guns, liquor, LEGOs
cards.teaser: Robert John Davison allegedly used nearly $419,000 of Fraternal Order of Eagles funds for personal expenses including firearms, DUI fees, and items for his personal LEGO business.
cards.body:
Robert John Davison, who served as secretary of Aerie 4374 Fraternal Order of Eagles in Vero Beach from February 2015 until November 2024, allegedly spent nearly $419,000 of the organization's money on personal purchases. The investigation began after a representative from the Grand Aerie examined why membership and finances were declining at the chapter. The representative discovered that Davison had been using the organization's debit card for unauthorized personal purchases.

The organization hired forensic accounting firm Clay Price & Associates, P.A. to review financial records. On February 24, 2025, the firm reported that Davison had used $418,899.26 in organization funds for personal expenses dating back to 2017. The alleged spending included $8,791.14 on firearms, ammunition, personal purchases and an NRA membership, $35,094.53 in personal grocery and liquor store purchases, and at least $2,461.37 in purchases for Davison's personal LEGO business.

Other alleged expenses included $4,463.52 in personal court payments including child support and DUI-related fees, $55,175.40 on personal bills including credit cards and vehicle payments, $115,087.49 in ATM withdrawals and associated fees, $9,861.27 in transfers to Davison's personal Cash App account, $16,038.66 in unauthorized flights and lodging, $5,930.98 in rideshare expenses, and $2,476.43 in personal fuel purchases. Davison is accused of embezzlement involving a value of $100,000 or more.
