hero.headline: Port St. Lucie mayoral candidates debate growth, traffic, and infrastructure ahead of Election Day
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie voters are deciding Tuesday who will lead the city, with incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin facing challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Strazzeri in a race focused on growth, traffic, development and infrastructure. The mayoral race is nonpartisan, and polls close Tuesday at 7 p.m. If one candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, that candidate wins outright. If no candidate reaches 50%, the top two vote-getters advance to the November general election.

The candidates offered different approaches to managing growth in one of Florida's largest cities. Giordano said he wants to slow down development and ensure existing infrastructure can handle what is already being built, focusing on drainage systems, roads and traffic infrastructure. Martin said many development rights were granted more than 20 years ago and cannot simply be taken away by the current City Council, but pointed to Rosser Lakes Preserve as an example where the city prevented a developer from building 86 homes and instead acquired the land as green space. Port St. Lucie has acquired more than 280 acres of green space since January 2025. Strazzeri said he supports responsible growth but believes roads, schools, utilities and emergency services need to be in place before communities are developed.

All three candidates acknowledged traffic as a major issue. Giordano called traffic in St. Lucie West a nightmare and said it takes almost 30 minutes to get from one end to the other, which he called totally unacceptable. He wants a new traffic study examining roadways, traffic signals and signal timing. Martin pointed to projects already underway, including work on Floresta Drive and Port St. Lucie Boulevard South, roundabouts in Torino and planned intersection improvements at Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway, Savona Boulevard and Gatlin Boulevard. Strazzeri said the city needs to be proactive and not reactive, calling for better traffic signal coordination, adaptive signal technology and road expansion where possible.

Martin has served as Port St. Lucie's mayor for the past five years and previously served on the City Council starting in 2010. She said the city has lowered its property tax rate each year for the past 11 years, reducing the rate by 25% over that period. Giordano said he has lived in Port St. Lucie since 1989 and has nearly 20 years of public service experience, including about a decade with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Strazzeri said he moved to Port St. Lucie in 2015, served in the Army and deployed to Iraq as a combat engineer, and later transitioned into information technology and cybersecurity.
hero.article_text: Lucie voters are deciding Tuesday who they want to lead one of Florida's largest cities, with growth, traffic, development and the future of the city among the major issues in the mayoral race. CBS12 News sat down with incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin and challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Strazzeri ahead of Election Day, asking them the same questions about some of the biggest concerns facing Port St. Lucie and what they would do if elected. Their answers reveal different approaches to managing a city that continues to grow. Lucie's growth Giordano said he believes the city needs to slow development and focus on whether existing infrastructure can handle what is already being built. "I want to slow down the growth and make sure that our infrastructure can handle what we already have," Giordano said. He said the city needs to make sure its drainage systems, roads and traffic infrastructure can keep up with development. Giordano also said he wants the city to focus more heavily on supporting local businesses and attracting higher-paying jobs. Martin said one challenge is that many development rights were granted decades ago and cannot simply be taken away by the current City Council. "What a lot of people don't realize still is that the developer rights were granted over 20 years ago," Martin said. "Where the developers do have those rights that were granted and those entitlements, we can't make that change." Martin pointed to Rosser Lakes Preserve as an example of an area where the city was able to prevent additional development. She said a developer wanted to build 86 homes on the property, but the city instead acquired the land to preserve it as green space. Lucie has acquired more than 280 acres of green space since January 2025. Strazzeri said he supports what he calls responsible growth but believes infrastructure should be in place before communities are developed. "Our roads, our schools, our utilities, our emergency services need to be in place prior to them developing in these communities because they're playing catch up right now," Strazzeri said. Traffic All three candidates acknowledged traffic as a major issue, but offered different approaches. Giordano called traffic in St. Lucie West a "nightmare" and said he wants a new traffic study examining roadways, traffic signals and signal timing. "It takes almost 30 minutes to get from one end to the other," Giordano said of St. "That's totally unacceptable." He said the city should examine where roads could be widened, whether medians need to be removed and where other changes could improve traffic flow. Martin pointed to projects already underway, including work on Floresta Drive and Port St. Lucie Boulevard South, roundabouts in Torino and planned intersection improvements at Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway, Savona Boulevard and Gatlin Boulevard. She said roundabouts can help move vehicles more efficiently and the city is extending turn lanes where possible. "We're going to continue to look at all of our areas and do those intersection improvements so that we can keep the flow of traffic going to reduce that traffic congestion," Martin said. Strazzeri said the city needs to be "proactive and not reactive," calling for better traffic signal coordination, adaptive signal technology and road expansion where possible. "We have to ensure that the infrastructure keeps pace with the development," Strazzeri said. Who should pay for growth? The candidates also addressed concerns over whether developers are paying enough toward the infrastructure needed to support new development. Giordano said developers should be held accountable for infrastructure needs associated with their projects. "They need to pay their fair share if they're going to be coming here and developing," Giordano said, adding that if a project requires sidewalks or lights, developers should be responsible for those needs. Martin pushed back on the idea that developers are not already paying toward infrastructure. "All the developers are required to pay mobility or impact fees for roads, for parks, for law enforcement and for civic space," Martin said. She said the city periodically reviews and increases those fees, but noted state law limits how much municipalities can levy through impact and mobility fees. Strazzeri said he also believes developers should carry more of the burden associated with growth. "The developers have to pay their fair share," Strazzeri said. "This should not be pushed off to the residents." He said roads, schools, emergency services and utilities should be addressed as part of the development process. Property taxes, CDDs and housing costs Martin also addressed a distinction she said residents should understand when looking at what they pay to live in Port St. She said the city does not control housing prices or interest rates, but does control its own property tax rate. Lucie has lowered its property tax rate each year for the past 11 years, reducing the rate by 25% over that period. She also said 22% of a resident's property tax bill goes to the city, with the remainder going to other taxing authorities. Martin also addressed Community Development District assessments, or CDDs, which are common in parts of Tradition. She said those assessments are determined by their respective CDD boards, not the Port St. On housing affordability, Giordano said higher-paying jobs are an important part of making it possible for residents to afford homes. "We need to bring the jobs," Giordano said. Strazzeri acknowledged the city does not control the housing market or interest rates but said it can work on affordable housing and ensuring housing options exist for everyday workers. "Everybody deserves the right to afford a home," Strazzeri said. Giordano also tied housing affordability to the need for higher-paying jobs. He said he wants to attract investors, medical centers and technology companies to Port St. We need those $100,000 jobs for our community, Giordano said. Why do we have to travel to West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale or Miami? Strazzeri also said attracting higher-paying jobs could help residents afford to stay in the city. He said he would like to see Port St. Lucie become a technology hub rather than having residents leave for higher-paying work elsewhere. Trash collection Trash service is another issue that has generated debate in Port St. The city currently provides garbage collection once a week. Lucie voters will also get a chance to weigh in on trash service in the November general election, when a nonbinding question will ask whether residents support twice-weekly garbage pickup. Giordano said he supports allowing residents to decide service frequency and proposed creating a city-run trash operation instead of outsourcing collection. He estimated the city currently spends roughly $61 million outsourcing trash service and said he believes a city operation could provide the service for around $55 million while creating jobs. Those cost estimates are Giordano's and were not independently verified by CBS12 News. Strazzeri said he remains frustrated with trash service and also believes voters should have a say in how often their trash is collected. "We're paying more for less service, whereas previously we were paying less and getting more service," Strazzeri said. He said he has heard from residents who want twice-a-week pickup and others who prefer different service levels. The city has previously said twice-weekly collection would require more equipment and workers and would cost residents approximately $130 more per household each year. Soccer stadium and a downtown for Port St. Lucie One of the clearest differences between the candidates involves the planned minor league soccer stadium and the broader effort to create a downtown-like destination. Martin supports the project and said the stadium is intended to serve as an anchor for redevelopment on the city's east side. She said the city is not paying for the stadium itself, its operations or maintenance, or debt associated with it. "It's supposed to be the anchor to start attracting all those different uses of the retail, the shopping, the hotels to really redevelop that entire area so that we can have that walkable downtown-like destination point," Martin said. Giordano opposes the stadium and said he would try to stop it if possible. "If I can stop the soccer stadium, I will stop it," Giordano said. However, he said that if the project cannot be stopped, he would work to make the venue as profitable as possible by using it for concerts, graduations and other community events. Giordano said he does support creating a downtown and floated attracting investors and even a Seminole Hard Rock casino as possibilities. Strazzeri said he is not opposed to a downtown but does not believe it or the soccer stadium should be the city's priority right now. "I would really like to improve the roads," Strazzeri said. "I would like to bring, you know, Trader Joe's, a Topgolf, higher-paying jobs." He said Port St. Lucie should first focus on quality of life and other needs. "I'm not saying that I'm against a downtown, but right now we need to focus on other things," Strazzeri said. Water quality Water quality also came up during the candidate interviews. Giordano said he wants the city to stop chemical spraying in lakes and waterways, pointing to a fish kill at Sawgrass Lakes as an example of his concern. He attributed the deaths to spraying and said the practice would stop if he becomes mayor. Strazzeri similarly said he would prefer natural approaches, including aeration or dredging, over what he described as harsh chemicals. "I would prefer to find natural ways to fix these issues rather than using these harsh chemicals and killing the fish," Strazzeri said. Martin pointed to the city's existing water-quality programs, including the McCarty Ranch Water Quality Project, stormwater baffle boxes and other projects aimed at reducing nutrients and pollution. "We constantly have projects going that are all about water quality," Martin said. What would they prioritize in office? Martin said her top priority if reelected would continue to be public safety, followed by infrastructure, reducing traffic congestion and maintaining quality of life. She also pointed to what she considers accomplishments during her time in office, including lowering the city's millage rate, reducing city debt by more than $400 million and adding parks. Giordano said that during his first 100 days, he would focus on Flock license plate readers and red-light cameras as well as traffic patterns and signal timing. He said he would seek new traffic data to determine where the city can reduce congestion. Strazzeri said his first year would focus on increasing transparency between City Hall and residents. He proposed creating a small-business owner committee and holding quarterly town halls where residents could hear about upcoming city plans and provide feedback before decisions are made. He said he would also focus on higher-paying jobs and additional entertainment and dining options. Martin has served as Port St. Lucie's mayor for the past five years and previously served on the City Council. She was first elected in 2010 and said she has lived in Port St. Before elected office, Martin worked as a paralegal. Giordano said he has lived in Port St. Lucie since 1989, grew up and attended school in the city and has nearly 20 years of public-service experience. He said he spent about a decade with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, later worked in security at the nuclear power plant and is a local business owner. Strazzeri said he moved to Port St. He served in the Army, deployed to Iraq as a combat engineer and later transitioned into information technology and cybersecurity. He said he decided to run after his son died from cancer and his experiences led him to believe residents needed a stronger voice in local government. Why should voters choose them? Martin points to her experience. "I have the knowledge, experience, and the results-driven leadership in order to continue to make that happen, to continue to make Port St. Lucie the best it possibly can be," Martin said. Giordano describes himself as an alternative to longtime political leadership. I'm a local business owner," Giordano said. "I want to bring a different style of leadership that works for the community." Strazzeri said his campaign is centered on transparency and accountability. Lucie deserves leadership that's transparent, accountable, and independent and is only responsible to the people and not special interests," Strazzeri said. Lucie voters will make that decision Tuesday. Election Day information The Port St. Lucie mayoral race is nonpartisan, meaning candidates do not run with a political party affiliation. Polls close Tuesday at 7 p.m. If one candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, that candidate wins the mayoral race outright. If no candidate receives more than 50%, the top two vote-getters will advance to the November general election. CBS12 News will be tracking the Port St. Lucie mayoral race and election results throughout the night.

hero.headline: Christopher 'Doc' Collins wins Martin County Commission District 2 seat
hero.body:
Christopher 'Doc' Collins won the open Martin County Commission District 2 seat Tuesday, defeating Susan O'Rourke and Althea Wiley in a Universal Primary Contest that decided the race outright. Collins received 14,657 votes, or about 49 percent, while O'Rourke received 12,065 votes, about 40 percent, and Wiley received 3,194 votes, nearly 11 percent. Because all three candidates were Republicans and no Democrat qualified, Tuesday's vote decided the seat with no November general election to follow.

Collins, a chiropractor and former Stuart city commissioner and mayor, stepped down from the Stuart City Commission earlier this year to run for the county seat, a move required under the city's charter before he could qualify for another elected office. He ran largely on a platform of slow growth, calling for tighter restrictions on new development across the county. During his time on the Stuart City Commission, Collins joined two other commissioners in voting to rescind the city's agreement with Brightline for a downtown train station, a position that put him at odds with O'Rourke throughout the campaign.

The campaign had a tense moment in its final week, when Collins accused a man named Jim Gallegos of stealing his campaign signs, posting a Facebook video with trail camera footage and Apple AirTag tracking he said showed Gallegos pulling one of his signs from the ground. Gallegos denied stealing anything, saying he removed roughly 30 signs for various candidates, including some of Collins', at a property owner's request. The dispute also drew in Derreck Ogden, a Stuart City Commission candidate, who publicly confronted Gallegos over the signs.

Collins will replace outgoing Commissioner Stacey Hetherington, who chose not to seek re election. O'Rourke, a former traffic engineer who previously served on Stuart's Local Planning Agency, ran on managing growth and easing traffic congestion. Her candidacy became the subject of a legal dispute earlier this year after Collins filed a challenge seeking to have her removed from the ballot, arguing she was not legally a Martin County resident when she qualified. A judge dismissed that challenge in July. Wiley, an author, Realtor and chef, ran on affordability, pointing to rising housing costs and other everyday expenses facing county residents.

Because all three candidates were Republicans and no Democrat qualified for the race, it was held as a Universal Primary Contest, meaning Tuesday's vote decided the seat outright with no November general election to follow. Collins received 14,657 votes, or about 49 percent. O'Rourke received 12,065 votes, about 40 percent, and Wiley received 3,194 votes, nearly 11 percent. Collins, a chiropractor and former Stuart city commissioner and mayor, stepped down from the Stuart City Commission earlier this year to run for the county seat, a move required under the city's charter before he could qualify for another elected office. He ran largely on a platform of slow growth, calling for tighter restrictions on new development across the county. During his time on the Stuart City Commission, Collins joined two other commissioners in voting to rescind the city's agreement with Brightline for a downtown train station, a position that put him at odds with O'Rourke throughout the campaign. See also: Martin, Giordano head to November runoff for PSL mayor The campaign also had a tense moment in its final week, when Collins accused a man named Jim Gallegos of stealing his campaign signs, posting a Facebook video with trail camera footage and Apple AirTag tracking he said showed Gallegos pulling one of his signs from the ground. Gallegos denied stealing anything, saying he removed roughly 30 signs for various candidates, including some of Collins', at a property owner's request. The dispute also drew in Derreck Ogden, a Stuart City Commission candidate, who publicly confronted Gallegos over the signs. Collins did not respond to CBS12's requests for an interview at any point during the campaign, and did not respond to a request for comment following the results. Collins will replace outgoing Commissioner Stacey Hetherington, who chose not to seek re-election. O'Rourke, a former traffic engineer who previously served on Stuart's Local Planning Agency, ran on managing growth and easing traffic congestion. Her candidacy became the subject of a legal dispute earlier this year after Collins filed a challenge seeking to have her removed from the ballot, arguing she was not legally a Martin County resident when she qualified. A judge dismissed that challenge in July. Wiley, an author, Realtor and chef, ran on affordability, pointing to rising housing costs and other everyday expenses facing county residents. The Brightline project remains a live issue for the incoming commission. Plans call for a roughly 10,200-square-foot station, a 660-foot platform, parking and other rail infrastructure, with completion targeted for 2029. Martin County has sought $69.3 million in federal funding for the project, and the commission is expected to keep playing a role in how it moves forward. Collins will also take office as the county braces for a possible November ballot measure, Amendment 3, which would expand the state's homestead exemption and cut into local government revenue. Commissioners previously voiced their concerns about the amendment during a public meeting in July, where the Martin County Fire Chief told the county about cuts he may have to make if the amendment passes in November.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County voters respond to arrest of Clerk and Comptroller Mike Caruso on primary election day
hero.teaser: Voters in Palm Beach County headed to the polls Tuesday amid a major shake-up after Republican candidate Mike Caruso was arrested and is being held without bond.
hero.body:
Mike Caruso served seven years in the Florida House, representing parts of Palm Beach County, before Governor Ron DeSantis appointed him as Palm Beach County Clerk and Comptroller in August of last year. His arrest came on primary election day. Although his name is not on the ballot as he is running uncontested, his removal from the race leaves Republicans without a candidate for the seat.

One voter called the development pretty shocking because Caruso is the Clerk of Court, saying people in that position should hold themselves to a higher level of standard. Another voter expressed frustration over losing their candidate, saying it sucks when a candidate drops off the map like that and expressing hope the Republican Party would be able to do some kind of referendum, while noting dislike for appointed candidates. Voters said the controversy should not keep people from participating and coming out to vote, and that their voices still matter at the polls.

Although his name is not on the ballot as he is running uncontested, voters are reacting to the news of his arrest and the serious allegations against him. His removal from the race leaves Republicans without a candidate for the seat."Pretty shocking because he is the Clerk of Court. You know, you would expect people like that to hold themselves to a higher level of standard…" one voter said.Another voter expressed frustration over losing their candidate."It sucks when you have your candidate kind of just drop off the map like that. So, I'm hoping the Republican Party is able to like do some kind of referendum. I don't like appointed candidates... I think it always gets sketchy," the voter said.Still, voters say the controversy shouldn't keep people from participating and coming out to vote. Even amid the controversy, voters say their voices still matter at the polls.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds wins Republican nomination for Florida governor, David Jolly takes Democratic nod
cards.body:
Byron Donalds won the Republican nomination for Florida governor on Tuesday, defeating opponents including former Lieutenant Governor Jay Collins and political newcomer James Fishback. Former U.S. Representative David Jolly captured the Democratic nomination, setting the stage for a November contest to replace outgoing Governor Ron DeSantis, who is barred from running for a third consecutive term.

Donalds, 47, triumphed with backing from President Trump and promises to push tax cuts, overhaul Florida's insurance regulations to lower consumer costs and seek greater price transparency from healthcare providers. There have been three elected Black governors in U.S. history, and Donalds could become Florida's first. Jolly, 53, is a former Republican U.S. representative who became a fierce critic of Trump, turned independent, and joined the Democratic Party last year. For the second time in a row, Florida Democrats have chosen a former Republican as their candidate for governor. Four years ago, Democrats backed former Republican Governor Charlie Crist, who was easily defeated by DeSantis by nearly 20 percentage points.

Trump has had an inconsistent record on picks for governor in primaries this year, and a strong showing by Donalds would leave Republicans in a more commanding position for November. Though DeSantis coasted to reelection in 2022, he squeaked into office in 2018 by little more than 32,000 ballots out of 8.1 million cast. Rich Chamberlin, a retiree in Port St. Lucie, said he supported Jolly in Tuesday's primary, spurred on by attack ads against him. Chamberlin said he saw anti-Jolly ads and decided if they were against him, then he must be for him, adding it did not matter to him that Jolly was once a Republican.

Tuesday's primaries gave final form to a November ballot whose races will test Trump's grip on his adopted state and Democrats' ability to resurrect Florida as a national political battleground. Florida has moved notably to the right since Trump won his first election in 2016, though Democrats hope to regain ground from his slumping popularity ratings. DeSantis, a leading conservative figure who has clashed and collaborated with Trump over the years, praised Donalds as ready to continue conservative policies in the state.

Trump ousted Vindman afterward.Floridians haven't sent a Democrat to the Senate since 2012.Serving in Congress since 2005 , she entered a new district — thanks to DeSantis' successful push for new congressional maps intended to boost Trump's midterm election prospects.It's not the first time Wasserman Schultz has had to sway new voters after Republicans tinkered with boundaries. Among allegations, Mills has denied accusations that he abused a former girlfriend. Leading Republicans, including DeSantis, had abandoned their support of Mills leading up to the primary.Elijah advances to the general election in a central Florida district that is considered reliably Republican.____Associated Press reporters Gisela Salomon in Miami and David Fischer in Port St. Lucie, Florida, contributed.

Ron DeSantis, who is finishing his second term and is barred from seeking a third consecutive termThere have been three elected Black governors in U.S. Yet the 47-year-old Donalds is more likely to tout his conservative credentials than the possibility of joining that select group as campaigning opens for November.He has promised to push tax cuts, overhaul Florida's insurance regulations to lower consumer costs and seek greater price transparency from healthcare providers.“The people of Florida want to make sure that the Florida dream is alive and well into the future,” he said recently. “Affordability is a problem for all Floridians. It doesn't matter what your politics are. It doesn't matter what the color of your skin is.”Trump has had an inconsistent record on picks for governor in primaries this year, and a strong showing by Donalds would leave him, and Republicans in general, in a more commanding position for November. Though DeSantis coasted to reelection in 2022, he squeaked into office in 2018 by little more of 32,000 ballots out of 8.1 million cast.Meanwhile, Jolly is hoping to prove a party-switching former Republican can actually carry the Democratic banner in a state where that's failed before. Democrats nominated former Republican Gov. Charlie Crist in 2022 only to see him lose by nearly 20 percentage points to DeSantis.Rich Chamberlin, a retiree in Port St. Lucie, said he supported Jolly in Tuesday's primary, spurred on by attack ads against him.“I saw anti-Jolly ads. I said ‘Ok, if they are against him, then I must be for him,'" Chamberlin said, adding it didn't matter to him that Jolly was once a Republican.Moody, a former state attorney general tapped for Rubio's seat in 2025, was already in a strong position as she pursued the GOP nomination. DeSantis, when he appointed her, praised her as a law-and-order prosecutor ready to help Trump “shut the border,” tame inflation, and overhaul a federal bureaucracy “run amok.”Democrats face a familiar theme of 2026 primaries, with the progressive Nixon confronting Vindman from the party's center-left establishment. Vindman's testimony in 2019 was notable in the Democrat-led House impeachment case that led to Trump's acquittal in the Republican-led Senate. Trump ousted Vindman afterward.Floridians haven’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 2012.Serving in Congress since 2005 , she entered a new district — thanks to DeSantis' successful push for new congressional maps intended to boost Trump's midterm election prospects.It’s not the first time Wasserman Schultz has had to sway new voters after Republicans tinkered with boundaries. But this time she was the only white candidate in a plurality Black district — the redrawn Florida 20th, concentrated in the most diverse parts of South Florida's Broward County. It's the most Democratic House district in Florida, meaning she will be a prohibitive favorite in November.Her four Black primary opponents — including Cherfilus-McCormick — had argued that the district requires a Black representative. But the voters went with a candidate who touted long experience from serving in Congress since 2005.Surrounded by her campaign staff Tuesday night, Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz tearfully thanked voters for having confidence in her. “(I will work) to make all of you proud, to make sure that the people we spoke to all across this district know that I will fight so they can pay their rent,” Schultz said.She said she hoped to live up to the legacy of Alcee Hastings, a long-time representative of District 20 who passed away in 2021. Schultz will be the first representative of the new District 20 despite controversy regarding her running in the historically Black-represented district.In other races, former television news reporter Ryan Elijah won the Republican nomination for Florida’s 7th Congressional District, ousting scandal-plagued U.S. Cory Mills.A two-term congressman, Mills had spent months denying allegations of domestic violence against a former girlfriend and other controversies. Among allegations, Mills has denied accusations that he abused a former girlfriend.Florida Republicans including DeSantis had abandoned Mills ahead of the primary. And Trump, though initially backing Mills in February, did not include him in a list of endorsements released this week.Elijah advances to the general election in a central Florida district that is considered reliably Republican.Associated Press reporters Gisela Salomon in Miami and David Fischer in Port St. Lucie, Florida, contributed.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office uses Flock cameras in search for Vero Beach homicide suspect
hero.teaser: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is using a network of automated license plate cameras and its Real Time Crime Center to search for Matthew Waggle.
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office confirmed Tuesday it has been using its Real Time Crime Center and a network of Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for 33-year-old Matthew Waggle and work to piece together what happened in the Sunday morning homicide of 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic. Waggle has been identified as a person of interest in the shooting death of Kriskewic, who was found in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach, Sunday morning.

A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle. Investigators say he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached. The Sheriff's Office said investigators believe Kriskewic had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the shooting as a domestic violence homicide.

The Sheriff's Office said there are no further updates ready for release at this time. The investigation remains ongoing.

Kriskewic was found in the 500 block of First Street , just outside Vero Beach, Sunday morning. Deputies performed lifesaving measures before she was taken to a trauma center, where she later died. cards.headline: Vero Beach shooting victim identified as Dawn Kriskewic, suspect Matthew Waggle still at large
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office has identified the woman shot and killed Sunday morning in Vero Beach as 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic. Kriskewic was found with an apparent gunshot wound in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street Sunday morning. Despite life-saving measures by deputies, she was pronounced dead at a trauma center.

The sheriff's office said there was a delay in releasing the victim's name because several out-of-state next of kin needed to be located and notified. Detectives are treating the case as a domestic violence homicide and continue searching for 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian, who has been identified as a person of interest. Investigators believe Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said a nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle, who should be considered armed and dangerous and may have fled the area. Flowers warned residents not to approach Waggle if they encounter him, saying it is possible he could harm other people or himself.

Close friends remembered Kriskewic as someone who was beautiful inside and out, a mother, hairdresser and author who was loved by many. The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie voters decide mayor race as growth and traffic top concerns
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie voters cast ballots Tuesday in a mayoral race focused on managing growth, traffic congestion, and infrastructure in one of Florida's largest cities. Incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin faces challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Strazzeri in a nonpartisan election where no candidate running with a party affiliation.

The candidates offered different approaches to the city's rapid development. Giordano said he wants to slow growth and ensure infrastructure can handle existing development, pointing to traffic in St. Lucie West that he called a nightmare, saying it takes almost 30 minutes to get from one end to the other. Martin said many development rights were granted over 20 years ago and cannot be taken away by the current City Council, but pointed to the city's acquisition of more than 280 acres of green space since January 2025, including Rosser Lakes Preserve where a developer wanted to build 86 homes. Strazzeri said roads, schools, utilities, and emergency services need to be in place prior to communities being developed.

A planned minor league soccer stadium proved a clear dividing line between the candidates. Martin supports the project as an anchor for redevelopment on the city's east side and said the city is not paying for the stadium itself, its operations, maintenance, or debt. Giordano said if he can stop the soccer stadium, he will stop it. Strazzeri said he is not opposed to a downtown but does not believe the stadium should be the city's priority right now, saying the city should focus on roads and higher-paying jobs.

Polls close at 7 p.m. Tuesday. If one candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote, that candidate wins outright. If no candidate receives more than 50 percent, the top two vote-getters will advance to the November general election. The race follows a campaign sign controversy that resulted in three Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on leave, including Lt. Aaron Martin, the mayor's husband.
hero.article_text: Lucie voters are deciding Tuesday who they want to lead one of Florida's largest cities, with growth, traffic, development and the future of the city among the major issues in the mayoral race. CBS12 News sat down with incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin and challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Strazzeri ahead of Election Day, asking them the same questions about some of the biggest concerns facing Port St. Lucie and what they would do if elected. Their answers reveal different approaches to managing a city that continues to grow. Lucie's growth Giordano said he believes the city needs to slow development and focus on whether existing infrastructure can handle what is already being built. "I want to slow down the growth and make sure that our infrastructure can handle what we already have," Giordano said. He said the city needs to make sure its drainage systems, roads and traffic infrastructure can keep up with development. Giordano also said he wants the city to focus more heavily on supporting local businesses and attracting higher-paying jobs. Martin said one challenge is that many development rights were granted decades ago and cannot simply be taken away by the current City Council. "What a lot of people don't realize still is that the developer rights were granted over 20 years ago," Martin said. "Where the developers do have those rights that were granted and those entitlements, we can't make that change." Martin pointed to Rosser Lakes Preserve as an example of an area where the city was able to prevent additional development. She said a developer wanted to build 86 homes on the property, but the city instead acquired the land to preserve it as green space. Lucie has acquired more than 280 acres of green space since January 2025. Strazzeri said he supports what he calls responsible growth but believes infrastructure should be in place before communities are developed. "Our roads, our schools, our utilities, our emergency services need to be in place prior to them developing in these communities because they're playing catch up right now," Strazzeri said. Traffic All three candidates acknowledged traffic as a major issue, but offered different approaches. Giordano called traffic in St. Lucie West a "nightmare" and said he wants a new traffic study examining roadways, traffic signals and signal timing. "It takes almost 30 minutes to get from one end to the other," Giordano said of St. "That's totally unacceptable." He said the city should examine where roads could be widened, whether medians need to be removed and where other changes could improve traffic flow. Martin pointed to projects already underway, including work on Floresta Drive and Port St. Lucie Boulevard South, roundabouts in Torino and planned intersection improvements at Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway, Savona Boulevard and Gatlin Boulevard. She said roundabouts can help move vehicles more efficiently and the city is extending turn lanes where possible. "We're going to continue to look at all of our areas and do those intersection improvements so that we can keep the flow of traffic going to reduce that traffic congestion," Martin said. Strazzeri said the city needs to be "proactive and not reactive," calling for better traffic signal coordination, adaptive signal technology and road expansion where possible. "We have to ensure that the infrastructure keeps pace with the development," Strazzeri said. Who should pay for growth? The candidates also addressed concerns over whether developers are paying enough toward the infrastructure needed to support new development. Giordano said developers should be held accountable for infrastructure needs associated with their projects. "They need to pay their fair share if they're going to be coming here and developing," Giordano said, adding that if a project requires sidewalks or lights, developers should be responsible for those needs. Martin pushed back on the idea that developers are not already paying toward infrastructure. "All the developers are required to pay mobility or impact fees for roads, for parks, for law enforcement and for civic space," Martin said. She said the city periodically reviews and increases those fees, but noted state law limits how much municipalities can levy through impact and mobility fees. Strazzeri said he also believes developers should carry more of the burden associated with growth. "The developers have to pay their fair share," Strazzeri said. "This should not be pushed off to the residents." He said roads, schools, emergency services and utilities should be addressed as part of the development process. Property taxes, CDDs and housing costs Martin also addressed a distinction she said residents should understand when looking at what they pay to live in Port St. She said the city does not control housing prices or interest rates, but does control its own property tax rate. Lucie has lowered its property tax rate each year for the past 11 years, reducing the rate by 25% over that period. She also said 22% of a resident's property tax bill goes to the city, with the remainder going to other taxing authorities. Martin also addressed Community Development District assessments, or CDDs, which are common in parts of Tradition. She said those assessments are determined by their respective CDD boards, not the Port St. On housing affordability, Giordano said higher-paying jobs are an important part of making it possible for residents to afford homes. "We need to bring the jobs," Giordano said. Strazzeri acknowledged the city does not control the housing market or interest rates but said it can work on affordable housing and ensuring housing options exist for everyday workers. "Everybody deserves the right to afford a home," Strazzeri said. Giordano also tied housing affordability to the need for higher-paying jobs. He said he wants to attract investors, medical centers and technology companies to Port St. We need those $100,000 jobs for our community, Giordano said. Why do we have to travel to West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale or Miami? Strazzeri also said attracting higher-paying jobs could help residents afford to stay in the city. He said he would like to see Port St. Lucie become a technology hub rather than having residents leave for higher-paying work elsewhere. Trash collection Trash service is another issue that has generated debate in Port St. The city currently provides garbage collection once a week. Lucie voters will also get a chance to weigh in on trash service in the November general election, when a nonbinding question will ask whether residents support twice-weekly garbage pickup. Giordano said he supports allowing residents to decide service frequency and proposed creating a city-run trash operation instead of outsourcing collection. He estimated the city currently spends roughly $61 million outsourcing trash service and said he believes a city operation could provide the service for around $55 million while creating jobs. Those cost estimates are Giordano's and were not independently verified by CBS12 News. Strazzeri said he remains frustrated with trash service and also believes voters should have a say in how often their trash is collected. "We're paying more for less service, whereas previously we were paying less and getting more service," Strazzeri said. He said he has heard from residents who want twice-a-week pickup and others who prefer different service levels. The city has previously said twice-weekly collection would require more equipment and workers and would cost residents approximately $130 more per household each year. Soccer stadium and a downtown for Port St. Lucie One of the clearest differences between the candidates involves the planned minor league soccer stadium and the broader effort to create a downtown-like destination. Martin supports the project and said the stadium is intended to serve as an anchor for redevelopment on the city's east side. She said the city is not paying for the stadium itself, its operations or maintenance, or debt associated with it. "It's supposed to be the anchor to start attracting all those different uses of the retail, the shopping, the hotels to really redevelop that entire area so that we can have that walkable downtown-like destination point," Martin said. Giordano opposes the stadium and said he would try to stop it if possible. "If I can stop the soccer stadium, I will stop it," Giordano said. However, he said that if the project cannot be stopped, he would work to make the venue as profitable as possible by using it for concerts, graduations and other community events. Giordano said he does support creating a downtown and floated attracting investors and even a Seminole Hard Rock casino as possibilities. Strazzeri said he is not opposed to a downtown but does not believe it or the soccer stadium should be the city's priority right now. "I would really like to improve the roads," Strazzeri said. "I would like to bring, you know, Trader Joe's, a Topgolf, higher-paying jobs." He said Port St. Lucie should first focus on quality of life and other needs. "I'm not saying that I'm against a downtown, but right now we need to focus on other things," Strazzeri said. Water quality Water quality also came up during the candidate interviews. Giordano said he wants the city to stop chemical spraying in lakes and waterways, pointing to a fish kill at Sawgrass Lakes as an example of his concern. He attributed the deaths to spraying and said the practice would stop if he becomes mayor. Strazzeri similarly said he would prefer natural approaches, including aeration or dredging, over what he described as harsh chemicals. "I would prefer to find natural ways to fix these issues rather than using these harsh chemicals and killing the fish," Strazzeri said. Martin pointed to the city's existing water-quality programs, including the McCarty Ranch Water Quality Project, stormwater baffle boxes and other projects aimed at reducing nutrients and pollution. "We constantly have projects going that are all about water quality," Martin said. What would they prioritize in office? Martin said her top priority if reelected would continue to be public safety, followed by infrastructure, reducing traffic congestion and maintaining quality of life. She also pointed to what she considers accomplishments during her time in office, including lowering the city's millage rate, reducing city debt by more than $400 million and adding parks. Giordano said that during his first 100 days, he would focus on Flock license plate readers and red-light cameras as well as traffic patterns and signal timing. He said he would seek new traffic data to determine where the city can reduce congestion. Strazzeri said his first year would focus on increasing transparency between City Hall and residents. He proposed creating a small-business owner committee and holding quarterly town halls where residents could hear about upcoming city plans and provide feedback before decisions are made. He said he would also focus on higher-paying jobs and additional entertainment and dining options. Martin has served as Port St. Lucie's mayor for the past five years and previously served on the City Council. She was first elected in 2010 and said she has lived in Port St. Before elected office, Martin worked as a paralegal. Giordano said he has lived in Port St. Lucie since 1989, grew up and attended school in the city and has nearly 20 years of public-service experience. He said he spent about a decade with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, later worked in security at the nuclear power plant and is a local business owner. Strazzeri said he moved to Port St. He served in the Army, deployed to Iraq as a combat engineer and later transitioned into information technology and cybersecurity. He said he decided to run after his son died from cancer and his experiences led him to believe residents needed a stronger voice in local government. Why should voters choose them? Martin points to her experience. "I have the knowledge, experience, and the results-driven leadership in order to continue to make that happen, to continue to make Port St. Lucie the best it possibly can be," Martin said. Giordano describes himself as an alternative to longtime political leadership. I'm a local business owner," Giordano said. "I want to bring a different style of leadership that works for the community." Strazzeri said his campaign is centered on transparency and accountability. Lucie deserves leadership that's transparent, accountable, and independent and is only responsible to the people and not special interests," Strazzeri said. Lucie voters will make that decision Tuesday. Election Day information The Port St. Lucie mayoral race is nonpartisan, meaning candidates do not run with a political party affiliation. Polls close Tuesday at 7 p.m. If one candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, that candidate wins the mayoral race outright. If no candidate receives more than 50%, the top two vote-getters will advance to the November general election. CBS12 News will be tracking the Port St. Lucie mayoral race and election results throughout the night.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie voters share priorities as polls open in mayoral election
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie voters heading to the polls Tuesday expressed priorities ranging from public safety to development concerns. The race follows a campaign sign controversy that resulted in three Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on leave.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie voters shared their priorities for the city's next mayor as they cast ballots Tuesday. One voter said safety is most important to them, while another voiced concerns about development, saying it was so beautiful and a lot of it has gone to development after living in the city for 20 years.

Other voters focused on the type of leadership they want to see at city hall. One voter said they would like the mayor to be somebody that has lived here, worked here, knows what it's like to be a working person, has kids, wants to keep them here, raise them here so they have a good future. A majority of voters expressed a desire for a mayor who is honest and committed to addressing issues that matter to residents.

The race follows a campaign sign controversy that resulted in three Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on leave. Police say the investigation involves two incidents earlier this month. Surveillance video shows a woman removing one of Mayor Shannon Martin's campaign signs, with her opponent Steven Giordano seen at the scene. In another incident, Giordano reported witnessing someone vandalizing his campaign sign. The officers placed on leave are Lt. Jason Vega, Detective Joseph Alves, and Lt. Aaron Martin, who is the mayor's husband. Polling places in Port St. Lucie are open until 7 p.m.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man in emotional distress from ocean
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office Marine Deputies and Aviation Unit joined a county lifeguard to save a man who stated he was going to swim out into the ocean in hopes of not returning.
cards.body:
Two divisions of the Martin County Sheriff's Office worked together Sunday to save a man suffering from a mental health crisis. The sheriff's office released a video from Sunday, August 16, showing Marine Deputies and the Aviation Unit working with a Martin County Lifeguard to rescue a man who was distraught and wanting to harm himself.

The man stated he was going to swim out into the ocean in hopes of not returning, according to the sheriff's office. When personnel located the man, they observed he was in emotional distress. Deputies entered the water and pulled the man out.

The sheriff's office said the man is getting the help he needs. The Suicide Crisis Lifeline is available by calling or texting 988, or through online chat. The 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast can be reached by dialing 211 or texting a ZIP code to 898211.

hero.headline: Shannon Ramsey-Chessman sworn in as interim Palm Beach County clerk after Michael Caruso arrest
hero.teaser: Shannon Ramsey-Chessman was sworn in Tuesday as Clerk Ad Interim after Palm Beach County Clerk of Court Michael Caruso was arrested on five felony child sex abuse charges and immediately suspended from office by Gov. Ron DeSantis.
hero.body:
Chief Judge Glenn Kelley of the 15th Judicial Circuit issued an administrative order Tuesday naming Ramsey-Chessman to the role, effective immediately. The appointment follows Caruso's arrest on charges including kidnapping, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious exhibition, luring or enticing a child, and child abuse causing mental injury, according to an arrest warrant and affidavit filed in Orange County Circuit Court.

Ramsey-Chessman has served as Chief Deputy Clerk, Chief of Staff and Chief Information Officer for the Palm Beach County Clerk of the Circuit Court & Comptroller since January 2021, according to court records. Her 29 years of public sector experience includes working with Palm Beach County's Office of Financial Management and Budget, the 15th Judicial Circuit, and the Martin County Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller.

Caruso, 67, faces serious charges stemming from allegations involving a child victim over nearly a year-long period. Caruso was appointed to the Palm Beach County Clerk position in August 2025 by DeSantis, following seven years of service in the Florida House of Representatives. He is running for election in November to retain his position, but his name is not on Tuesday's primary ballot since he is running uncontested.

cards.headline: Miami woman accused of posing as bank representative in Martin County credit card scam
cards.teaser: A Florida woman took a scam beyond phone lines, showing up at a Martin County resident's door pretending to represent a bank and demanding a credit card on Monday.
cards.body:
Monique Love Turnbull, of Miami, was seen at a victim's doorstep claiming the victim's bank account had been compromised, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Turnbull asked for the victim's credit card and said she would dispose of it. As law enforcement investigated, deputies were alerted to another call identifying Turnbull in a separate case.

Body camera video shows deputies pulling Turnbull over and asking her to step out of the car. The arresting deputy then tells Turnbull she is under arrest for fraud before placing her in handcuffs.

The sheriff's office is warning residents never to allow someone into their home if the person was not scheduled to visit. Residents should also never hand over credit cards, cash, gold or other valuables to someone who shows up unexpectedly. MCSO says anyone who comes to a resident's home claiming to represent a bank or financial institution and asking for valuables should be treated with suspicion. Residents are urged to call 911.

cards.headline: Vero Beach shooting victim identified as Dawn Kriskewic, suspect Matthew Waggle still at large
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office identified the woman shot and killed Sunday morning in Vero Beach as 52-year-old Dawn Kriskewic. Kriskewic was found with an apparent gunshot wound in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street Sunday morning. Despite life-saving measures by deputies, she was pronounced dead at a trauma center.

Detectives are treating the case as a domestic violence homicide and continue searching for 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian, who has been identified as a person of interest. Investigators believe Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship. Sheriff Eric Flowers said a nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle, who should be considered armed and dangerous and may have fled the area.

The sheriff's office said there was a delay in releasing the victim's name because several out-of-state next of kin needed to be located and notified. Close friends remembered Kriskewic as someone who was beautiful inside and out, a mother, hairdresser and author who was loved by many.

Flowers warned residents not to approach Waggle. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers. Waggle is described as having brown hair and blue eyes, about 6 feet 1 inch tall and weighing about 200 pounds.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Nuclear Plant back at full power after control rod failure prompted shutdown
hero.body:
Florida Power & Light says Unit 1 at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant is back at 100% power after being manually shut down Wednesday following an equipment issue. According to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, three control rods dropped into the reactor's core, prompting crews to shut the unit down for repairs. FPL says there was no danger to the public or staff, and no customers lost power.

Forrest Blanton lives on the Indian River Lagoon in St. Lucie County, where the plant's towering concrete structures are visible across the water. He said he was relieved by how the situation was handled and praised the company's openness about the incident.

Dr. Donald Wall, a nuclear engineering professor at the University of Florida, said residents living nearby had no reason to be alarmed. Wall said staff followed correct safety procedures by shutting the reactor down and noted the plant has multiple layers of protection built in. Wall compared the decision to a driver pulling over when a check engine light comes on.

Wall pointed to an NRC report of a similar incident in November 2024, in which Unit 1 was also manually shut down after three rods dropped during rod control maintenance. He raised questions about what the two events may have in common.

cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will head to the polls Tuesday to decide who will lead the city as its next mayor. All three candidates spoke about their priorities for the city Monday, with issues ranging from infrastructure and public safety to government spending and quality of life.

Giordano said he wants to bring a different approach to city hall, with a focus on spending, transparency and adding more amenities for families. Strazzeri said fiscal responsibility is at the top of his list, along with improving roads, drainage and overall quality of life.

Polls in Port St. Lucie open Tuesday at 7 a.m.

hero.headline: Stuart awarded $79 million federal grant to replace 100-year-old St. Lucie River Railroad Bridge
hero.body:
The City of Stuart has been awarded $79 million in federal funding to replace the aging St. Lucie River Railroad Bridge as part of a $5.3 billion nationwide investment in rail safety and infrastructure announced by U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy on Tuesday. The grant, part of the National Railroad Partnership Program, will fund the replacement of the 100-year-old single-track bridge with a modern double-track structure featuring dramatically improved clearances for boats and vessels navigating the Okeechobee Waterway.

Florida received a total of $496 million from the program, with the Stuart bridge project representing the second-largest allocation in the state. The new bridge will increase horizontal clearance from 50 feet to approximately 90 feet, while vertical clearance will jump from just 6.5 feet to 17.75 feet when in the closed position. These improvements will allow more than 90% of vessels to pass without requiring the bridge to open, significantly reducing delays for marine traffic on the federal navigation channel.

Congressman Brian Mast said the century-old bridge is too low, too narrow, and stuck in the closed position more often than it should be. He called it a daily headache for boaters and a safety risk for everyone who shares that corridor.

The bridge serves both Brightline passenger trains and Florida East Coast Railway freight operations, making it a critical piece of infrastructure for the region's transportation network.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies and lifeguard rescue man in emotional distress from ocean
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office marine deputies, the aviation unit, and a county lifeguard rescued a man Sunday who had entered the ocean stating he was not planning to return.
cards.body:
Two divisions of the Martin County Sheriff's Office worked together Sunday to save a man suffering from a mental health crisis. The sheriff's office released a video from Sunday, Aug. 16, showing its marine deputies, aviation unit, and a Martin County lifeguard saving a man who was distraught and wanting to harm himself.

According to the sheriff's office, the man stated he was going to swim out into the ocean in hopes of not returning. When personnel located the man, they observed he was in emotional distress. Deputies entered the water and pulled the man out of the water. The sheriff's office said the man is getting the help he needs.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce City Council selects former St. Lucie County attorney as interim city attorney
hero.body:
Fort Pierce City Council voted Monday to appoint Daniel S. McIntyre as interim city attorney when Sara Hedges ends her tenure in September. McIntyre, who served as St. Lucie County's chief legal counsel from 1985 to 2025, will negotiate salary terms with the city before assuming the role.

The council voted 4-1 to hire McIntyre after rejecting Commissioner Michael Broderick's motion to extend Hedges' contract through December 31. Mayor Linda Hudson supported Broderick's proposal, but Commissioners Chris Dzadovsky, Arnold Gaines and Curtis Johnson Jr. voted against it. The motion failed 2-3, with only Broderick voting against McIntyre's appointment.

Hedges became head of the city attorney's office in September 2023 after serving as an assistant city attorney. Her tenure became contentious in May following controversy over a wage garnishment for an unpaid credit card account owed by Johnna Morris, the city's finance director. City officials also reported friction between Hedges and City Manager Richard Chess over Chess' wish to consult outside counsel in the matter and Hedges' claim that Chess excluded her from staff employment issues.

McIntyre has 43 years of local government law experience, including three years as assistant Martin County attorney from 1982 to 1985. He holds a bachelor's degree from University of Miami and a law degree from Wake Forest School of Law. City officials said McIntyre has stepped in multiple times over the years to serve as Fort Pierce interim city attorney during vacancies. The city's Human Resources Department also offered John J. Anastasio, former counsel for Port St. Lucie Mayor JoAnn Faiella, as another candidate for the interim position.

hero.headline: Vero Beach shooting suspect remains at large as 911 calls released
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's detectives continue searching for Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, a person of interest in a fatal shooting Sunday at a mobile home complex along 1st Street in Vero Beach. Authorities believe Waggle is armed and dangerous and may have fled the area. The victim was a 52-year-old woman whose identity has not been released while next of kin is being notified.

The 911 calls released Tuesday captured neighbors' reactions moments after shots were fired. One caller told dispatchers, "I, I don't know there's a lady like in the street I think she's dead or somebody killed her I don't know." The neighbor described the victim as "new over here" when asked by the dispatcher if they knew who she was. Close friends remembered the victim as a mother, hairdresser, and author who was loved by many.

Detectives are treating the case as a domestic violence incident. The victim and Waggle were previously in a relationship, according to the sheriff's office. Sheriff Eric Flowers said investigators have issued a nationwide be on the lookout alert for Waggle. "We have put out a nationwide BOLO for him at this point and our team is working with real time crime center," Flowers said.

Flowers urged anyone with information to come forward. "If anybody saw anything, heard anything, please either reach out to crime stoppers or give our detectives a call," Flowers said. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org, or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant reactor returns to full power after control rod incident
hero.body:
Florida Power & Light says Unit 1 at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant is back at 100% power after being manually shut down Wednesday following what the company called an equipment issue. According to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, three control rods dropped into the reactor's core, prompting crews to shut the unit down for repairs. FPL says there was no danger to the public or staff, and no customers lost power.

Forrest Blanton lives on the Indian River Lagoon in St. Lucie County, where the plant's towering concrete structures are visible across the water. He said he was relieved by how the situation was handled and praised the company's openness about the incident. Dr. Donald Wall, a nuclear engineering professor at the University of Florida, said residents living nearby had no reason to be alarmed. Wall said staff followed correct safety procedures by shutting the reactor down, comparing the decision to pulling off the road when a check engine light comes on.

Wall noted the plant has multiple layers of protection built in. However, Wall pointed to an NRC report of a similar incident in November 2024, in which Unit 1 was also manually shut down after three rods dropped during rod control maintenance. He raised questions about what the two events may have in common.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office warns of law enforcement impersonation scam with 50 reports
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is sounding the alarm after receiving more than 50 reports from people targeted by a scam involving callers impersonating law enforcement officers.
cards.body:
According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, scammers have been using the names of the Civil Judicial Services Bureau, Lt. Michael O'Brien and retired Sgt. Jeff Buchanan when making fraudulent calls. Deputies said the scam follows a repeated pattern. A caller claims the victim missed court or jury duty and that there is a warrant for their arrest. hero.headline: Martin County deputies and lifeguard rescue man in emotional distress from ocean
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office marine deputies, the Aviation Unit, and a Martin County lifeguard rescued a man suffering from a mental health crisis on Sunday, August 16. The man had told officials he was going to swim out into the ocean in hopes of not returning.

When sheriff's office personnel located the man, they observed he was in emotional distress. Deputies entered the water and pulled the man out of the water. The sheriff's office released a video of the rescue on Tuesday.

The man is getting the help he needs, according to the sheriff's office. The rescue involved two divisions of the sheriff's office working together to save the man who was distraught and wanting to harm himself.

People in crisis can talk with the Suicide Crisis Lifeline by calling or sending a text message to 988, or by chatting online. The 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast can be reached by dialing 211 or by texting a ZIP code to 898211.

hero.headline: Florida lawmaker plans bill to ban elective cat declawing statewide
hero.body:
State Rep. Rob Long announced plans to introduce legislation during the 2027 Legislative Session that would prohibit elective cat declawing across Florida while still allowing veterinarians to perform the procedure when medically necessary. Long said declawing involves amputating the last bone of a cat's toes, not simply removing claws. The proposal would revive and update a bill first introduced by former State Sen. Lauren Book in 2020. Long said the basic framework is simple: prohibit declawing for cosmetic or convenience reasons while preserving a veterinarian's ability to perform the procedure when it is genuinely medically necessary.

Long said he learned about a cat recently adopted from Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control that was later returned after being declawed, which he said led to behavioral issues commonly associated with the procedure. Janet Steele, director of Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control, said declawed cats that come through the shelter often need extra accommodations including litter that does not irritate their sensitive paws and spaces that do not require large distance leaps. Steele said the behavioral impacts of declawing can cause pain redirecting actions such as biting or swatting towards people or other pets, difficulties using certain litters resulting in urinating or defecating outside the litter box, and an overall pulling back from social activities.

Long pointed to a shift within the veterinary industry, saying Banfield and VCA, two of the largest veterinary systems in the country, no longer support elective declawing. Organizations including the American Veterinary Medical Association and the American Animal Hospital Association also discourage medically unnecessary declawing, according to Long. Animal advocacy group The Paw Project said five states have banned declawing within the past nine years: New York, Maryland, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and California. All ten Canadian provinces have also banned the procedure.

The Paw Project said there is no evidence that declaw bans result in cats losing their homes, and that shelter intake numbers declined in every jurisdiction where data is available. The group said shelter intake of cats in Los Angeles dropped by 43.5 percent in the years after the city banned declawing. Long said his goal next session is to update Book's work and get it across the finish line, adding that an irreversible amputation should be performed because the animal medically needs it, not simply for human convenience.

Deputies said scammers use fear, urgency and threats of arrest to pressure victims into taking immediate action.

If residents have questions about a legitimate court matter, they should contact the appropriate agency using a verified phone number.

cards.headline: Indian River County manhunt continues for armed suspect in fatal Vero Beach shooting
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's detectives continue searching for 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle, a person of interest in a fatal shooting Sunday in Vero Beach. Authorities believe Waggle is armed and dangerous and may have fled the area. The sheriff's office released 911 calls from the incident on Tuesday.

The shooting happened Sunday at a mobile home complex along 1st Street in Vero Beach. The victim, a 52-year-old woman whose identity is not being released while next of kin is being notified, was found in the street. Neighbors called 911 moments after shots were fired. One caller told dispatchers, "I don't know there's a lady like in the street I think she's dead or somebody killed her I don't know." Close friends remembered the victim as a mother, hairdresser, and author who was loved by many.

Detectives are treating the case as a domestic violence incident. The victim and Waggle were previously in a relationship. Sheriff Eric Flowers said investigators have issued a nationwide alert for Waggle. "We have put out a nationwide BOLO for him at this point, be on the look out. And our team is working with real time crime center. Our detectives have been working on this and its our goal to ultimately locate him," Flowers said.

Flowers urged anyone with information to come forward. "If anybody saw anything, heard anything, please either reach out to crime stoppers or give our detectives a call," Flowers said. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org, or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.
