hero.headline: Port St. Lucie to reconsider LED sign rules after church request
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council will revisit regulations governing LED signs after a Tulip Boulevard church pastor requested permission to install a larger display than current code allows. Pastor Manzie of Central Baptist Church asked the council to increase the permitted LED sign size from 20 square feet to 25 square feet and to allow images in addition to text-only displays. The pastor explained in an email that LED signs are manufactured in specific sizes, and the current 20-square-foot limit would force the church to choose a 15.44-square-foot sign, losing nearly eight square feet of display space. The LED screen the church wants to purchase measures 88.2 inches by 37.7 inches, or 23.09 square feet.

Councilman Anthony Bonna brought the request to the council at its Aug. 10 meeting, calling it reasonable and suggesting the city make its code compatible with how LED panels are manufactured. The issue reopens a controversy council members thought they had settled in 2024 when they amended the Sign Code to limit LED signs to 20 square feet and text-only displays. That earlier change followed a dispute between two Prima Vista Boulevard churches, one of which had erected an LED sign without a permit while another sought permission for a similar sign.

Mayor Martin and Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo, who both participated in the earlier LED discussions, expressed caution about allowing images on LED displays. Mayor Martin cited the U.S. Supreme Court decision in Reed v. Gilbert as a distinct reason the city had restricted LED signs to text only. Vice-Mayor Caraballo noted concerns included light pollution, though she acknowledged LED technology has changed and the city now uses LED in some of its own signage. Council members agreed to separate the discussions on size and images to avoid delaying the pastor's request for a larger sign.

City Attorney Richard Berrios said changing the code would require input from Planning and Zoning officials. Assistant Planning and Zoning Director Anne Cox explained the process would require a workshop, followed by review at the Planning and Zoning Board and then two readings at City Council. A workshop scheduled for Aug. 17 was subsequently canceled. Councilman Bonna pushed to separate the size and image discussions so the more complicated image question would not delay approval of a modest size increase for Central Baptist Church.
hero.article_text: LUCIE – A recent request by the pastor of a Tulip Boulevard church for a larger LED sign than currently permitted by the city’s Sign Code has reopened a conversation and controversy that City Council members here thought they’d finally settled two years ago. Not too many years back, city officials found themselves embroiled in a controversy between two Prima Vista Boulevard churches, one of which had purportedly erected an LED sign without a city permit, followed by the other requesting permission for just such a sign. That propelled Council members and staff into action, who also worried about compliance with a U.S. Supreme Court decision related to church signs and free speech. They thought the dust had finally settled on that issue in 2024 when they amended the Sign Code to limit LED signs to 20 square feet in diameter broadcasting text only. Pastor Manzie’s email, however, led to an Aug. 10 discussion launched by Councilman Anthony Bonna. “The request was quite reasonable to me, so I just wanted to bring it to Council to see what the temperature of Council was,” he said. “Essentially, he’s not asking for the monument to be any larger; it’s just these LED panels are constructed in such a way that he would have to reduce the LED portion significantly, which would reduce the impact of his sign. The LED portion is currently allowed to be 20 square feet, so simply by increasing that to 24 square feet we can address that. There may be similar requests in the future, and it might make sense to make the code compatible with how these panels are constructed.” Councilman Bonna was referring to part of Manzie’s email that spoke of a significant size limitation in current LED sign choices. The pastor insisted he needed more space to advertise the churches annual events since the city forced him to stop using large banners for that purpose. “Our church has been seeking quotes for various LED signs,” he wrote. “We were told that – according to the statute – we could only have a 20-square-foot LED sign displaying text only. The LED screen we would like to purchase is 88.2 inches by 37.7 inches, or 23.09 square feet. To comply with the code, we would need to select the next smaller size, which would be 15.44 square feet. I would loose a dramatic amount of space all because of how LED signs are made. I respectfully request that we adjust the code to allow 25 square feet and permit pictures.” City Attorney Richard Berrios then provided the Council his initial legal guidance on that request. “Upon first review, it looks like it would be a comprehensive amendment to the code to allow for a larger square footage,” he said. “Alternatively, there might be some other paths from staff they might have.” Councilman David Pickett initially thought Central Baptist might proceed with the larger sign in the interim, but the city attorney shot that idea down. “We would have to change the code first,” Berrios explained. “What is the pastor’s ETA on putting the sign in?” Councilman Pickett asked. Councilman Bonna tackled that question. “I think they’re looking to do it soon, but they’ve been a part of the community for a long time and they want to work through our processes,” he said. “My preference would be to change the code and not look for a work-around and do it as soon as possible. The other thing he would like to do – which may be more controversial – is have some imagery in his LED display.” Mayor Martin, who was vice-mayor during those earlier conversations immediately hit the brakes. “There were reasons why that was done that way,” she said. “We need to go back and relook at that, especially as it related to the Reed v. “I think this is a two-prong thing, but I believe there are distinct reasons why we didn’t allow the imagery portion of it.” Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo also took part in that earlier LED discussion. “There was a lot more than just imagery,” she said. “There was also concern with light pollution, but LEDs have changed. We even utilize LED in some of our signage, so I think there is an opportunity to relook at where technology is and Reed vs Gilbert. I would like a comprehensive discussion and then make the changes on the Sign Code that we can come up with.” Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan, in turn, described the prior church controversy that led to the earlier Sign Code changes. “This came up because the Methodist Church on Prima Vista placed an LED sign without a permit,” she recalled. Andrews across the street wanted to construct one but was told they couldn’t. So, it was like, how do we fix this? It was not even two years ago that we changed it to allow for that, and it was for messaging only.” Councilman Bonna still sought a timetable from staff, with Berrios acknowledging he would need input from Planning Zoning officials as well. “I would definitely need to coordinate with staff and have an understanding of what the appetite is,” he said. “Square footage seems simple in concept, but I don’t want to rummage around in the code without talking to them first and understanding the background.” Assistant Planning Zoning Director Anne Cox then provided the formal framework. “You said you’d like to workshop it first,” she said. “Then, if the language is agreed to, it’s a zoning text amendment. It would have to go to the Planning Zoning Board and then two readings at Council.” “So, it’s going to take a few months then,” Mayor Martin responded. Councilman Bonna, in turn, insisting on separating the discussions on size and images so as not to logjam the pastor’s request. Vice-Mayor Caraballo agreed. “I think the second piece of it’s going to be more complicated,” she said. “The way I see it in Reed v. Gilbert, once we allow images, we won’t be able to discriminate against additional images. So, I think that’s going to be the challenge. I agree with separating the issues, but I would like to see where we’re currently at with best practices looking at the top largest cities and the size of signs with LEDs as well.” Council members and staff then suggested holding the workshop that same month, but the Aug. 17 workshop was subsequently canceled. hero.headline: Home insurance premiums drop in Indian River County in first half of 2026
hero.teaser: Indian River County saw the largest decrease in average home insurance premiums among Treasure Coast counties in the first six months of 2026.
hero.body:
Average home insurance premiums in Indian River County fell from $4,453 in January 2026 to $4,334 in July 2026, a decrease of 2.7 percent, according to the July 2026 Property Insurance Stability Report from Florida's Insurance Commissioner. The decrease was the largest among Treasure Coast counties.

Martin County saw average premiums drop from $5,993 to $5,899, a decrease of 1.6 percent, while St. Lucie County saw premiums fall from $3,522 to $3,491, a decrease of 0.9 percent. The report showed decreasing property insurance premiums in 51 of 67 Florida counties.

The report cited reduced litigation from state reforms as one of the main drivers in lowering rates for many insurers. Palm Beach County Commissioner Gregg Weiss, who dropped wind coverage on his West Palm Beach home several years ago, said dropping insurance coverage carries risks, especially if a damaging storm hits, and is an option available only to homeowners who don't have a mortgage.

For many, the reductions may seem modest, and for others, relief is still not being seen. "It has been going up, never went down," Barry Garcia, a Palm Beach County resident, said. cards.headline: Vero Beach woman shot dead in roadway; Indian River County authorities search for Sebastian man nationwide
cards.body:
A 52-year-old woman died Sunday morning after being shot in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach, and the Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching nationwide for 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian as a person of interest in what investigators are treating as a domestic violence homicide.

The sheriff's office received a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway. Deputies found the woman with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said investigators believe Waggle and the victim were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle. Authorities have issued a nationwide be on the lookout for Waggle, who should be considered armed and dangerous. Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area whose siblings live in the complex, said his brother heard the shot. Cardenas said the neighborhood is typically quiet.

Flowers said detectives are using resources such as flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts. State Rep. Debra Tendrich, who sponsored House Bill 277 to strengthen protections for domestic violence survivors, said domestic violence is not contained in a specific area and that tracking someone across state lines is very difficult. The bill, signed into law by Gov. Ron DeSantis in July, adds victim relocation allowance, protection for military families and pets, and stronger protections for victims. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org, or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant Unit 1 returns to full power after control rod incident
hero.teaser: Florida Power & Light says Unit 1 at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant is back at 100% power after being manually shut down Wednesday following an equipment issue.
hero.body:
Unit 1 at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant returned to full power after being manually shut down last week when three control rods fell into the reactor's core. According to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the three control rods dropped into the reactor's core, prompting crews to shut the unit down for repairs. FPL says there was no danger to the public or staff, and no customers lost power.

Forrest Blanton lives on the Indian River Lagoon in St. Lucie County, where the plant's towering concrete structures are visible across the water. He said he was relieved by how the situation was handled and praised the company's openness about the incident. Dr. Donald Wall, a nuclear engineering professor at the University of Florida, said residents living nearby had no reason to be alarmed and that staff followed correct safety procedures by shutting the reactor down.

Wall pointed to an NRC report of a similar incident in November 2024, in which Unit 1 was also manually shut down after three rods dropped during rod control maintenance. He raised questions about what the two events may have in common.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man arrested on attempted murder charge after firing through bathroom door during domestic dispute
cards.body:
A 23-year-old Fort Pierce man faces multiple felony charges after deputies say he fired a gun through a bathroom door at a victim who had locked herself inside during a domestic disturbance Sunday morning. Nathan Hsu is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on no bond, charged with attempted felony murder, kidnapping, tampering with a witness, simple battery and grand theft of a motor vehicle.

Deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to a home on the 1700 block of Wyoming Avenue at around 11:30 a.m. Sunday for a reported domestic disturbance. During the incident, the victim locked herself inside a bathroom. Hsu allegedly fired a round through the bathroom door before fleeing the residence in a car.

Fort Pierce police later located the car near Porpoise Beach, prompting an extensive search of the area. While the search was underway, detectives with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators executed a search warrant at the residence on Wyoming Avenue.

At around 2:30 p.m., Hsu's family located him and alerted a passing Fort Pierce police officer. Hsu was taken into custody without incident and a firearm was recovered. Authorities said the incident was isolated and there is no ongoing threat to the public. The investigation remains active.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office warns of law enforcement impersonation scam with 50 reports
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office received more than 50 reports from people targeted by a scam involving callers impersonating law enforcement officers.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is sounding the alarm after receiving more than 50 reports from people targeted by a scam involving callers impersonating law enforcement officers. According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, scammers have been using the names of the Civil Judicial Services Bureau, Lt. Michael O'Brien and retired Sgt. Jeff Buchanan when making fraudulent calls.

Deputies said the scam follows a repeated pattern. A caller claims the victim missed court or jury duty and that there is a warrant for their arrest. The sheriff's office warned that scammers may use official-sounding language and personal information to make the call appear legitimate. The sheriff's office said scammers use fear, urgency and threats of arrest to pressure victims into taking immediate action.

Deputies said residents who receive one of these calls should hang up, not provide personal or financial information, not send money or make any payments, and not trust the caller ID or the name provided by the caller. If you have questions about a legitimate court matter, contact the appropriate agency using a verified phone number.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police officers rescue ducklings trapped in storm drain
cards.teaser: A routine call for service turned into a rescue mission for two Port St. Lucie police officers after a group of ducklings became trapped in a storm drain.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department said Officers Ortiz and Garcia responded Friday to the area of Southeast Oakridge Drive and Southeast Oaklyn Street, where the young ducks had fallen into the drain. Body camera video released by the department shows officers working around the storm drain and reaching inside to retrieve the ducklings one by one. Their mother remained nearby as officers worked to free her babies.

After carefully removing the ducklings from the drain, officers reunited them with their mother, bringing the unusual call to a happy ending. The department wrote in a Facebook post that it may have been a small rescue, but it made for a pretty great start to the weekend. Police used the rescue as a reminder that protecting the community can sometimes include its smallest residents.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide in ocean
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies pulled a distressed man from the ocean Monday after he swam out with no intention of returning, according to the agency.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office responded to a call about a man who said he was going to swim into the ocean without intending to return. Marine deputies, the aviation unit, and a Martin County lifeguard located the man in the water and jumped in to stop him from continuing.

Video from the Martin County Sheriff's Office shows several deputies surrounding the man in the water during the rescue. The agency said the responders quickly realized the situation and acted to prevent the man from continuing.

The man was pulled from the water and is now receiving help, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

hero.headline: Florida lawmaker proposes statewide ban on elective cat declawing
hero.body:
State Rep. Rob Long plans to introduce legislation during the 2027 Legislative Session that would prohibit elective cat declawing across Florida while still allowing veterinarians to perform the procedure when medically necessary. Long said declawing is widely misunderstood and involves amputating the last bone of a cat's toes, not simply removing claws. The proposal would revive and update a bill first introduced by former State Sen. Lauren Book in 2020.

Long said the basic framework would prohibit declawing for cosmetic or convenience reasons while preserving a veterinarian's ability to perform the procedure when genuinely medically necessary. He cited personal experience with rescue cats and a recent visit to Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control during cat season, where he learned about a cat that was adopted and later returned after being declawed, which led to behavioral issues. Janet Steele, director of Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control, said declawed cats that come through the shelter often need extra accommodations including litter that doesn't irritate their sensitive paws and spaces that don't require large distance leaps. Steele said the behavioral impacts of declawing can cause pain redirecting actions such as biting or swatting towards people or other pets, difficulties using certain litters resulting in urinating or defecating outside the litter box, and an overall pulling back from social activities.

Long pointed to a growing shift within the veterinary industry, saying Banfield and VCA, two of the largest veterinary systems in the country, no longer support elective declawing. Organizations including the American Veterinary Medical Association and the American Animal Hospital Association also discourage medically unnecessary declawing. Animal advocacy group The Paw Project said five states, New York, Maryland, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and California, have banned declawing within the past nine years, as have all ten Canadian provinces.

The Paw Project said there is no evidence that declaw bans result in cats losing their homes, and that shelter intake numbers declined in every jurisdiction where data is available. The group highlighted Los Angeles as one example, saying shelter intake of cats dropped by 43.5% in the years after the city banned declawing. Long said an irreversible amputation should be performed because the animal medically needs it, not simply for human convenience, and his goal next session is to update Book's work and get it across the finish line.

cards.headline: Florida emergency management chief Kevin Guthrie joins Jay Collins gubernatorial ticket hours before primary
cards.teaser: Jay Collins has chosen Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie as his running mate in the Republican race for governor, announcing the pick just hours before Tuesday's primary.
cards.body:
Collins announced the pick as he tries to close a significant polling gap with frontrunner Byron Donalds, who has held a commanding lead in many polls. Collins said he spent weeks considering who could serve as his second-in-command and wanted competence, leadership, character and someone who could step in and lead on day one, rather than someone chosen for demographic or geographic reasons.

cards.headline: Home insurance premiums decrease in 51 Florida counties in first half of 2026
cards.teaser: New state data show decreasing property insurance premiums in the first six months of 2026 in 51 of 67 counties, according to Florida's Insurance Commissioner.
cards.body:
The July 2026 Property Insurance Stability Report from January 2026 to July 2026 showed average premiums in Palm Beach County decreased from $6,412 to $6,323, a decrease of 1.4%. Martin County saw premiums drop from $5,993 to $5,899, a decrease of 1.6%. St. Lucie County premiums fell from $3,522 to $3,491, a decrease of 0.9%. Indian River County dropped from $4,453 to $4,334, a decrease of 2.7%. Okeechobee County fell from $3,754 to $3,730, a decrease of 0.6%.

The report cited reduced litigation from state reforms as one of the main drivers in lowering rates for many insurers. Palm Beach County resident Barry Garcia said his insurance has been going up and never went down. Palm Beach County Commissioner Gregg Weiss, who dropped wind coverage on his West Palm Beach home several years ago, said he has saved tens of thousands of dollars. Experts said dropping insurance coverage carries risks, especially if a damaging storm hits, and it is an option available only to homeowners who don't have a mortgage.

Weiss said he and other county commissioners still hear from residents about high insurance costs. He said one of the big ticket items of living in Florida is the cost of homeowners insurance.

hero.headline: More than 50 St. Lucie County residents targeted in law enforcement impersonation scam
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office received more than 50 reports from people targeted by a scam involving callers impersonating law enforcement officers. Scammers have been using the names of the Civil Judicial Services Bureau, Lt. Michael O'Brien and retired Sgt. Jeff Buchanan when making fraudulent calls, according to the sheriff's office.

Deputies said the scam follows a repeated pattern. A caller claims the victim missed court or jury duty and that there is a warrant for their arrest. The sheriff's office warned that scammers may use official-sounding language and personal information to make the call appear legitimate.

The sheriff's office said scammers use fear, urgency and threats of arrest to pressure victims into taking immediate action. Deputies said residents who receive one of these calls should hang up and not provide personal or financial information. Victims should not send money or make any payments and should not trust the caller ID or the name provided by the caller.

If residents have questions about a legitimate court matter, they should contact the appropriate agency using a verified phone number, according to the sheriff's office.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie officers rescue ducklings trapped in storm drain on Southeast Oakridge Drive
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police officers rescued a group of ducklings that fell into a storm drain Friday, reuniting them with their mother.
cards.body:
Officers Ortiz and Garcia responded Friday to the area of Southeast Oakridge Drive and Southeast Oaklyn Street, where young ducks had fallen into a storm drain. Body camera video released by the Port St. Lucie Police Department shows officers working around the storm drain and reaching inside to retrieve the ducklings one by one. Their mother remained nearby as officers worked to free her babies.

After carefully removing the ducklings from the drain, officers reunited them with their mother. The department wrote in a Facebook post that it may have been a small rescue, but it made for a great start to the weekend. The police department said protecting the community can sometimes include its smallest residents.

Nathan Hsu faces charges of attempted felony murder, kidnapping, tampering with a witness, simple battery, and grand theft of a motor vehicle.

Deputies responded to the residence around 11:30 a.m. Sunday for a reported domestic disturbance. During an argument with a woman, the victim locked herself inside a bathroom. Hsu fired a round through the bathroom door before fleeing the residence in a vehicle, according to the sheriff's office.

Fort Pierce police located the vehicle near Porpoise Beach on Hutchinson Island, prompting an extensive search of the surrounding area by both agencies. While the search was underway, detectives with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators executed a search warrant at the Wyoming Avenue residence.

He remains in the St. Lucie County Jail on no bond. The sheriff's office said the incident was isolated and there is no ongoing threat to the public.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce approves $183,200 pilot program for two code enforcement officers in redevelopment areas
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency voted unanimously on Aug. 11 to approve an interlocal funding agreement with the city for a yearlong pilot program that will employ two new code enforcement officers to work solely in community redevelopment areas of Fort Pierce. The first year of the program will cost up to $183,200.

Community and Economic Development Director Shyanne Harnage told the board that the program will provide enhanced code enforcement services within the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency boundaries only. The officers will focus on eliminating slum and blight, addressing non-operable vehicles, litter and illegal dumping. Harnage said other community redevelopment agencies are implementing similar programs and have been successful. Community Response Director Shaun Coss said the officers will conduct daily sign sweeps on main corridors within the FPRA boundaries and potentially deal with noise complaints once the city revises its noise ordinance.

Mayor Linda Hudson said the program will be aggressive and proactive rather than complaint driven. Commissioner Arnold Gaines expressed concerns about potential misunderstandings by residents, asking that the city get the word out that certain neighborhoods are not getting picked on doubly because of the new program. He also said officials should ensure that information reaches residents in languages they can understand, noting that what one culture thinks looks bad might be considered beautiful by another.

Coss said vehicles parked with flat tires and clearly not operable, or with expired tags or no tags on private property, will be addressed by the new officers. The Police Department will continue to handle vehicles within the right of way or on the streets. Coss said a very big focus for the officers is going out and speaking with residents and business owners and educating the public. The program includes quarterly reporting requirements, and the board will decide on an annual basis whether to renew it.
hero.article_text: FORT PIERCE – The members of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency here voted unanimously Aug. 11 to approve an interlocal funding agreement with the city for the cost of a yearlong pilot program employing two new code-enforcement officers to work solely in the community redevelopment areas of Fort Pierce. Community and Economic Development Director Shyanne Harnage introduced the resolution to the Board that evening, whose members are made up of city commissioners wearing different hats. “We have outlined this pilot program to provide enhanced code-enforcement services within the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency boundaries only,” she said. “These will go above and beyond the baseline code enforcement services that are currently offered through the City of Fort Pierce. If you read through the redevelopment plan, you’ll see multiple goals that talk about elimination of slum and blight, vehicles, litter [and] illegal dumping. We think this is a very creative way to eliminate those issues, be more proactive and have relationships with our residents that maybe our code-enforcement officers don’t have the time to do.” Harnage then provided clarification on the pilot program oversight. “There are quarterly reporting requirements,” she continued. “They would come to you all and discuss how it’s going [and] what’s happening. Then on an annual basis, we’ll decide if we want to renew this program. I will say that other CRAs are implementing similar programs, and they have been very successful. I don’t think this should be looked at negatively in terms of double enforcement for the residents who live in the CRA, but more so of additional beautification and how we can work together and engage.” Community Response Director Shaun Coss also provided his input on the program, whose first year will cost up to $183,200. “Shyanne hit the nail on the head,” he said. “We’re definitely looking at very focused, supplemental enforcement [of] non-operable vehicles, illegal dumping, the trash and litter. There will be daily sign sweeps on the main corridors within the FPRA boundaries and we’ll potentially deal with the noise complaints once we revise the noise ordinance. These are issues the typical code-enforcement officers are not going to be addressing. This is all proactive in nature and supplemental to what code enforcement typically does.” Mayor Linda Hudson immediately expressed her satisfaction with the parameters of the new code-enforcement service. “So, this is not necessarily complaint driven, but it is going to be aggressive and people are going to be looking out,” she said. “I think we need eyes on our streets and our properties and identifying it rather than somebody having to call it in. I am pleased about that.” Commissioner Arnold Gaines, however, expressed concerns about potential misunderstandings by CRA residents directly impacted by the work of the two new code-enforcement officers. “Let’s be very clear that we get the word out that certain neighborhoods are not getting picked on doubly because of this new program,” he said. “If we’re going to look for cars, you need to let people understand what they can and can’t do. If you have a car that might have a flat tire, but the car is registered, has insurance and is parked on their property, a homeowner’s saying, why are you messing with me when my car has a tag on it? Another thing is to make sure with the different cultures that we get the right information out with the language they can understand. Because what somebody things looks bad to us, their culture might think think is beautiful. Let’s be proactive and get the word out instead of getting all these emails after you guys start.” Commissioner Curtis Johnson Jr. agreed, hoping the new officers will solve the issue of illegal signs in the city’s rights of way. “I think we should do a campaign to let people know who they are and what their assignments will be,” he said of the new officers. “I think it’s a really good program and I’m really interested to get the community to understand we’ve got to change the behaviors here to clean our city up. One of the things I want to talk to you about is trash cans. That’s becoming a problem because they’re in the street now, and people are hitting them causing damage not only to their cars but to the cans.” Mayor Hudson posed a final clarification question related to the renewed enforcement of non-operable vehicle in the community redevelopment areas. “So, you’re talking about on private property if somebody leaves a vehicle and it’s parked there forever and it doesn’t move and grass grows around it,” she asked. “Is that the kind of code enforcement you’re talking about in terms of the vehicles?” Coss tackled that inquiry. “Vehicles parked there with flat tires and clearly not operable, have expired tags or no tags on private property. The Police Department will continue to handle vehicles within the right of way or on the streets. The key component to this campaign is public education. A very big focus for these officers is going out and speaking with the residents and business owners and educating the public.” The FPRA Board then voted unanimously for approval. cards.headline: Flock license plate cameras aid search for Vero Beach homicide person of interest
cards.teaser: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is using a network of automated license plate cameras to search for Matthew Waggle, a person of interest in a Sunday homicide outside Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers took reporters inside the agency's Real Time Crime Center on Monday, where analysts are using Flock license plate cameras to search for 33-year-old Matthew Waggle. Waggle has not been charged but was identified as a person of interest after a 52-year-old woman was found shot near her home Sunday morning in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach. Flowers said investigators believe the woman had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the killing as a domestic violence homicide.

Flock's automated license plate readers capture information about vehicles as they pass, including license plates, locations and timestamps. Indian River County operates 140 license plate readers. Flowers pointed to a deadly hit-and-run investigated by the Florida Highway Patrol last week as one recent example where analysts used Flock data to help build a case that otherwise had no leads.

Flowers defended the county's use of the cameras against growing national privacy concerns. He said law enforcement should be able to use available technology to protect the public. A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle, who investigators say should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.
cards.article_text: A network of license plate cameras facing growing privacy scrutiny across the country is now part of the search for a person of interest in a Vero Beach-area homicide. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers took CBS12 News Reporter Katie Bente inside the agency's Real Time Crime Center on Monday, where analysts are using Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for 33-year-old Matthew Waggle. Waggle has not been charged in the killing. Deputies identified him as a person of interest after a 52-year-old woman was found shot near her home Sunday morning in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach. Deputies performed lifesaving measures before the woman was taken to a trauma center, where she later died. Flowers said investigators believe the woman had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the killing as a domestic violence homicide. "One of the first places that we go, Real Time Crime Center gets activated," Flowers said. "They're looking at all the Flock cameras. They're looking at the traffic in the area." How Flock plays a role Flock's automated license plate readers capture information about vehicles as they pass, including license plates, locations and timestamps. That allows investigators to search for vehicles connected to crimes and potentially piece together where they traveled. Indian River County has previously said it operates 140 license plate readers. Flowers pointed to a deadly hit-and-run investigated by the Florida Highway Patrol last week as one recent example. He said analysts in the Real Time Crime Center used Flock data to help build a case that otherwise had no leads. He said the technology can also work in reverse helping investigators eliminate someone as a suspect. "If we're able to show that that person's vehicle was nowhere near the homicide," Flowers said, "that's a great way for us to show that somebody is innocent as well." A crime-fighting tool and a privacy fight The ability to reconstruct where vehicles have traveled is also at the heart of a growing national debate over Flock. Privacy and civil liberties advocates have questioned how extensively law enforcement should be able to track drivers, how information is shared between agencies and what safeguards exist to prevent misuse. More than 50 jurisdictions have reportedly ended relationships with Flock. The company announced new safeguards last week, including plans to reduce its recommended default data retention period from 30 days to seven days and require searches to be connected to case numbers. Flowers strongly defended Indian River County's use of the cameras. "You're on camera every time you go to Walmart. You're on camera every time you go to Walgreens," Flowers said. "Everywhere you go, your bank transactions are being tracked." Flowers said law enforcement should be able to use available technology to protect the public. "Don't you want your law enforcement protecting your community and making it safer by leveraging technology?" he said. Flowers said Indian River County has largely avoided the public backlash seen elsewhere because the Sheriff's Office explained its use of the technology early and, he argues, residents have seen results. He pointed to auto burglaries as an example, saying the county recorded more than 800 in 2015 compared with roughly 250 last year. Flowers attributed at least part of that decline to the camera network and proactive policing. Now, the technology is being used in an active homicide investigation. See also: 12 pounds of meth, 12,000 rounds,12 guns, and fentanyl found in Boynton Beach SWAT raid Flowers said investigators spent Monday speaking with the victim's coworkers and examining her relationship with Waggle as they work to determine what led to the shooting. "It really looks like she was trying to break up with him," Flowers said. He wasn't ready for it to be over." A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle. Investigators have said he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County population jumps 22% since 2020, adding more than 73,000 residents
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County's population reached 402,449 as of July 1, 2025, up from 329,226 in 2020, according to new Census estimates. Port St. Lucie now accounts for roughly two-thirds of the county's population.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County's population reached 402,449 as of July 1, 2025, up from 329,226 in 2020, according to Census Bureau estimates. That's an increase of more than 73,000 residents, or 22.2%, in just over five years. For comparison, neighboring Palm Beach County grew from 1,492,191 residents in 2020 to an estimated 1,575,726 in 2025, an increase of about 5.6%. St. Lucie County has grown at roughly four times the rate of Palm Beach County since 2020.

Much of St. Lucie County's population is concentrated in Port St. Lucie. The Census Bureau estimates 268,062 people now live in Port St. Lucie, meaning the city accounts for roughly two-thirds of the county's entire population. Port St. Lucie has also grown faster than the county overall. The city's population is up nearly 31% from its 2020 estimates base of 204,826.

Jason Coley with Atlantic Shores Realty, Expertise ERA Powered, said affordability remains one of the biggest factors he sees among his clients. According to Coley, a buyer spending between $400,000 and $500,000 in St. Lucie County can find a four-bedroom, two-bathroom home with a two-car garage on a quarter-acre lot. He estimated a comparable newer home in Palm Beach County could cost between $600,000 and $800,000. Coley said some of his clients are willing to make a longer commute, while others are able to work remotely.

That's an increase of more than 73,000 residents, or 22.2%, in just over five years. For comparison, neighboring Palm Beach County grew from 1,492,191 residents in 2020 to an estimated 1,575,726 in 2025 an increase of about 5.6%. Lucie County has grown at roughly four times the rate of Palm Beach County since 2020. Lucie County started the decade with less than one-quarter of Palm Beach County's population, but has added nearly as many residents. RELATED: Census data shows St. Lucie surging while Palm Beach growth nearly stops Much of St. Lucie County's population is concentrated in Port St. The Census Bureau estimates 268,062 people now live in Port St. Lucie, meaning the city accounts for roughly two-thirds of the county's entire population. Lucie has also grown faster than the county overall. The city's population is up nearly 31% from its 2020 estimates base of 204,826. So what's drawing people there? Jason Coley with Atlantic Shores Realty, Expertise ERA Powered, said affordability remains one of the biggest factors he sees among his clients. "It's been picking up big time," Coley said. "People are moving here because we have a heck of a deal with the bang for your buck. You can get a really nice house." Coley works throughout the Treasure Coast and into Palm Beach County, but said about 60% of his business is in St. He said his clients moving into the area are coming from both outside Florida and communities farther south in South Florida. "A lot of them are coming from down south," Coley said. "They're coming from Broward, Palm Beach. They can just get much more of a home up in our area than they can down south." Coley said his own clients are roughly split between people relocating from out of state and those coming from other parts of Florida. He said he also sees buyers coming from Miami-Dade County. For some South Florida buyers, he believes the decision to continue north into St. Lucie County instead of buying in Palm Beach County comes down largely to price. "I just strictly think it is pricing," Coley said. "When they look at what they're going to be able to get and what they can afford, it just makes it that much harder for them to really have the family dream of what they want." According to Coley, a buyer spending between $400,000 and $500,000 in St. Lucie County can find a four-bedroom, two-bathroom home with a two-car garage on a quarter-acre lot. See also: Florida left lane law: Deputies crack down on slow drivers lingering in the fast lane He estimated a comparable newer home in Palm Beach County could cost between $600,000 and $800,000, though prices vary significantly by neighborhood, property and market conditions. Coley said he sees a range of people making the move, from retirees to young couples and families looking for more space. For some buyers, living farther north also means a longer commute. Coley said some of his clients are willing to make that tradeoff, while others are able to work remotely. "A lot of people are working from home nowadays when we talk to people," Coley said. "They're either working remote or willing to make that drive just to have a nicer house." New construction helping attract buyers New construction is another part of Port St. Communities in and around Tradition continue to add homes as builders compete for buyers. Coley said some builders are offering incentives such as closing-cost assistance and temporary or permanent mortgage-rate buydowns, which can make new construction more attractive to buyers facing higher borrowing costs. "They're giving them cash to close, which is like covering their closing costs," Coley said. "And they're also buying down their interest rates." The exact incentives and mortgage rates vary by builder, development, buyer and loan. Coley also believes Port St. Lucie's expanding selection of restaurants, entertainment and other amenities is helping make the city more attractive to families. "I think it's just drawn people in because it's newer," Coley said. Another report highlights Port St. Lucie's growth The Census numbers are not the only recent data highlighting Port St. A private analysis from workplace technology company Blink recently ranked Port St. cities in an index examining population growth and indicators of small-business activity. The analysis considered population growth along with retail, food and hospitality business density, workforce growth, online search activity and walkability. The report cited Census data showing Port St. Lucie added 11,880 residents between 2023 and 2024. The Blink ranking should not be confused with an official Census ranking of America's fastest-growing cities. It is a private analysis that combines population growth with several economic and business-related factors. The newer Census estimates now put Port St. Lucie's population above 268,000. See also: West Palm Beach man arrested after police say he faked coma to cover up $190K embezzlement With more people arriving, the question becomes whether St. Lucie County can maintain its affordability advantage as demand increases. Coley said he does not expect interest in the area to disappear anytime soon. "My crystal ball is broken, so I can't tell you for sure if it'll last," Coley said. "But I will say that people have to live somewhere." When asked whether he sees Port St. Lucie's growth stopping soon, his answer was simple. "I don't see it anytime soon."

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man arrested on attempted murder charge after firing through bathroom door during domestic dispute
cards.body:
A 23-year-old Fort Pierce man was arrested Sunday after he fired a gun through a bathroom door during a domestic disturbance at a home on the 1700 block of Wyoming Avenue and fled before being captured hours later, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said. Deputies responded to the residence at around 11:30 a.m. Sunday for a reported domestic disturbance. During the incident, the victim locked herself inside a bathroom. Nathan Hsu allegedly fired a round through the bathroom door before fleeing the residence in a car.

Fort Pierce police later located the car near Porpoise Beach, prompting an extensive search of the area. While the search was underway, detectives with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators executed a search warrant at the residence on Wyoming Avenue.

At around 2:30 p.m., Hsu's family located him and alerted a passing Fort Pierce police officer. Hsu was taken into custody without incident and a firearm was recovered.

Hsu is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on no bond. He faces multiple felony charges, including attempted felony murder, kidnapping, tampering with a witness, simple battery and grand theft of a motor vehicle. Authorities said the incident was isolated and there is no ongoing threat to the public. The investigation remains active.

cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin is fighting to hold on to her office as she faces two challengers, Steve Giordano and Eric Strazzeri, who have criticized her leadership over the city's handling of garbage collection issues. Dating back to the pandemic, trash has been a serious issue in the city and many residents say it's why the mayor's race is in the balance.

The city told residents they would be getting a tax credit, not a refund check in the mail, after the city won $24 million from a lawsuit against WastePro for years of shoddy service. Sometime later, the cost of trash collection went up. The question of how many times a week trash should be collected will be a ballot issue in November.

The mayor's race has also been overshadowed in recent days by a dispute over campaign signs that has led to a state investigation. Port St. Lucie police officers, including Mayor Shannon Martin's husband, Lt. Aaron Martin, were placed on paid administrative leave as the Florida Department of Law Enforcement took over a criminal investigation into two campaign-sign incidents involving mayoral challenger Steve Giordano. If there's a clear majority winner this week, the race will be decided, but if it's close, two finalists will advance to the General Election in November.

The department wrote in a Facebook post that protecting the community can sometimes include its smallest residents. hero.headline: Florida couple with full insurance and FEMA aid still unable to rebuild two years after 2024 hurricanes
hero.body:
A Florida couple who carried both flood and homeowners insurance before the 2024 hurricane season received payments from their insurer and FEMA but remain on an empty lot nearly two years later, unable to rebuild. Jen and RJ Garbowicz lost their home to flooding during Hurricane Helene in 2024, then sustained roof damage 13 days later during Hurricane Milton. The couple paid between $18,000 and $20,000 annually for both types of insurance.

The Garbowicz couple's flood insurance through FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program paid out the maximum of $250,000. Their mortgage holder is holding $200,000 of that payout, leaving the couple only $50,000 to rebuild. FEMA required the couple to rebuild under the 50% rule. After appealing four times by submitting the same documentation repeatedly, they received approval for a $33,000 FEMA disaster grant. The couple qualified for an SBA disaster loan but were told they must first cover the difference between insurance payments received and the total cost of rebuilding with their own cash. They also must repay the $33,000 FEMA grant before receiving the SBA loan.

Florida Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie, who served on the President's FEMA Review Council, told an insurance workshop in June that the average FEMA payout is $4,500. Guthrie urged insurance companies to ensure policyholders understand that FEMA will not make homeowners whole. The Garbowicz couple traveled to Washington, D.C., with the Extreme Weather Survivors group to advocate for the FEMA Act, a House proposal that would reform the agency. The bill would make FEMA an independent agency by removing it from the Department of Homeland Security, create a universal application process for disaster recovery, process FEMA grants faster by providing money to homeowners before recovery rather than as reimbursement, and facilitate investment in mitigation efforts and damage prevention before storms hit.

The couple estimates they have another 18 to 24 months of rebuilding ahead. RJ Garbowicz said the proposed reforms would have helped them rebuild sooner. Jennifer Garbowicz said getting their story out through interviews and putting pressure on lawmakers is what it will take to drive change. The couple remains in legal discussions with their homeowners insurance company over one claim.

So you have to cover the gap with your own cash," RJ said.And then the couple said that before they could receive an SBA disaster loan they had qualified for, they now had to repay that $33,000 grant to FEMA."It's really unfortunate that we did all the right things. We took all the right steps. We had insurance, we did everything as homeowners that we were supposed to do, and at the end of the day when we were counting on it, it didn't work like we thought that it would," Jennifer said.AVERAGE FEMA PAYOUTIn June, the Scripps News Group's Nadeen Yanes traveled to an insurance workshop where Florida Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie spoke as a guest. Guthrie also served on the President's FEMA Review Council. He nearly urged insurance companies to make sure policyholders understand that FEMA will not make homeowners whole."Let's just be very, very candid. The average person is going to get a $4,500 payout from this, from FEMA," Guthrie said.FIGHTING FOR FEMA REFORMThe Garbowicz traveled to Washington, D.C., as part of the Extreme Weather Survivors group to push for both FEMA and insurance reform."Everyone here today knows that disasters don't end when the news coverage does," a speaker at the event said."The important thing for us was just to get the conversation going, get the message out there," RJ said.The couple met with lawmakers to advocate for the FEMA Act, a House proposal that would completely reform the agency. Key provisions of the bill include:Makes FEMA and independent agency by removing FEMA from under the Department of Homeland SecurityCreating a universal application process for disaster recoveryProcessing FEMA grants faster, providing money to homeowners before recovery rather than as reimbursementFacilitates investment, mitigation efforts, and damage prevention before a storm hitsRELATED STORY | The hidden risk in your insurance policy: Why state minimums may not save you'WE NEED LONG-TERM SOLUTIONS'"Long-term disaster recovery, as you can see, doesn't end a day, a week, a month, or even in this case a year after the storm. It's many, many years of recovery, and we need long-term solutions," said one of the speakers at the Extreme Weather Survivors group in DC.The couple says those reforms would have helped them rebuild sooner, instead of still standing on an empty lot nearly two years after the storms. They estimate they have another 18 to 24 months of rebuilding ahead."It's been a long time coming, two years, and we probably still have another 18 to 24 months still left," RJ said."The important thing for us was just to get the conversation going, get the message out there," Jennifer added. "Just tell our story as much as possible because I think that's what it's going to take. It's going to take interviews like this, getting out there and really putting pressure."This story was originally published by Nadeen Yanes with the Scripps News Group in Tampa.

He said he ultimately had no choice but to stop trying to save the home. 'So I called it quits. I can't keep up,' he said. hero.headline: Fort Pierce man arrested after firing bullet through bathroom door during domestic disturbance
hero.body:
A 23-year-old Fort Pierce man faces attempted felony murder and kidnapping charges after firing a gun through a bathroom door during a domestic disturbance Sunday morning and fleeing before being captured hours later near Porpoise Beach on Hutchinson Island. Hsu was arrested Sunday and is also charged with tampering with a witness, simple battery, and grand theft of a motor vehicle.

St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to a home on the 1700 block of Wyoming Avenue at around 11:30 a.m. Sunday for a reported domestic disturbance. During the incident, the victim locked herself inside a bathroom. Hsu allegedly fired a round through the bathroom door before fleeing the residence in a car.

Fort Pierce Police Department officers later located the car near Porpoise Beach, prompting an extensive search of the area by both agencies. While the search was underway, detectives with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators executed a search warrant at the residence.

At around 2:30 p.m., Hsu's family located him and alerted a passing Fort Pierce police officer. Hsu was taken into custody without incident and a firearm was recovered. Hsu is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on no bond. Authorities said the incident was isolated and there is no ongoing threat to the public.

hero.headline: Woman shot to death in Vero Beach roadway; sheriff's office searches for Sebastian man
hero.body:
A 52-year-old woman died after being shot Sunday morning in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach, and the Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching for 33-year-old Matthew Allen Waggle of Sebastian as a person of interest in what investigators are treating as a domestic violence homicide. Deputies responded at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday after receiving a 911 call reporting a woman in the roadway. Deputies located the woman with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said investigators believe Waggle and the victim were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home. Flowers said the sheriff's office has put out a nationwide BOLO for Waggle and warned he should be considered armed and dangerous. Flowers said investigators believe Waggle has left the Vero Beach area and are using resources such as flock cameras to investigate his whereabouts.

Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home. His brother heard the shot and went inside to check on his sister. Cardenas said the neighborhood is typically quiet and he hopes an arrest comes soon.

Flowers said the sheriff's office has a domestic violence investigator working alongside homicide detectives. He called the incident a tragedy and said detectives have been working on the case all day. Authorities are warning anyone who sees Waggle not to approach him and to call 911. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org, or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: 36 dogs rescued from Palm City home prompt call for tougher animal cruelty laws
hero.teaser: Thirty-six dogs were rescued from a Palm City residence where animals lived in filth covered in matted fur and feces. State lawmakers and Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek toured the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast facility and pledged to push for stronger animal protection laws.
hero.body:
Thirty-six dogs were rescued from a Palm City home where animals lived in filth covered in matted fur and their own feces. The dogs were taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which is treating the animals for severe neglect. Staff members said they are removing an average of six pounds of matted fur per dog, with some mats containing four-inch shards of glass and metal. The shelter has groomed 20 of the 36 dogs so far and is using all available space to house and treat the animals.

State Representatives Meg Weinberger and John Snyder, State Senator Gayle Harrell, and Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek visited the facility to see the condition of the rescued dogs. The officials agreed current laws are insufficient to prevent such cases. Weinberger said the case was horrific because no one could access the property to check on the dogs.

Sheriff Budensiek said the owner had been a breeder years ago and called for stricter regulations on breeders. Snyder said lawmakers need to work in the upcoming legislative session to ensure such cases do not happen again. Harrell said the state needs to empower sheriffs to take necessary steps to protect animals. The humane society is working around the clock to provide medical care and grooming for the traumatized animals, which are slowly beginning to recover.
hero.article_text: Thirty-six dogs are now safe and beginning a long road to recovery after being rescued from what officials are calling a "house of horror" in Palm City. The animals were discovered living in filth, covered in matted fur and their own feces. The horrific discovery has prompted state lawmakers and the Martin County Sheriff's Office to call for new laws to prevent this from happening again.The dogs were rushed to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which is now dealing with its second massive hoarding case in the last month.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Staff at the humane society are working around the clock to provide medical care and grooming for the traumatized animals. According to officials, the condition of the dogs was shocking."We're averaging about six pounds of mat per dog," one staff member said.Crews performing emergency grooming have found 4-inch shards of glass and metal hidden in the dense, matted fur. The shelter is using every available space to house and treat the animals, with 20 of the 36 dogs having been groomed so far.The severity of the situation drew a swift response from local leaders. State Representatives Meg Weinberger and John Snyder, State Senator Gayle Harrell, and Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek toured the facility to see the dogs' condition firsthand."It's time to really roll up our sleeves, get up to Tallahassee this session, and to try and make sure we're doing everything we can to make sure this never happens again," Rep. Snyder said."We need to work with our sheriffs in particular to really gain that experience as to what they are seeing out there," said Senator Harrell. "We need to empower our sheriffs to be able to take the steps that they are that they need to take from our conversations today. We need to empower them to do what's necessary to protect the animals."Rep. Weinberger added, "Sadly, I've seen cases like this, but this was really bad... the fact that nobody could get in to check on these dogs, it was horrific."The officials agreed that current laws are not enough. Sheriff Budensiek said the owner of the dogs had been a breeder years ago and called for more stringent regulations."We need some teeth in the breeder law where we can inspect them," Sheriff Budensiek stated. "And then, oh, by the way, after the fact, we're still going to come back and inspect to make sure you're following the parameters that we put forward."Despite the monstrous ordeal, some of the dogs are already showing signs of recovery. They are slowly learning what it is like to experience love, clean food, and water.For these 36 dogs, the journey is just beginning, but for the first time, they are safe.

hero.headline: Melbourne man, 82, dies after single-vehicle crash on I-95 in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
An 82-year-old Melbourne man died Friday afternoon after a single-vehicle crash on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. The driver was pronounced dead at the scene after his 2002 Jeep Wrangler left the roadway and struck a tree in the median.

The crash was reported at 3:14 p.m. on August 14 on northbound Interstate 95 south of Gatlin Boulevard. According to investigators, the driver was traveling north in the inside lane when his Jeep Wrangler traveled off the roadway to the left and onto the paved left shoulder.

The vehicle continued in a northwest direction into the grass median, where the front end struck a tree. The Jeep came to rest in the median, facing west.

The driver was entrapped and sustained serious injuries. Investigators are still working to determine why the vehicle left the roadway. The crash remains under investigation.

The vehicle continued in a northwest direction into the grass median, where the front end struck a tree. The Jeep came to rest in the median, facing west. hero.headline: Vero Beach Art Club hosts summer camp for 91 young artists
hero.body:
The Vero Beach Art Club held its annual Summer Art Camp over 10 weeks, serving 91 students from the Vero Beach area and a few children visiting grandparents. The program taught children how to draw, mix colors, and create projects using paper, glue and other art materials while learning to work cooperatively, listen to instructions and express themselves through art.

hero.headline: Woman found shot in Vero Beach roadway dies; homicide investigation underway
hero.body:
A woman found with a gunshot wound in a Vero Beach roadway Sunday morning died at a hospital, and the Indian River County Sheriff's Office is investigating her death as a homicide. Indian River County Sheriff's Office 911 dispatch received a call at 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman was in the roadway in the 500 block of First Street in Vero Beach. Responding deputies located the woman with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. The woman was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead.

Detectives and crime scene personnel are processing the scene. A person of interest has been identified and detectives are actively searching for him. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office did not release the identities of the victim or the person of interest.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact the Indian River County Sheriff's Office or to remain anonymous, contact the Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers. The sheriff's office asks anyone who has seen the person of interest or knows his whereabouts to not approach him.

cards.headline: Martin County corrections deputy Mark Budensiek dies from cancer
cards.teaser: Deputy Mark Budensiek, cousin of Martin County Sheriff John M. Budensiek, died Saturday after battling cancer. He served as a corrections officer for 15 years.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office Deputy Mark Budensiek, the cousin of Sheriff John M. Budensiek, died Saturday after a courageous battle with cancer, the agency said. Mark Budensiek, 42, was hired under Sheriff Robert Crowder in the Corrections Department in 2011.

He leaves behind his wife and 14-year-old daughter who were the center of his life, MCSO posted. The sheriff's office said his dedication, sacrifice and service to the community will never be forgotten.

Sheriff John M. Budensiek was sworn into office on Jan. 7, 2025, and has been employed by the agency since 1997.

cards.headline: Palm City woman jailed after 36 Border Collies rescued from home on Southwest Alligator Street
cards.teaser: Paige Anne ODonnell, 62, was arrested after deputies and Animal Services found 36 Border Collies living in deplorable conditions at her home in the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street.
cards.body:
Paige Anne ODonnell, 62, of the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City, was arrested on Aug. 10 after Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Animal Services Unit employees confiscated 36 dogs from what Sheriff John Budensiek said were deplorable conditions. ODonnell remains in the Martin County Jail on a $275,000 bond.

ODonnell faces 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air. A judge ordered that ODonnell may not own or possess, either temporarily or permanently, any animals as a condition of the bond.

The conditions inside the home near Southwest Mapp Road and south of Southwest Martin Highway were so deplorable that deputies and Animal Services officers had to wear Tyvek protective clothing. Feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris throughout the residence made the process of locating and safely removing the animals extremely challenging. All the animals were turned over to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City.

MARTIN COUNTY – The owner of 36 Border Collies rescued on Aug. 10 from her Palm City home remains in the Martin County Jail on a $275,000 bond, as of Aug. 12, according to the jail web site. Paige Anne O’Donnell, 62, of the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City, was arrested on Aug. 10 after Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies and Animal Services Unit employees confiscated the 36 dogs from what Sheriff John Budensiek said were living in “deplorable conditions.” O’Donnell faces 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death; and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air. During her first appearance in court on Aug. 11, a judge set the bail and ordered that O’Donnell may not own or possess, either temporarily or permanently, any animals as a condition of the bond, the sheriff’s office wrote in a Facebook posting. All the animals were turned over to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City where they are being evaluated, cleaned, treated and care for, the sheriff’s office noted in its Facebook posting. The home is near Southwest Mapp Road and south of Southwest Martin Highway. “From the outside, the home appeared well-maintained, neatly groomed and fenced off. Inside was a much different story,” the sheriff’s office wrote in the Facebook posting. “The conditions were so deplorable that deputies and Animal Services officers had to wear Tyvek protective clothing while working inside the home. Feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris throughout the residence made the process of locating and safely removing the animals extremely challenging.” Throughout the investigation, which actually began in 2020, O’Donnell claimed she had no more than five dogs inside the home, the Sheriff’s Office noted. However, once the sheriff’s office was able to obtain a search warrant, officers discovered the 36 Border Collies inside the house “under conditions that failed to provide a sanitary and appropriate living environment and restricted their ability to obtain appropriate exercise and adequate environmental conditions,” according to an arrest affidavit. In addition, an “inoperable air-conditioning system demonstrated that the animals had been maintained in conditions that subjected them to unnecessary suffering,” according to the arrest affidavit. The Humane Society is asking for the public’s help by donating what it can towards the care of the 36 dogs. To donate, go to hstc1.org/Donate . Your comment has been submitted. hero.headline: St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant Unit 1 manually shut down after control rods drop into reactor core
hero.body:
St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant Unit 1 was manually shut down Wednesday morning after three control rods dropped into the reactor core, according to a notification filed with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The manual reactor trip occurred at 9:47 a.m. on August 13, 2026, while Unit 1 was operating at 100 percent power. The NRC classified the event as a non-emergency.

The trip was uncomplicated with all systems responding normally after the shutdown, according to the licensee. Operations stabilized the plant in Mode 3, known as Hot Standby. Decay heat is being removed by discharging steam to the main condenser using the turbine bypass valves and main feedwater.

Unit 2 at the Saint Lucie facility was not affected by the incident. According to the NRC website, Unit 1 remains shut down.

The licensee reported that at the time of the manual trip, the reactor was in Mode 1 at 100 percent power. All systems responded normally following the shutdown procedure, and operations successfully stabilized the plant.

hero.headline: Palm City woman jailed on $275,000 bond after 36 dogs rescued from Southwest Alligator Street home
hero.body:
Paige Anne ODonnell, 62, remains in the Martin County Jail on a $275,000 bond after Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Animal Services Unit employees rescued 36 Border Collies from her home in the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City on August 10. ODonnell faces 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air.

The home near Southwest Mapp Road and south of Southwest Martin Highway appeared well-maintained from the outside, but inside deputies discovered deplorable conditions. Feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris throughout the residence made locating and safely removing the animals extremely challenging. Deputies and Animal Services officers had to wear Tyvek protective clothing while working inside the home. An inoperable air-conditioning system demonstrated that the animals had been maintained in conditions that subjected them to unnecessary suffering, according to an arrest affidavit.

During her first appearance in court on August 11, a judge set the bail and ordered that ODonnell may not own or possess any animals as a condition of the bond. Throughout the investigation, which began in 2020, ODonnell claimed she had no more than five dogs inside the home. Once the sheriff's office obtained a search warrant, officers discovered the 36 Border Collies inside the house under conditions that failed to provide a sanitary and appropriate living environment and restricted their ability to obtain appropriate exercise and adequate environmental conditions.

All 36 animals were turned over to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City where they are being evaluated, cleaned, treated and cared for. Sheriff John Budensiek said the dogs were living in deplorable conditions. The Humane Society is asking for the public's help by donating towards the care of the 36 dogs.

hero.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office deputy dies from cancer at 42
hero.teaser: Deputy Mark Budensiek, cousin of Sheriff John M. Budensiek, died Saturday after a battle with cancer.
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office Deputy Mark Budensiek died Saturday after a battle with cancer. He was 42 years old and the cousin of Sheriff John M. Budensiek.

Mark Budensiek was hired under Sheriff Robert Crowder in the Corrections Department in 2011 and served as a corrections officer for 15 years. He leaves behind his wife and 14-year-old daughter who were the center of his life, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

The agency posted on Facebook that their hearts are with Mark's family, friends, fellow deputies and all those who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him. The agency said his dedication, sacrifice and service to the community will never be forgotten.

cards.headline: Melbourne man, 82, dies after Jeep strikes tree in median of Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: The single-vehicle crash happened Friday afternoon on northbound Interstate 95 south of Gatlin Boulevard.
cards.body:
An 82-year-old Melbourne man died Friday afternoon after his vehicle left northbound Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County and struck a tree in the median. The crash was reported at 3:14 p.m. on August 14 on northbound Interstate 95 south of Gatlin Boulevard. The driver was traveling north in the inside lane when, for reasons still under investigation, his 2002 Jeep Wrangler traveled off the roadway to the left and onto the paved left shoulder.

The vehicle continued in a northwest direction into the grass median, where the front end struck a tree. The Jeep came to rest in the median, facing west. The driver was entrapped and sustained serious injuries. He was later pronounced dead on scene by a St. Lucie County paramedic. The crash remains under investigation.
